121468.e: Research, preclinical tests, three phases of clinical trials and the approval review take a lot of time. Usually 10 to 15 years pass.
121468.m: A new medicine usually takes 10 to 15 years to be approved.

121469.q: What do chemists do once they have found a substance with the desired effect?
a: They change it on purpose to improve its effect and tolerability
They sell it in pharmacies straight away
They have Swissmedic approve it directly
They test it only on plants from then on
121469.e: Such a starting substance is called a lead compound. Small chemical changes turn it into a candidate that is more effective, more stable and better tolerated.
121469.m: Optimising a lead compound produces a drug candidate.

121470.q: Which method is used in pharmaceutical research to test hundreds of thousands of substances for an effect automatically?
121470.e: In high-throughput screening, robots test large libraries of substances against a biological target. Hits are then examined more closely.
121470.m: High-throughput screening quickly finds active substances in huge libraries.

121471.q: What is the biological molecule, usually a protein, that a medicine is meant to act on called?
121471.e: The target is, for example, a receptor or an enzyme involved in a disease. Identifying the target is the first step in many development projects.
121471.m: A medicine is developed specifically for a biological target.

121472.q: As a rule, how long does a patent for a new active ingredient last from the date of filing?
121472.e: Patents usually protect an invention for 20 years from the filing date. Because development takes a long time, often only part of this is left for sales after approval.
121472.m: A patent generally protects an invention for 20 years.

121473.q: What are medicines for rare diseases called that receive special support during approval?
121473.e: Orphan drugs (medicines for rare diseases) are not very attractive commercially because only a few people are affected. That is why authorities, including Swissmedic, make things easier for them.
121473.m: Orphan drugs are medicines for rare diseases.

121474.q: Which well-known antibiotic did Alexander Fleming discover by chance in 1928?
121474.e: Fleming noticed that a mould on a bacterial culture was stopping the bacteria from growing. Mass production only succeeded in the 1940s.
121474.m: Penicillin was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.

121475.q: Roughly what proportion of drug candidates that enter clinical trials reach approval?
121475.e: Many candidates fail because they do not work well enough or have side effects. Depending on the study and disease area, only about one in ten candidates from phase I reaches the market.
121475.m: Most drug candidates fail in clinical trials.

121476.q: What is mainly studied in preclinical research before an active ingredient is tested on humans for the first time?
a: Effect and toxicity in cell cultures and animal experiments
121476.e: Preclinical studies provide data on the mechanism of action, pharmacology and toxicology. Only if these results are convincing may a clinical trial be applied for.
121476.m: Preclinical research checks effect and safety before the first use in humans.

121477.q: What do the three Rs of the 3R principle for animal experiments stand for?
121477.e: The 3R principle of Russell and Burch (1959) calls for replacing animal experiments, reducing the number of animals and lessening their suffering. Switzerland promotes it through the Swiss 3R Competence Centre.
121477.m: The 3R principle aims to replace, reduce and refine animal experiments.

a: Testing in a test tube or in cell cultures
121478.e: In vitro literally means “in glass”. In vivo, by contrast, means experiments on a living organism, and in silico means computer simulations.
121478.m: In vitro means in the test tube.

121479.q: What is checked with a mutagenicity test for a new active ingredient?
a: Whether it can damage genetic material
How expensive it is to make
121479.e: Mutagenic substances change DNA and can cause cancer. A standard test for this is the Ames test with bacteria.
121479.m: Mutagenicity tests look for substances that damage genetic material.

121480.q: Which drug disaster around 1961 led to much stricter testing rules for medicines?
a: Contergan with the active ingredient thalidomide
121480.e: Thalidomide was sold as a sleeping pill and caused severe malformations in children whose mothers had taken it during pregnancy. After that, tests for harm to unborn babies became compulsory.
121480.m: The thalidomide scandal led to stricter testing of medicines.

121481.q: How did Swiss voters decide in February 2022 on the initiative to ban animal and human experiments?
121481.e: On 13 February 2022, the initiative was rejected by about 79 per cent of voters and by all cantons. Animal experiments remain allowed in Switzerland under strict licensing conditions.
121481.m: A ban on animal experiments was clearly rejected in 2022.

121482.q: Which quality standard regulates how preclinical safety studies must be planned, carried out and documented?
121482.e: GLP (Good Laboratory Practice) ensures that study data are traceable and reliable. Authorities only accept safety studies if they follow GLP.
121482.m: Preclinical safety studies follow Good Laboratory Practice.

a: A microsystem with human cells that copies organ functions
A computer chip for hospital bills
121483.e: Cells are arranged on a few centimetres so that they imitate, for example, a lung or a liver. Such models can partly replace animal experiments.
121483.m: Organ-on-a-chip models copy organs in miniature.

121484.q: Who typically takes part in a phase I trial of a new medicine?
a: A small group of mostly healthy volunteers
121484.e: Phase I mainly tests safety, tolerability and how the active ingredient behaves in the body. With very toxic substances, for example in cancer medicine, patients take part too.
121484.m: In phase I, an active ingredient is tested on a few people for the first time.

121485.q: What is the main aim of a phase II trial?
a: To show first signs of effectiveness in patients and find the dose
To record long-term side effects after approval
To test the medicine in animals
121485.e: In phase II, a few hundred patients receive the active ingredient. It is checked whether it works and which dose is best.
121485.m: Phase II clarifies effectiveness and the right dose.

121486.q: What characterises a phase III trial?
a: It compares the active ingredient with a standard treatment or a placebo in hundreds to thousands of patients.
It takes place only in a test tube.
It includes at most ten people.
It is carried out only after the medicine goes on sale.
121486.e: Phase III provides the decisive data for approval. Because of the large number of participants, rarer side effects can also be detected.
121486.m: Phase III provides the large comparison data for approval.

121487.q: What is the trial phase called that observes everyday use and rare side effects after approval?
121487.e: Phase IV studies collect data from a very large number of people treated in everyday life. This is how rare or late side effects are discovered.
121487.m: Phase IV observes a medicine after approval.

121488.q: What characterises a so-called phase 0 trial (microdosing)?
a: A few people receive a very small, ineffective dose to measure how the substance behaves in the body.
Thousands of patients receive the full dose.
The active ingredient is tested only on cell cultures.
The medicine is already on sale.
121488.e: In microdosing studies, usually less than a hundredth of the effective dose is given. This shows early on whether a candidate behaves in humans as expected.
121488.m: Phase 0 trials test tiny doses to check early how a substance behaves in the body.

121489.q: Why are participants in clinical trials assigned to the groups at random (randomisation)?
a: So that the groups differ only in the treatment
So that the trial is cheaper
So that everyone gets the placebo
So that the doctors can choose the groups
121489.e: Random assignment spreads known and unknown influencing factors evenly across the groups. Differences in the result can then be put down to the treatment.

121490.q: Which Swiss law has regulated research involving humans, including clinical trials, since 2014?
121490.e: The Human Research Act (HRA) came into force on 1 January 2014. Among other things, it requires approval by an ethics committee and the informed consent of participants.
121490.m: The Human Research Act protects people who take part in research.

121491.q: Which international document of the World Medical Association from 1964 sets out ethical principles for research involving humans?
121491.e: Among other things, the Declaration of Helsinki requires voluntary, informed consent and review by an ethics committee. It has been revised several times since.
121491.m: The Declaration of Helsinki is the ethical foundation of research involving humans.

121492.q: What is the difference between the active ingredient and an excipient in a tablet?
a: The active ingredient does the healing, excipients give shape, shelf life and make it easy to take.
Both have the same healing effect.
The active ingredient is only the colouring.
121492.e: Excipients such as fillers, binders or coatings turn the active ingredient into a form you can take. The pharmacological effect comes from the active ingredient.
121492.m: The active ingredient heals, the excipients make it possible to take.

121493.q: What is an active ingredient called that binds to a receptor and blocks it without activating it?
121493.e: An antagonist occupies the receptor and stops the body's own messengers from working. An agonist, by contrast, activates the receptor like a natural messenger.

121494.q: Which doctor, born in Einsiedeln, came up with the idea “Only the dose makes a thing not a poison”?
121494.e: Paracelsus (about 1493 to 1541) came from Einsiedeln. His principle is still seen today as the basis of toxicology.
121494.m: According to Paracelsus, the dose decides whether a substance is poisonous.

a: An inactive precursor that is only converted into the active ingredient in the body
A medicine without an active ingredient
121495.e: Prodrugs are activated, for example, in the liver. This can improve absorption or tolerability. One example is codeine, part of which is converted into morphine.
121495.m: A prodrug only becomes the active ingredient inside the body.

121496.q: What does the therapeutic window of an active ingredient describe?
a: The gap between the effective dose and the toxic dose
The number of diseases it cures
121496.e: The wider the therapeutic window, the safer an active ingredient is. With a narrow window, as with digoxin, the dose must be monitored closely.
121496.m: A wide therapeutic window makes an active ingredient safer.

121497.q: What are medicines called whose active ingredients are made in living cells using biotechnology, such as antibodies?
121497.e: Biologics are large, complex molecules such as monoclonal antibodies or insulin. They are produced in cell cultures and not made purely by chemical synthesis.
121497.m: Biologics are made with the help of living cells.

121498.q: From which plant was a forerunner of aspirin's active ingredient known for a long time?
121498.e: Willow bark contains salicin, from which salicylic acid forms in the body. Acetylsalicylic acid, derived from it, came on the market as aspirin in 1899. Foxglove provides heart medicines, the poppy morphine and cinchona bark quinine.
121498.m: Aspirin's active ingredient is related to a substance from willow bark.

a: The path of an active ingredient through the body, from uptake to excretion
The transport of medicines to pharmacies
121500.e: Pharmacokinetics studies how an active ingredient is released, absorbed, distributed in the body, broken down and excreted.
121500.m: Pharmacokinetics describes the path of a medicine through the body.

121501.q: A patient takes 400 mg of an active ingredient with a half-life of 6 hours. How much is still in the body after 18 hours (simplified)?
121501.e: 18 hours are three half-lives. 400 mg halves to 200, then 100, then 50 mg.
121501.m: After each half-life, only half of the active ingredient is left.

121502.q: How do pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics differ?
a: Kinetics describes what the body does to the drug, dynamics what the drug does to the body.
Both terms mean the same thing.
Kinetics studies only animals, dynamics only humans.
Kinetics is about prices, dynamics about patents.
121502.e: Pharmacokinetics studies absorption, distribution, breakdown and excretion. Pharmacodynamics describes the mechanism of action and the effect at the target site.
121502.m: Pharmacokinetics asks what the body does to the medicine.

a: Part of a swallowed active ingredient is broken down on its first pass through the liver.
The first tablet always works most strongly.
An active ingredient is only absorbed the first time.
The kidney excretes the active ingredient immediately.
121503.e: Substances absorbed from the gut first reach the liver through the portal vein. There a large part can be metabolised before the active ingredient reaches the circulation.
121503.m: The first-pass effect reduces the amount of a swallowed active ingredient.

121504.q: What is the bioavailability of an active ingredient that is injected directly into a vein?
121504.e: When given intravenously, all of the active ingredient goes directly into the bloodstream. Other routes of administration are compared with this reference.
121504.m: Active ingredients given intravenously are fully bioavailable.

121505.q: An active ingredient has a bioavailability of 40 per cent when taken as a tablet. How much of a 200 mg tablet reaches the bloodstream?
121505.e: 40 per cent of 200 mg is 0.4 times 200 mg, which is 80 mg. The rest is not absorbed or is broken down beforehand.
121505.m: Bioavailability shows what share reaches the circulation.

121506.q: Why are many medicines taken at regular intervals?
a: So that the level in the blood stays evenly within the effective range
So that the stomach gets used to the tablets
So that the tablets do not expire
So that the body stops making its own defences
121506.e: The body breaks down active ingredients all the time. Taking them regularly makes up for this, so that the level in the blood is neither too low nor too high.
121506.m: Taking medicine regularly keeps the level of the active ingredient even.

121507.q: In which organ are most medicines broken down chemically?
121507.e: The liver contains many enzymes that convert and break down active ingredients. The breakdown products are then usually excreted through the kidneys.
121507.m: The liver breaks down most medicines.

121508.q: Why should you avoid grapefruit juice with some medicines?
a: It blocks the breakdown enzyme CYP3A4 in the gut, so the level of the active ingredient can rise.
It neutralises all active ingredients immediately.
It thins the blood like water.
121508.e: Substances in grapefruit block CYP3A4 in the gut wall. As a result, less of the active ingredient is broken down, and an overdose can occur.
121508.m: Grapefruit juice can slow down the breakdown of some medicines.

121509.q: What do antibiotics NOT work against?
121509.e: Antibiotics attack structures and metabolic pathways of bacteria that viruses do not have. That is why they are useless against flu or a cold and only encourage resistance.
121509.m: Antibiotics help against bacteria, not viruses.

121510.q: What does the abbreviation MRSA stand for?
121510.e: MRSA are staphylococci that are resistant to methicillin and many other beta-lactam antibiotics. They are a common cause of hospital infections.
121510.m: MRSA is a feared resistant hospital germ.

121511.q: How can bacteria exchange resistance genes with each other?
a: Through plasmids by horizontal gene transfer
Only through cell division in humans
Through the air as a gas
121511.e: In conjugation, bacteria pass small DNA rings, the plasmids, to other bacteria. This is how resistance also spreads between different species.
121511.m: Bacteria exchange resistance genes through plasmids.

121512.q: How do many bacteria make penicillin ineffective?
a: They make an enzyme that breaks down penicillin
They hide in red blood cells
They build penicillin into their cell wall
121512.e: The enzyme is called beta-lactamase and destroys the ring that penicillin needs to work. That is why some antibiotics are combined with substances that block this enzyme.
121512.m: Some bacteria destroy penicillin with an enzyme.

121513.q: Why does unnecessary use of antibiotics encourage resistance?
a: Sensitive bacteria die, resistant ones survive and multiply.
121513.e: Every use creates selection pressure. The few resistant bacteria then have an advantage and spread.

121514.q: The Swiss Strategy on Antibiotic Resistance (StAR) follows the One Health approach. What does that mean?
a: People, animals and the environment are considered together
Each person gets only one antibiotic in their life
Only hospitals need to take action
Antibiotics are only given to animals from now on
121514.e: Resistant bacteria move between people, farm animals, food and the environment. That is why the StAR strategy, adopted by the Federal Council in 2015, works in all these areas.
121514.m: One Health means that the health of people, animals and the environment belong together.

121515.q: What job does the Swiss centre ANRESIS have?
a: It monitors antibiotic resistance in hospitals and laboratories
It vaccinates farm animals against bacteria
121515.e: ANRESIS is the Swiss Centre for Antibiotic Resistance at the University of Bern. It collects resistance data across the country and so supports the federal strategy.
121515.m: ANRESIS monitors antibiotic resistance in Switzerland.

121516.q: According to a large study in the journal “The Lancet”, how many deaths worldwide in 2019 were directly caused by bacterial antibiotic resistance?
121516.e: The study, published in 2022, estimated about 1.27 million deaths directly caused in 2019. Including other cases where resistance played a part, there were almost five million.
121516.m: Antibiotic resistance causes more than a million deaths worldwide each year.

121517.q: What is the basic idea of personalised medicine?
a: To match treatments to a patient's individual features, such as their genes
To give all patients the same medicine
To choose medicines only by age
121517.e: Biomarkers, genetic tests and tumour analyses show which treatment is likely to work for a person. The aim is to increase effectiveness and reduce side effects.
121517.m: Personalised medicine adapts treatment to the individual person.

121518.q: Why is a breast cancer tested before it is treated with the antibody Herceptin?
a: Because the drug only works on tumours with a particular feature
Because the test replaces the medicine
Because the drug works the same on all tumours
Because the test prepares the anaesthetic
121518.e: Herceptin binds to the receptor HER2, which is present in large amounts in only some breast tumours. The medicine only helps with these HER2-positive tumours.
121518.m: Herceptin only works on tumours with a particular feature.

121519.q: What are cancer drugs such as imatinib called that specifically block an altered protein of the cancer cells?
121519.e: In one form of leukaemia, imatinib (Glivec) specifically blocks an abnormally altered protein. Healthy cells are harmed far less than with classic chemotherapy.
121519.m: Targeted therapies attack specific features of cancer cells.

a: A test that shows before treatment whether a medicine can work for a patient
A companion who takes patients to the doctor
121520.e: Companion diagnostics are developed together with a medicine. One example is a test for a particular gene change in a tumour before targeted cancer therapy.
121520.m: A companion diagnostic shows who will benefit from a medicine.

a: How genes affect the action and breakdown of medicines
121521.e: Gene variants in breakdown enzymes such as CYP2D6 mean that some people break down medicines very quickly or very slowly. The dose can be adjusted to this.
121521.m: Pharmacogenetics explains why medicines work differently depending on genes.

121522.q: How does a CAR-T cell therapy work?
a: The patient's own immune cells are genetically modified so that they recognise cancer cells.
Cancer cells are heated with rays.
121522.e: T cells are taken out, fitted with a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) and given back. The first CAR-T therapy, Kymriah by Novartis, was approved in the USA in 2017.
121522.m: CAR-T cells are reprogrammed immune cells against cancer.

121523.q: Which international research project had largely decoded the human genome by 2003?
121523.e: The Human Genome Project sequenced the roughly three billion base pairs of the human genome. It laid the foundation for genome-based personalised medicine.
121523.m: The Human Genome Project laid the basis for personalised medicine.

121524.q: Which national initiative has promoted the use of health data for personalised medicine in Switzerland since 2017?
121524.e: The SPHN is building an infrastructure so that hospitals and universities can share health data for research. It is funded by the federal government.
121524.m: The SPHN connects health data for research in Switzerland.

121525.q: Who founded the company in Basel in 1896 from which Roche developed?
121525.e: Fritz Hoffmann-La Roche founded the firm F. Hoffmann-La Roche & Co. in 1896. The company still has its headquarters in Basel today.
121525.m: Roche was founded in 1896 by Fritz Hoffmann-La Roche.

121526.q: Which US biotech company did Roche take over completely in 2009?
121526.e: Roche had been the majority shareholder of Genentech since 1990 and bought the remaining shares in 2009. Genentech produced important cancer drugs such as trastuzumab.
121526.m: Genentech has been wholly owned by Roche since 2009.

121527.q: Which Roche building in Basel, at 205 metres, is the tallest building in Switzerland (as of 2025)?
121527.e: Building 2 opened in 2022 and overtook the 178-metre Building 1 from 2015. Both towers were designed by Herzog & de Meuron.
121527.m: Roche Tower Building 2 is the tallest building in Switzerland.

121528.q: In which field, besides medicines, is Roche a world-leading supplier?
121528.e: Roche has two divisions: Pharma and Diagnostics. The diagnostics division makes laboratory tests and equipment, for example for blood analysis.
121528.m: Roche is strong in pharma and diagnostics.

121529.q: Which chemist working at Roche developed the sedative diazepam (Valium)?
121529.e: At Roche, Leo Sternbach discovered the benzodiazepines, including chlordiazepoxide and diazepam. Valium came on the market in 1963 and became one of the best-selling medicines.
121529.m: Leo Sternbach developed Valium at Roche.

121530.q: Which chemical disaster in Italy in 1976 involved a Roche subsidiary?
121530.e: A cloud of dioxin escaped from the Icmesa factory near Seveso, which belonged to Roche through Givaudan. The disaster led to the European Seveso Directive on major accidents.
121530.m: The Seveso disaster of 1976 involved a Roche subsidiary.

121531.q: Which Roche flu medicine was stockpiled in large amounts worldwide as part of pandemic preparations?
121531.e: Tamiflu, with the active ingredient oseltamivir, blocks the neuraminidase of flu viruses. Many countries built up stocks of it in case of a flu pandemic.
121531.m: Roche's Tamiflu is used against flu viruses.

121532.q: What role did Roche play with vitamin C from the 1930s?
a: Roche was one of the first firms to start industrial synthesis.
Roche discovered vitamin C in oranges.
Roche banned vitamin C in Switzerland.
Roche made vitamin C only from apples.
121532.e: In 1933, Tadeus Reichstein developed a process for synthesising vitamin C, which Roche took over. This meant vitamin C was made on a large scale for the first time.
121532.m: Roche made vitamin C industrially at an early stage.

121533.e: The Basel companies Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz merged in 1996 to form Novartis. At the time it was one of the largest mergers in business history.
121533.m: Novartis was formed in 1996 from Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz.

121534.q: What does the Latin origin of the name Novartis mean?
121534.e: The name goes back to “novae artes”. It was meant to express a fresh start after the merger.

121535.q: Which generics division did Novartis spin off as an independent company in 2023?
121535.e: Sandoz was listed on the Swiss stock exchange in October 2023. Since then, Novartis has focused on innovative, patent-protected medicines.
121535.m: Sandoz has been independent of Novartis since 2023.

121536.q: Which insecticide, whose effect was discovered at Geigy in Basel in 1939, helped against malaria but was later largely banned because of environmental damage?
121536.e: The Geigy chemist Paul Hermann Müller received the Nobel Prize for it in 1948. But DDT built up in food chains and harmed, for example, birds of prey.
121536.m: DDT was discovered at Geigy and later banned because of environmental damage.

121537.q: Which fire in a Sandoz warehouse badly polluted the Rhine in 1986?
121537.e: On 1 November 1986, a chemical store burned in Schweizerhalle near Basel. The water used to fight the fire carried poisons into the Rhine, and huge numbers of fish died.
121537.m: The Schweizerhalle fire in 1986 caused a massive fish kill in the Rhine.

121538.q: What is special about the Novartis therapy Zolgensma for spinal muscular atrophy?
a: It replaces a missing gene with a single infusion
It is a vaccine against a virus
It is an antibiotic against bacteria
121538.e: Zolgensma is a gene therapy and replaces the missing SMN1 gene. When it was approved in 2019, at about 2.1 million dollars it was considered the most expensive medicine in the world.
121538.m: Zolgensma is a one-off gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy.

121539.q: Which medicine discovered at Sandoz revolutionised organ transplants from 1983 by preventing rejection?
121539.e: Ciclosporin suppresses the immune system in a targeted way so that transplanted organs are not rejected. Its immunosuppressive effect was discovered at Sandoz by Jean-François Borel.
121539.m: Sandoz's ciclosporin made organ transplants much more successful.

121540.q: Which disease is the Novartis medicine Coartem used against, whose active ingredient comes from a medicinal plant of Chinese medicine?
121540.e: Coartem is based on a derivative of artemisinin from sweet wormwood. Novartis supplies it in malaria areas at a not-for-profit price.
121540.m: Novartis's Coartem is used against malaria.

121541.q: From which branch of industry did the Basel chemical and pharmaceutical industry develop in the 19th century?
a: From making dyes for the silk ribbon industry
121541.e: Basel firms made synthetic dyes, so-called coal tar dyes, for the textile industry. Pharmaceutical companies later grew out of this chemical know-how.
121541.m: Basel's pharma industry grew out of the dye industry.

121542.q: Which advantage of its location played an important role for early chemistry in Basel?
a: The Rhine as a water source and transport route
121542.e: The Rhine supplied water for production and served as a transport route. In addition, Basel was close to France and Germany with their markets and raw materials.
121542.m: The Rhine was an important location advantage for Basel's chemical industry.

121543.q: Why could Swiss chemical firms easily copy foreign dyes in the 19th century?
a: For a long time Switzerland had no patent protection for chemical processes.
Switzerland bought up all the patents.
Switzerland was a member of the EU.
121543.e: Switzerland only had a patent law from 1888, and chemical processes only became patentable in 1907. This favoured firms that took over processes from abroad.
121543.m: A lack of patent protection helped early chemistry in Basel.

121544.q: What is the cross-border life sciences region around Basel, with parts of France and Germany, called?
121544.e: BioValley links companies, universities and clinics on the Upper Rhine in Switzerland, France and Germany. The term Crypto Valley, by contrast, refers to the blockchain sector in Zug.
121544.m: BioValley is the three-country life sciences region on the Upper Rhine.

121545.q: Which institute of the University of Basel has been a centre of molecular life sciences since 1971?
121545.e: The Biozentrum of the University of Basel was founded in 1971 and was one of the first interdisciplinary institutes for molecular biology. It attracts researchers from all over the world.
121545.m: The Biozentrum is a well-known research institute of the University of Basel.

121546.q: Which group of goods is Switzerland's largest export sector (as of 2024)?
121546.e: Chemical and pharmaceutical products make up well over a third of Swiss goods exports. A large part of them come from the Basel region.
121546.m: Pharmaceutical products are Switzerland's most important export.

121547.q: What do the big Basel pharmaceutical companies spend billions of francs on every year?
a: On research and development of new medicines
121547.e: Roche and Novartis are among the companies with the highest spending on research and development in the world. Bringing a new medicine to approval often takes more than ten years.
121547.m: Basel pharmaceutical companies invest a great deal in research.

121549.q: When may generics of a medicine be put on the market?
a: When the patent protection has expired
Immediately after the original is approved
121549.e: As long as the patent is valid, only the patent holder may market the active ingredient. After that, generics manufacturers can apply for a simplified approval.
121549.m: Generics come on the market after the patent ends.

121550.q: What must a manufacturer mainly prove to get a generic approved?
a: A phase III trial with thousands of patients
121550.e: Bioequivalence means that the active ingredient reaches the blood in a comparable amount and at a comparable speed. Effectiveness does not need to be proved again, because it is known from the original.
121550.m: Generics must be bioequivalent to the original.

121551.q: Why are generics usually cheaper than original products?
a: The manufacturers do not bear the costs of researching and clinically developing the active ingredient.
They are not tested by the authorities.
121551.e: The expensive research and trial costs do not apply to the generic. In addition, competition between several suppliers lowers prices.
121551.m: Generics are cheaper because there are no development costs.

121552.q: What is the copy version of a medicine made by biotechnology called?
121552.e: Biologics are so complex that an identical copy is not possible. A biosimilar is therefore only very similar and must prove its comparability with extra studies.
121552.m: Copies of biologics are called biosimilars.

121553.q: Since 2024, how high is the deductible in Switzerland if you get a more expensive original product instead of an available generic (without a medical reason)?
121553.e: The differentiated deductible was raised from 20 to 40 per cent at the start of 2024. The federal government wants to encourage the use of cheaper generics.
121553.m: Anyone who chooses the more expensive original without a reason pays a higher deductible.

121554.q: What may differ in a generic compared with the original?
a: The excipients, colour and shape of the tablet
The amount of active ingredient per tablet
121554.e: The active ingredient and dosage must be the same. Appearance, name and excipients can differ, which must be considered for allergies to certain excipients.
121554.m: Generics may differ from the original in colour, shape and excipients.

121555.q: Which professional does Swiss law allow to replace an original product with a cheaper generic, as long as the doctor does not explicitly ask for the original?
a: The patient in every case without advice
121555.e: Pharmacists have a right of substitution. They may hand out a generic unless the doctor asks for the original product for medical reasons.
121555.m: In the pharmacy, an original can be replaced by a generic.

121556.q: What legal form does Swissmedic have?
a: A federal institution under public law
A company listed on the stock exchange
An association under the Civil Code
A department of a health insurer
121556.e: Swissmedic is an institution under public law with its own legal personality and belongs to the Federal Department of Home Affairs. It is largely funded by fees.
121556.m: Swissmedic is a federal institution under public law.

121557.q: Since when has Swissmedic been working as the authority for therapeutic products?
121557.e: Swissmedic started work on 1 January 2002, when the Therapeutic Products Act came into force. It replaced the Intercantonal Office for the Control of Medicines (IKS).

121558.q: Which law regulates the approval and monitoring of medicines in Switzerland?
121558.e: The Therapeutic Products Act (TPA) is meant to ensure that only high-quality, safe and effective therapeutic products come on the market. Swissmedic puts it into practice.
121558.m: The Therapeutic Products Act regulates medicines and medical devices.

121559.q: Which three criteria does Swissmedic mainly check in an application for approval?
121559.e: A medicine is only approved if it meets these three criteria. Whether basic health insurance pays for it is then decided separately by the FOPH.
121559.m: Swissmedic checks quality, safety and effectiveness.

121560.q: Which authority decides whether an approved medicine is added to the list of pharmaceutical specialities and paid for by basic health insurance?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
121560.e: Approval by Swissmedic is only the first step. The FOPH then checks effectiveness, suitability and cost-effectiveness and sets the price.
121560.m: The FOPH decides on payment, Swissmedic on approval.

121561.q: Why can you only get some medicines with a doctor's prescription?
a: They can be dangerous if used wrongly
They have not been approved yet
121561.e: Prescription medicines have stronger effects or risks. A doctor should check whether they are suitable. Other medicines are available with or without advice in pharmacies and chemist's shops.
121561.m: Riskier medicines are only available on prescription.

121562.q: When did Swissmedic grant its first approval for a Covid-19 vaccine (Pfizer/BioNTech)?
121562.e: On 19 December 2020, Swissmedic approved the mRNA vaccine from Pfizer and BioNTech. It was the first approval of a Covid-19 vaccine in Switzerland through the regular procedure.
121562.m: The first Covid-19 vaccine was approved in Switzerland in December 2020.

121563.q: What is meant by pharmacovigilance, for which Swissmedic is responsible in Switzerland?
121563.e: Doctors, pharmacies and companies report unwanted effects to Swissmedic. This way risks can be recognised and, for example, warnings can be added.
121563.m: Pharmacovigilance monitors the safety of medicines in everyday use.

121564.q: Why does Swissmedic work together with authorities from other countries on approvals?
a: To review applications together and faster
121564.e: In the Access Consortium, for example, several authorities share the assessment work. This allows new medicines to be reviewed faster, but each country still makes its own decision.
121564.m: Through cooperation, Swissmedic reviews approvals faster.

121565.q: What is meant by drug repurposing?
a: Using a known active ingredient for a new disease
121565.e: Because safety data for an approved active ingredient already exist, development for a new use can be faster and cheaper. One example is thalidomide, which is used today against a form of bone marrow cancer.
121565.m: In drug repurposing, a known active ingredient gets a new job.

a: Antibiotics used only when others fail because of resistance
Antibiotics you keep in stock at home
121566.e: Reserve antibiotics such as colistin should be used as rarely as possible so that they keep working. The WHO sorts antibiotics into groups for this purpose.
121566.m: Reserve antibiotics are saved for serious cases with resistance.

121567.q: Which feature do prokaryotes lack, unlike eukaryotes?
a: A nucleus with a nuclear envelope
121567.e: In prokaryotes, the DNA lies freely in the cytoplasm without being surrounded by a nuclear envelope. A cell membrane, ribosomes and cytoplasm, on the other hand, are found in all cells.

121568.q: Which two domains of life belong to the prokaryotes?
121568.e: In Carl Woese's three-domain system, bacteria and archaea are prokaryotic, and the eukaryotes form the third domain. Viruses are not considered living things with their own cells.
121568.m: Bacteria and archaea are the two groups of prokaryotes.

121569.q: What is the region in a bacterium's cytoplasm called where the ring-shaped chromosome lies?
121569.e: The nucleoid is a nuclear region without a membrane in which the bacterial chromosome is tightly packed. The nucleolus, by contrast, is part of the nucleus of eukaryotes.
121569.m: Bacterial DNA lies in the nucleoid without an envelope.

121570.q: Which type of ribosome do prokaryotes have?
121570.e: Prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes, while eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Many antibiotics use this difference and specifically block the 70S ribosomes.

121571.q: What substance is the cell wall of most bacteria mainly made of?
121571.e: Murein, also called peptidoglycan, is a network of sugar chains and short peptides. Cellulose is found in plant cell walls, chitin in fungi and insects.
121571.m: The bacterial cell wall is made of murein.

121572.q: What are the long, rotating structures that many bacteria use to move called?
121572.e: Bacterial flagella are turned like a propeller by a motor in the cell envelope. Cilia and pseudopodia, by contrast, are found in eukaryotic cells.

121573.q: What are the small, usually ring-shaped DNA molecules called that bacteria can have in addition to their chromosome?
121573.e: Plasmids copy themselves independently of the chromosome and often carry useful extra genes. Plastids, by contrast, are organelles of plant cells.
121573.m: Plasmids are small rings of DNA in bacteria.

121574.q: After which Danish doctor is the staining method named that divides bacteria into two groups by the structure of their cell wall?
121574.e: Hans Christian Gram developed the stain in 1884. Bacteria with a thick cell wall layer stain blue-violet, those with a thin layer and an outer membrane stain red.
121574.m: Gram staining distinguishes bacteria by their cell wall.

121575.q: What is the reproductive cycle of a phage called in which the host cell bursts after new phages have formed?
121575.e: In the lytic cycle, the bacterium immediately produces new phages until the cell is dissolved and releases them. Lysis means dissolving.
121575.m: In the lytic cycle, the bacterial cell is destroyed.

121576.q: What is the phage DNA called that is built into the bacterial chromosome in the lysogenic cycle?
121576.e: The prophage is copied along with every cell division without killing the bacterium. Only under stress can it be cut out and trigger the production of new phages.
121576.m: A built-in phage is called a prophage.

121577.q: What is the protein shell called that surrounds the genetic material of a phage?
121577.e: The capsid consists of many identical protein building blocks. In typical phages such as T4, it sits as a head on a tail with fibres.
121577.m: The capsid protects a virus's genetic material.

121578.q: What did Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase prove with bacteriophages in 1952?
a: That DNA is the genetic material
That proteins are the genetic material
That viruses have their own cells
121578.e: They labelled the DNA with radioactive phosphorus and the proteins with radioactive sulphur. Only the labelled DNA got into the bacteria.
121578.m: The Hershey-Chase experiment proved that DNA carries genetic information.

121579.q: What would people like to use bacteriophages for more often in medicine?
121579.e: Phages attack particular bacteria specifically, including those against which antibiotics no longer work. This phage therapy has a long tradition, especially in Georgia.
121579.m: Phages are a hope against resistant bacteria.

121580.q: Why are bacteriophages basically harmless to humans?
a: They do not survive in water
They are bigger than human cells
They are digested by the stomach at once
121580.e: Phages use their tail fibres to recognise very specific surface structures of bacteria. They cannot dock onto human cells.

121581.q: What does the Greek part “phage” in “bacteriophage” mean?
121581.e: Phagein means to eat or devour in Greek. A bacteriophage is therefore literally a bacteria eater.

121582.q: What is the transfer of bacterial genes from one cell to another with the help of phages called?
121582.e: In transduction, phages accidentally package pieces of bacterial DNA and carry them into the next bacterium. In transformation, by contrast, a bacterium takes up free DNA from its surroundings.
121582.m: In transduction, phages carry bacterial genes.

121583.q: What is the transfer of plasmids between two bacteria through direct cell contact via a pilus called?
121583.e: In conjugation, a donor bacterium forms a bridge to the recipient and transfers a copy of the plasmid. In this way resistance genes spread quickly, even between different species.
121583.m: Conjugation transfers plasmids through direct contact.

121584.q: Which enzyme makes many bacteria resistant to penicillins by splitting the active substance?
121584.e: Beta-lactamases destroy the penicillin molecule before it can work. That is why penicillins are often combined with inhibitors such as clavulanic acid.

121585.q: What is the approach called that looks at antibiotic resistance in humans, animals and the environment together?
121585.e: Resistant bacteria move back and forth between people, farm animals, food and water. That is why, in the One Health approach, human and veterinary medicine, farming and environmental protection work together.
121585.m: Resistance is best fought with the One Health approach.

121586.q: Which evolutionary process explains why resistant bacteria increase during antibiotic treatment?
121586.e: The antibiotic kills sensitive bacteria, while resistant ones survive and multiply. In this way resistance spreads through the bacterial population.

121587.q: What is meant by horizontal gene transfer in bacteria?
a: Genes are exchanged between existing cells
Genes are only passed on to daughter cells
121587.e: In horizontal gene transfer, genes pass not through division but sideways from one bacterium to another. This can even happen between different bacterial species.
121587.m: Horizontal gene transfer spreads resistance genes between bacteria.

121588.q: When is a germ described as multi-resistant?
a: When it is resistant to several classes of antibiotics
When disinfectants do not affect it
121588.e: Multi-resistant germs no longer respond to several groups of antibiotics. This makes treatment difficult and expensive.
121588.m: Multi-resistant germs defy several groups of antibiotics.

121589.q: What is the main aim of the Swiss Strategy on Antibiotic Resistance (StAR)?
a: To keep antibiotics effective in the long term
To sell antibiotics without a prescription
121589.e: The StAR strategy was adopted by the Federal Council in 2015. It includes measures in human and veterinary medicine and in farming so that antibiotics remain effective.
121589.m: Switzerland fights antibiotic resistance with the StAR strategy.

121590.q: Which behaviour by patients encourages antibiotic resistance to develop?
a: Stopping or changing the course without talking to the doctor
Telling the doctor about side effects
121590.e: Anyone who stops antibiotics on their own, takes the wrong dose or later takes leftover tablets themselves exposes bacteria to the drug unnecessarily or insufficiently. This helps resistant germs survive.
121590.m: Take antibiotics exactly as the doctor prescribes.

121591.q: Which aminopenicillin is very often prescribed today, for example for middle ear infections?
121591.e: Amoxicillin is a penicillin with a wider range of action that is well absorbed from the gut. Ciprofloxacin, doxycycline and clarithromycin belong to other classes of antibiotics.
121591.m: Amoxicillin is a commonly used penicillin.

121592.q: What did Alexander Fleming observe in 1928 that led to the discovery of penicillin?
a: A mould stopped bacteria growing in a culture dish
121592.e: Fleming noticed that no bacteria grew around a mould of the genus Penicillium. The mould produced a substance that he called penicillin.

121593.q: Why was penicillin only used as a medicine more than ten years after its discovery?
a: It was difficult to make it pure and in large amounts
It was banned at the time
At first it only worked on plants
Nobody had recognised bacteria as germs
121593.e: Only around 1940 did Howard Florey and Ernst Chain in Oxford manage to purify penicillin and show its healing effect. For this they received the Nobel Prize with Fleming in 1945.
121593.m: Florey and Chain turned penicillin into a medicine.

121594.q: How does penicillin act on bacteria?
a: It blocks the building of the cell wall
It dissolves the cell membrane at once
121594.e: Penicillin blocks enzymes that cross-link the network of sugar chains and peptides in the cell wall. Growing bacteria therefore become unstable and burst.
121594.m: Penicillin disrupts the building of the bacterial cell wall.

121595.q: Which ring structure in the molecule is crucial for penicillin's effect?
121595.e: The strained four-membered beta-lactam ring binds to the enzymes that build the cell wall and blocks them. Cephalosporins also have this ring.
121595.m: Penicillins belong to the beta-lactam antibiotics.

121596.q: Against which bacteria does penicillin G mainly work?
121596.e: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick cell wall layer that is easy to reach. In gram-negative bacteria, an outer membrane protects the thin cell wall layer.
121596.m: Penicillin G works especially well against gram-positive germs.

121597.q: Why is penicillin G usually injected rather than swallowed?
a: It is destroyed by stomach acid
It does not dissolve in water
It is stored straight away by the liver
121597.e: Penicillin G is sensitive to acid and would be largely broken down in the stomach. Penicillin V is more stable in acid and can be taken as a tablet.

121598.q: Which unwanted reaction to penicillin is the best known?
121598.e: Penicillin allergies are among the most common drug allergies and range from skin rashes to anaphylactic shock. Discoloured teeth, by contrast, are typical of tetracyclines.

121599.q: What do staphylococci typically look like under the microscope?
a: Spheres in clusters like bunches of grapes
121599.e: Staphylé is the Greek word for a bunch of grapes. Spherical bacteria in chains, by contrast, are streptococci.
121599.m: Staphylococci lie together like bunches of grapes.

121600.q: Where does Staphylococcus aureus live in many healthy people without making them ill?
121600.e: Around 20 to 30 per cent of people carry Staphylococcus aureus in their nose, some of them permanently. It only becomes dangerous when it gets into the body, for example through wounds.
121600.m: Many healthy people carry staphylococci in their nose.

121601.q: Which measure is most important in hospital to prevent MRSA from being passed on?
a: Taking the temperature of all visitors
121601.e: MRSA is mainly carried from patient to patient on the hands of staff. Hand disinfection breaks this route most effectively.
121601.m: Hand disinfection stops MRSA from spreading.

121602.q: What does the “R” in the abbreviation MRSA stand for?
121602.e: MRSA means methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. These bacteria are not affected by methicillin and related antibiotics such as penicillins.
121602.m: MRSA is resistant to methicillin and related antibiotics.

121603.q: Why are MRSA infections harder to treat than ordinary staphylococcal infections?
a: Many common antibiotics no longer work
121603.e: The usual beta-lactam antibiotics fail against MRSA. Doctors have to switch to a few reserve drugs such as vancomycin, which can have more side effects.
121603.m: Many common antibiotics do not work against MRSA.

121604.q: What does decolonisation mean for MRSA carriers?
a: The bacteria are removed from the skin and mucous membranes
The person is moved to another country
The bacteria are grown in the laboratory
The person is given a vaccine against MRSA
121604.e: Nasal ointments and antiseptic washes, for example, are used for several days. The aim is that the person no longer carries the bacteria and passes them on.

121605.q: In which decade was MRSA first described, shortly after methicillin was introduced?
121605.e: Methicillin came onto the market in 1959, and resistant strains were already described in Great Britain in 1961. This shows how quickly bacteria adapt.
121605.m: MRSA appeared as early as the 1960s.

121606.e: Prions contain no genetic material but are proteins with an abnormal three-dimensional folding. This makes them fundamentally different from viruses and bacteria.
121606.m: Prions are disease-causing proteins without genetic material.

121607.q: Who coined the term prion and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it in 1997?
121607.e: In 1982 the American Stanley Prusiner described prions as protein-like infectious particles. His theory was controversial for a long time.

121608.q: Which animal disease, which also concerned Switzerland in the 1990s, is caused by prions?
121608.e: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy, known as mad cow disease, also occurred in Swiss cattle. The other diseases are caused by viruses.
121608.m: BSE is a prion disease of cattle.

121609.q: Which human disease is caused by prions?
121609.e: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease quickly destroys nerve tissue in the brain and is fatal. One variant has been linked to eating beef contaminated with BSE.
121609.m: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is a prion disease.

121610.q: How do prions multiply in the body?
a: They make normal proteins fold wrongly too
They build their genetic material into the DNA
They form spores in the nerve cells
121610.e: A misfolded prion protein acts like a template and changes the shape of healthy proteins. This creates a chain reaction, and the faulty proteins build up as deposits.
121610.m: Prions multiply by refolding healthy proteins.

121611.q: Why do surgical instruments need special treatment if prions are suspected?
a: Prions survive many usual sterilisation methods
121611.e: Prions are very resistant to heat, radiation and many disinfectants. That is why especially strict cleaning rules apply to them.

121612.q: What is the prion disease of sheep and goats called?
121612.e: Scrapie has been known since the 18th century; sick animals often rub themselves against fences. Distemper, foot rot and mange have other causes.
121612.m: Scrapie is the prion disease of sheep.

121613.q: In which country did the prion disease kuru occur?
121613.e: Kuru affected the Fore people in the highlands of Papua New Guinea. It was passed on through ritual funeral customs and disappeared after these were given up.
121613.m: Kuru was a prion disease in Papua New Guinea.

121614.q: Which enzyme in retroviruses copies RNA into DNA?
121614.e: Reverse transcriptase reverses the usual flow of information from DNA to RNA. This is also where the name retrovirus comes from.
121614.m: Retroviruses copy their RNA into DNA.

121615.q: Which is the best-known retrovirus that makes humans ill?
121615.e: The human immunodeficiency virus is a retrovirus and, if untreated, can lead to the disease AIDS. Flu, measles and hepatitis A viruses are not retroviruses.
121615.m: HIV is one of the retroviruses.

121616.q: Which immune cells does HIV mainly attack?
121616.e: HIV docks onto the surface protein CD4, which is carried mainly by T helper cells. If these cells fail, the whole immune defence is weakened.
121616.m: HIV mainly destroys T helper cells.

121617.q: What is the DNA of a retrovirus called once it is built into the host cell's genome?
121617.e: The provirus stays permanently in the cell's genome and is copied with every division. That is why an HIV infection cannot yet be cured completely.
121617.m: Built-in retrovirus DNA is called a provirus.

121618.q: Which enzyme of a retrovirus builds the newly made viral DNA into the host genome?
121618.e: Integrase cuts open the host DNA and inserts the viral DNA. Integrase inhibitors are an important part of HIV treatment today.
121618.m: Integrase builds viral DNA into the genome.

121619.q: Why was the discovery of reverse transcriptase around 1970 so important?
a: It showed that genetic information can also flow from RNA to DNA
It showed that viruses have no genetic information
It proved that DNA is made of proteins
It led directly to a cure for AIDS
121619.e: People had assumed that information only flows from DNA to RNA. But retroviruses copy their RNA into DNA. The discoverers received the Nobel Prize in 1975.
121619.m: Retroviruses reverse the flow of information.

121620.q: What kind of genetic material do retroviruses carry in the virus particle?
121620.e: Each retrovirus particle contains two copies of single-stranded RNA. Only in the host cell is it turned into double-stranded DNA.
121620.m: Retroviruses carry their genetic material as RNA.

121621.q: What are endogenous retroviruses in the human genome?
a: Remains of old virus infections passed down for generations
Active viruses that make every person ill
Bacteria living in the cell nucleus
Genes that only appear during illness
121621.e: Millions of years ago, retroviruses built their DNA into the germ cells of our ancestors. These traces have been inherited ever since and are mostly inactive.
121621.m: Our genome contains many remains of old retroviruses.

121622.q: What is typical of a parasite?
a: It lives at the expense of a host
It lives only on dead material
121622.e: A parasite takes nutrients from its host and harms it, but usually does not kill it straight away. When both partners benefit, it is called symbiosis.
121622.m: A parasite lives at the expense of its host.

121623.q: Which of these organisms is an ectoparasite?
121623.e: Ectoparasites live on the outside of the host's body, like the tick on the skin. Tapeworm, roundworm and liver fluke live inside the body and are endoparasites.
121623.m: Ectoparasites live on the outside of their host.

121624.q: What is the host called in which a parasite reaches its adult stage?
121624.e: In the definitive host, the parasite becomes adult and reproduces. Only larval or young stages live in the intermediate host.
121624.m: A parasite becomes adult in the definitive host.

121625.q: Which animals are the typical intermediate hosts of the fox tapeworm?
121625.e: Mice take in the worm eggs, and larvae grow in their liver. When a fox eats the mouse, the cycle is complete; humans can be infected as accidental hosts.
121625.m: Mice are the intermediate hosts of the fox tapeworm.

121626.q: What is a relationship called in which one partner benefits and the other neither benefits nor is harmed?
121626.e: In commensalism, an animal might for example use another's food scraps without harming it. In parasitism, by contrast, the host is harmed.
121626.m: Commensals help themselves without harming their partner.

121627.q: Which native bird is a well-known brood parasite?
121627.e: The female cuckoo lays her eggs in other birds' nests. The host birds raise the cuckoo chick, often at the expense of their own young.
121627.m: The cuckoo has its young raised by other birds.

121628.q: Which bacterial disease is most often passed on by ticks in Switzerland?
121628.e: Lyme disease is caused by bacteria of the genus Borrelia and can be treated with antibiotics. There is a vaccine against TBE, which is also passed on by ticks but is caused by a virus.
121628.m: In Switzerland, ticks mainly pass on Lyme disease.

121629.q: Which animal is the definitive host of the parasite Toxoplasma gondii?
121629.e: Only in cats and other felines can Toxoplasma complete its full life cycle. Mice and also humans are intermediate hosts.
121629.m: Cats are the definitive hosts of Toxoplasma.

121630.q: Which mosquitoes pass the malaria parasites on to humans?
121630.e: Only females of the genus Anopheles pass on plasmodia when they suck blood. The tiger mosquito passes on other diseases, such as dengue.
121630.m: Malaria is spread by Anopheles mosquitoes.

121631.q: To which group of disease-causing organisms do plasmodia belong?
121631.e: Plasmodia are single-celled organisms with a nucleus, in other words eukaryotes. That is why antibiotics against bacteria do not help against malaria.
121631.m: Malaria is caused by single-celled organisms.

121632.q: Which species of Plasmodium causes the most dangerous form of malaria?
121632.e: Plasmodium falciparum causes falciparum malaria, which is often fatal if untreated. Infected blood cells stick together in small vessels, for example in the brain.
121632.m: Plasmodium falciparum is the most dangerous malaria parasite.

121633.q: Which blood cells do plasmodia attack in the human body?
121633.e: The parasites multiply in the red blood cells and make them burst. Many cells bursting at the same time leads to bouts of fever.
121633.m: Plasmodia multiply in red blood cells.

121634.q: Which organ do plasmodia travel to first after a mosquito bite?
121634.e: The parasites first multiply unnoticed in liver cells. Only after that do they get into the blood and cause the signs of illness.
121634.m: Plasmodia first multiply in the liver.

121635.q: For discovering which malaria drug did the Chinese researcher Tu Youyou receive the Nobel Prize in 2015?
121635.e: Tu Youyou obtained artemisinin from sweet wormwood, a plant used in traditional Chinese medicine. Combination therapies with artemisinin are standard today against falciparum malaria.
121635.m: Artemisinin is an important malaria drug from a plant.

121636.q: Which inherited blood disease, in its mild form with only one copy of the gene, partly protects against malaria?
121636.e: Carriers with one copy of the sickle cell gene are less likely to become seriously ill with falciparum malaria. That is why the gene is common in the malaria regions of Africa.
121636.m: The sickle cell gene gives some protection against malaria.

121637.q: What best protects travellers in malaria regions from infection?
a: Protection against mosquitoes and, depending on the region, preventive medicines
Having no contact with sick people
A single vaccination before the trip
121637.e: Malaria is spread by mosquito bites, not by water or direct contact. Mosquito nets, long clothing and insect repellent help, and in some regions tablets as well.
121637.m: Protection against mosquitoes is the main defence against malaria.

a: An infection caught in hospital or a care home
An infection that only affects animals
121638.e: Nosocomial comes from the Greek nosokomeion, hospital. It means infections that arise in connection with a stay or treatment in a healthcare facility.

121639.q: From when after admission to hospital is an infection usually considered nosocomial?
a: At the earliest about 48 hours after admission
121639.e: If an infection only appears after about 48 hours and was not present or incubating on admission, it is put down to the hospital. Earlier infections were usually brought in from home.
121639.m: After about 48 hours in hospital, a new infection counts as nosocomial.

121640.q: Which doctor reduced childbed fever in Vienna in 1847 through handwashing with chlorinated lime?
121640.e: Semmelweis realised that doctors were carrying disease material from corpses to patients. With a chlorinated lime solution, the death rate on his ward fell sharply.
121640.m: Ignaz Semmelweis is considered a pioneer of hand hygiene.

121641.q: Which medical device especially increases the risk of a urinary tract infection in hospital?
121641.e: Bacteria can get directly into the bladder through the catheter tube. That is why a urinary catheter should only stay in for as long as necessary.
121641.m: Urinary catheters encourage urinary tract infections.

121642.q: What is the Swiss national centre for infection prevention called, which records hospital infections?
121642.e: Swissnoso carries out surveillance of wound infections after operations and runs infection prevention programmes. Swissmedic, by contrast, is the authority for medicines.
121642.m: Swissnoso deals with hospital infections in Switzerland.

121643.q: According to the WHO, for how long should hands be rubbed with an alcohol-based disinfectant?
121643.e: The WHO recommends rubbing in the product for 20 to 30 seconds until the hands are dry. In this way every part of the hands is reached.
121643.m: Hand disinfection takes about half a minute.

121644.q: How many moments for hand hygiene does the WHO describe for healthcare staff?
121644.e: The moments are: before touching a patient, before clean or aseptic procedures, after contact with body fluids, after touching a patient and after touching the patient's surroundings.
121644.m: The WHO names five moments for hand hygiene.

121645.q: What is the federal strategy for monitoring, preventing and fighting hospital infections called?
121645.e: The Federal Council adopted the NOSO strategy in 2016. It aims to reduce infections in hospitals and care homes in Switzerland.
121645.m: The NOSO strategy fights hospital infections in Switzerland.

121646.q: Why are patients in intensive care especially at risk of hospital infections?
a: They often have catheters, tubes and a weakened immune system
They always lie in single rooms
121646.e: Breathing tubes and venous catheters open direct routes into the body for germs. In addition, the defences of seriously ill people are often weakened.
121646.m: Intensive care patients have a high risk of infection.

121647.q: According to today's definition, what is sepsis?
a: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a misdirected response to an infection
Harmless reddening of the skin after an insect bite
121647.e: Since the Sepsis-3 definition of 2016, the focus is not on the infection itself but on the excessive and harmful reaction of the body. It can make organs such as the kidneys, lungs or circulation fail.
121647.m: In sepsis, the defence reaction damages the body's own organs.

121648.q: Which everyday expression is often used for sepsis?
121648.e: The term blood poisoning is widespread but inaccurate, as there is no poison in the strict sense. Lockjaw is an everyday name for tetanus.
121648.m: In everyday language, sepsis is called blood poisoning.

121649.q: Which signs during an infection can point to the start of sepsis?
121649.e: If a sick person breathes noticeably fast, seems confused or has low blood pressure, sepsis may be present. Then medical help is needed immediately.
121649.m: Fast breathing and confusion during an infection are warning signs.

121650.q: What is typical of septic shock?
a: A drop in blood pressure that needs circulation-supporting drugs despite fluids
High fever with no other symptoms
121650.e: In septic shock, the circulation is so badly disturbed that vasopressors are needed despite drips. The death rate is then especially high.
121650.m: Septic shock is the most severe form of sepsis.

121651.q: According to guidelines, within what time should antibiotics be given if septic shock is suspected?
a: Only after all lab results are in
121651.e: With every hour of delay, the risk of death rises considerably. That is why international guidelines recommend giving antibiotics within the first hour if possible.

121652.q: According to a large study in “The Lancet”, roughly how many deaths worldwide in 2017 were due to sepsis?
121652.e: The study estimated around 49 million cases of sepsis and about 11 million deaths for 2017. That was around one fifth of all deaths worldwide.
121652.m: Sepsis is one of the most common causes of death worldwide.

121653.q: Which people have an especially high risk of developing sepsis?
a: Babies, older people and people with weak immune systems
121653.e: In very young, old or immunocompromised people, the defence system is less able to contain an infection. Sepsis is therefore more common in them.
121653.m: Very young, old and immunocompromised people are especially at risk.

121654.q: Which blood value is measured in sepsis as a sign that the tissues are not getting enough oxygen?
121654.e: When cells lack oxygen, they get energy anaerobically and produce lactate. A raised lactate level shows a dangerous circulatory disorder.
121654.m: A high lactate level warns of a lack of oxygen in the tissues.

121655.q: If sepsis is suspected, what should be taken if possible before the first dose of antibiotics?
a: A saliva sample for a genetic test
121655.e: In blood cultures, the germs can be grown and tested for resistance. After antibiotics have been given, they often no longer grow, so the blood is taken beforehand.
121655.m: Blood cultures help to find the germ causing sepsis.

121656.q: In which year did the WHO declare the spread of COVID-19 a pandemic?
121656.e: On 11 March 2020, the WHO classified the worldwide spread of the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 as a pandemic. The first cases had appeared in China at the end of 2019.
121656.m: The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020.

121657.q: On which day did the WHO constitution come into force in 1948, a day now marked as World Health Day?
121657.e: The WHO constitution came into force on 7 April 1948. Since then, World Health Day has been held every year on this day with a focus theme.
121657.m: World Health Day is on 7 April.

121658.q: Which list has the WHO published regularly since 1977 as a guide for healthcare?
a: The Model List of Essential Medicines
The list of World Heritage Sites
The Red List of Threatened Species
The list of banned doping substances
121658.e: The model list names medicines that are important for basic healthcare in every country. It is revised about every two years.
121658.m: The WHO keeps a list of essential medicines.

121659.q: Who is Director-General of the WHO (as of 2026)?
121659.e: The Ethiopian Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has led the WHO since 2017 and was re-elected in 2022. Margaret Chan was his predecessor, and António Guterres is UN Secretary-General.
121659.m: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus leads the WHO.

121660.q: What is the highest decision-making body of the WHO, in which all member states are represented, called?
121660.e: The World Health Assembly meets every year in Geneva and sets the WHO's policy and budget. The Security Council is a body of the UN.
121660.m: The World Health Assembly is the highest body of the WHO.

121661.q: What status does the WHO have in the United Nations system?
a: It is a specialised agency of the UN
It is an authority of the European Union
121661.e: The WHO is a legally independent specialised agency of the United Nations with its own member states. It coordinates international health work.
121661.m: The WHO belongs to the UN as a specialised agency.

121662.q: Why does the WHO call for antibiotics to be used only in a targeted and sparing way?
a: So that fewer resistant bacteria develop
Because antibiotics only work in winter
Because there are hardly any antibiotics left worldwide
121662.e: Every use of antibiotics favours bacteria that are not affected by them. If resistance becomes more common, the medicines no longer work for dangerous infections.
121662.m: Using antibiotics sparingly slows down resistance.

121663.q: How does the WHO constitution define health?
a: As a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
As simply the absence of illness
As the ability to work fully
As the result of regular visits to the doctor
121663.e: The definition in the constitution stresses that health is more than the absence of disease or infirmity. It includes mental and social well-being.
121663.m: For the WHO, health is more than the absence of illness.

121664.q: Light with a wavelength of 600 nm falls on a double slit with a slit separation of 0.3 mm. How far apart are neighbouring bright fringes on a screen 2 m away?
121664.e: For small angles, fringe spacing equals wavelength times screen distance divided by slit separation. So 600 nm · 2 m / 0.3 mm = 0.004 m = 4 mm.
121664.m: The fringe spacing grows with wavelength and screen distance.

121665.q: What path difference between the two partial waves leads to a bright fringe with a double slit?
a: An odd multiple of half the wavelength
Exactly a quarter of the wavelength
121665.e: With a path difference of k times lambda, crest meets crest and the waves reinforce each other. With an offset of half a wavelength, on the other hand, they cancel out.
121665.m: Bright fringes form when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.

121666.q: Which property of light does the fringe pattern behind a double slit prove?
121666.e: Alternating bright and dark fringes can only come from interference, the overlapping of waves. Pure particles would produce two bright stripes behind the slits.
121666.m: The interference pattern shows that light behaves like a wave.

121667.q: What do you observe if you send electrons through a double slit one at a time?
a: After many electrons, an interference pattern forms
Each electron splits into two halves
121667.e: Each electron lands at a single point, but the hits are distributed according to an interference pattern. This is a key example of wave-particle duality.
121667.m: Even single electrons show wave behaviour.

121668.q: What happens to the interference pattern if you measure which slit each particle goes through?
a: The pattern becomes twice as bright
121668.e: As soon as there is which-way information, the two possibilities can no longer interfere. What remains is a distribution like that of classical particles.
121668.m: Measuring the path destroys the interference.

121669.q: How does the spacing of the bright fringes change if you double the slit separation and change nothing else?
121669.e: The fringe spacing is inversely proportional to the slit separation. So double the slit separation gives half the fringe spacing.
121669.m: A greater slit separation gives narrower fringes.

121670.q: Which light produces the most widely spaced fringes with the same double slit?
121670.e: Red light has the longest wavelength of the colours listed. Since the fringe spacing is proportional to the wavelength, its fringes are furthest apart.
121670.m: Long-wavelength light gives wider interference fringes.

121671.q: Behind a double slit with a slit separation of 0.2 mm, the bright fringes on a screen 1 m away are 3 mm apart. What is the wavelength of the light?
121671.e: Wavelength equals fringe spacing times slit separation divided by screen distance. So 3 mm · 0.2 mm / 1 m = 0.0000006 m = 600 nm.
121671.m: The double slit can be used to measure the wavelength of light.

121672.q: When did Thomas Young present his interference experiments with light?
a: At the beginning of the 19th century
In the middle of the 17th century
At the end of the 18th century
At the beginning of the 20th century
121672.e: Young published his work on interference in London between 1801 and 1803. It was among the most important evidence for the wave nature of light.
121672.m: Thomas Young showed the interference of light around 1801.

121673.q: Whose particle theory of light did Thomas Young call into question with his experiments?
121673.e: Newton’s corpuscular theory described light as a stream of tiny particles and was the dominant view at the time. Huygens, on the other hand, had already put forward a wave theory, which Young supported.
121673.m: Young strengthened the wave theory against Newton’s particle picture.

121674.q: Thomas Young made important contributions to deciphering which script?
121674.e: Young studied the Rosetta Stone and recognised that certain hieroglyphs stand for sounds. The full decipherment was achieved by Jean-François Champollion in 1822.
121674.m: Thomas Young also worked on hieroglyphs.

121675.q: Which material property is called “Young’s modulus” in English after Thomas Young?
121675.e: The modulus of elasticity tells you how much a material deforms under tension or compression. A high value means a stiff material such as steel.
121675.m: In English, the modulus of elasticity bears Young’s name.

121676.q: Which theory of colour vision goes back to Thomas Young and Hermann von Helmholtz?
121676.e: According to the Young-Helmholtz theory, the eye has three kinds of colour receptors for red, green and blue. All colours come from their different levels of stimulation.
121676.m: The eye sees colours with three types of receptor.

121677.q: What profession did Thomas Young have alongside his research?
121677.e: Young studied medicine, including in Göttingen, and worked as a doctor in London. His knowledge of the eye fed into his research on optics.
121677.m: Thomas Young was a doctor by profession.

121678.q: Which part of Britain was Thomas Young from?
121678.e: Thomas Young was born in 1773 in Milverton in the English county of Somerset. He died in London in 1829.

121679.q: Which experiment did Thomas Young use to show the wave nature of light?
121679.e: Light behind two narrow slits forms bright and dark fringes. This interference pattern can only be explained by waves.
121679.m: The double slit shows that light interferes.

121680.q: Which equation describes the position of the maxima for an optical grating with grating spacing g?
121680.e: A maximum forms when the path difference between neighbouring slits, g · sin α, is a whole number of wavelengths. k is the order of the maximum.
121680.m: For a grating, g times sin alpha equals k times lambda.

121681.q: Which of these gratings deflects light of the same wavelength most strongly in the first order?
a: A grating with 1200 lines per mm
A grating with 600 lines per mm
A grating with 300 lines per mm
A grating with 100 lines per mm
121681.e: More lines per millimetre mean a smaller grating spacing. According to sin α = λ / g, the angle then becomes larger.
121681.m: The more lines per millimetre, the stronger the diffraction.

121682.q: A grating has a spacing of 2 µm. Up to which order at most can maxima be observed for light of 600 nm?
121682.e: Since sin α is at most 1, k is at most g / λ = 2 µm / 600 nm, about 3.3. So the highest whole order is 3.
121682.m: The sine limits the number of grating orders.

121683.q: Why are the maxima of a grating much sharper than with a double slit?
a: Because very many slits interfere at the same time
Because the grating focuses light like a lens
Because the grating only lets one colour through
121683.e: With many slits, the waves cancel out almost completely even at small deviations from the angle of the maximum. What remains are narrow, bright lines.

121684.q: An optical grating has 500 lines per millimetre. What is its grating spacing?
121684.e: The grating spacing is the distance between neighbouring lines: 1 mm / 500 = 0.002 mm. That is 2 µm.
121684.m: The grating spacing is the reciprocal of the number of lines per length.

121685.q: What colour is the zero-order maximum when white light falls on a grating?
121685.e: In the zero order, the path difference is zero for all wavelengths. All the colours overlap there again to give white light.
121685.m: The central maximum of a grating stays white.

121686.q: Why does the underside of a CD shimmer in rainbow colours?
a: The closely spaced data tracks act as a reflection grating
The plastic layer acts as a prism
The light is converted by fluorescence
121686.e: The tracks of a CD are about 1.6 µm apart. The reflected light interferes as at a grating and is fanned out by wavelength.
121686.m: A CD acts like an optical grating.

121687.q: How can you better separate two very similar wavelengths with an optical grating?
a: By placing the screen closer to the grating
121687.e: The resolving power of a grating is the product of the order and the number of lines illuminated. The more lines take part, the sharper the lines become.
121687.m: More lines and a higher order separate wavelengths better.

121688.q: A 633 nm laser produces the first-order maximum at 30 degrees with a grating. What is the grating spacing?
121688.e: From g · sin α = λ, g = 633 nm / sin 30° = 633 nm / 0.5. That gives 1266 nm, about 1.27 µm.
121688.m: The grating spacing can be calculated from the diffraction angle.

121689.q: What does an optical spectrometer measure?
a: The intensity of light depending on wavelength
The speed of light in a vacuum
The temperature of a light source directly
121689.e: A spectrometer splits light by wavelength and measures how much light arrives at each wavelength. This gives a spectrum.
121689.m: A spectrometer splits light into its wavelengths.

121690.q: Why can a prism split light into colours?
a: The refractive index of the glass depends on the wavelength
The prism acts as a double slit
The light is diffracted at the tip
121690.e: This dependence is called dispersion. In normal glass, short-wavelength light is refracted more strongly than long-wavelength light.
121690.m: Dispersion splits light in a prism.

121691.q: Why is a spectrometer illuminated with a lamp with known lines, such as a mercury vapour lamp?
a: To remove dust from the grating
121691.e: The lines of the lamp lie at precisely known wavelengths. By matching them to the measured positions on the detector, you can assign a wavelength to every position.
121691.m: Spectrometers are calibrated with known spectral lines.

121692.q: Which component at the entrance of a spectrometer only lets in a narrow beam of light?
121692.e: The narrow entrance slit is imaged in the spectrometer. The narrower it is, the sharper the spectral lines, but the less light gets in.
121692.m: The entrance slit helps determine how sharp the lines are.

121693.q: Which detector records the whole spectrum at once in modern compact spectrometers?
a: A CCD or CMOS line sensor
121693.e: The line sensor consists of many light-sensitive pixels side by side. Each pixel measures a small range of wavelengths.
121693.m: Modern spectrometers measure with line sensors.

121694.q: Which method did the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz use in 1995 to find the first exoplanet around a Sun-like star?
121694.e: With a high-precision spectrograph, they measured how the lines of the star 51 Pegasi shift periodically. From this they concluded that a planet was orbiting it, and they received the Nobel Prize in 2019.
121694.m: Spectrometers can find exoplanets through the wobbling of their stars.

121695.q: What is a spectrometer’s ability to show two close wavelengths separately called?
121695.e: A high spectral resolution makes it possible to separate closely spaced lines such as the sodium double line. It depends on the grating, slit and detector.
121695.m: Spectral resolution shows how finely a spectrometer separates.

121696.q: Why do spectrometers for ultraviolet often use optics made of quartz glass instead of ordinary glass?
a: Ordinary glass absorbs much of the UV light
Ordinary glass does not refract light
