121945.e: One Health starts from the idea that many health risks arise where people, animals and the environment meet. This is especially important for zoonoses.
121945.m: One Health connects people, animals and the environment.

121946.q: Which group of animals is considered an important natural reservoir for many coronaviruses and lyssaviruses?
121946.e: Bats carry many viruses without becoming seriously ill themselves. These include coronaviruses and various lyssaviruses.
121946.m: Bats are a reservoir for many viruses.

121947.q: What happens to an epidemic if the reproduction number stays below 1?
121947.e: If each case infects fewer than one person on average, there are fewer cases from generation to generation. The outbreak dies out.

121948.q: With R0 equal to 4, what proportion of a population must at least be immune to reach herd immunity?
121948.e: The threshold is calculated as 1 minus 1 divided by R0. This gives 1 minus 0.25, which is 0.75.
121948.m: The herd immunity threshold is 1 minus 1 divided by R0.

121949.q: Why must a very high proportion of the population be vaccinated against measles?
a: Its basic reproduction number is very high
It is only spread through water
121949.e: Measles has one of the highest known basic reproduction numbers, about 12 to 18. This gives a threshold of over 90 per cent.
121949.m: Measles is extremely infectious and needs high vaccination coverage.

121950.q: R0 is 3 and 40 per cent of the population are immune. How many people does an infected person then still infect on average?
121950.e: Only 60 per cent are still susceptible. 3 times 0.6 gives 1.8.
121950.m: Immunity lowers the number of infections per case.

121951.q: An infected person has 10 contacts a day, the chance of passing it on per contact is 5 per cent and they are infectious for 6 days. Roughly what is R0?
121951.e: You multiply contacts, probability of transmission and duration. 10 times 0.05 times 6 gives 3.
121951.m: R0 depends on contacts, risk of infection and duration.

121952.q: With R equal to 2, a chain starts with one case. How many new cases are there in the fifth generation of infection?
121952.e: Each generation doubles the number of cases. 2 to the power of 5 gives 32.
121952.m: With R equal to 2, exponential growth doubles with every generation.

121953.q: Why is R0 not a fixed natural constant of a pathogen?
a: It also depends on the behaviour and contact patterns of the population
It only changes with the phases of the moon
It is set by law every year
It is the same for all pathogens
121953.e: R0 comes from both the pathogen's properties and human behaviour. The same pathogen can therefore have different R0 values in different societies.
121953.m: R0 depends on the pathogen and on how people behave.

121954.q: What is the reproduction number called that takes the current situation, with immunity and measures, into account?
121954.e: The effective reproduction number, often called Re or Rt, changes over the course of an epidemic. It falls, for example, through vaccinations or fewer contacts.
121954.m: The effective reproduction number shows the current spread.

121955.q: What makes a pandemic different from an epidemic?
a: A pandemic spreads across countries and continents
A pandemic is always less dangerous
A pandemic stays limited to one city
121955.e: An epidemic is a cluster of cases in a certain time and place. If it spreads worldwide, it is called a pandemic.
121955.m: A pandemic is a worldwide epidemic.

121956.q: On which day did the WHO classify Covid-19 as a pandemic?
121956.e: The Director-General of the WHO described the spread as a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Shortly afterwards, many countries took strict measures.
121956.m: The WHO declared Covid-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020.

121957.q: Which situation did the Federal Council declare in March 2020 because of Covid-19?
121957.e: On 16 March 2020 the Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation under the Epidemics Act. This allowed it to order measures across the whole country.
121957.m: In 2020 the Federal Council declared the extraordinary situation.

121958.q: Which three situations does the Swiss Epidemics Act distinguish?
121958.e: Depending on the situation, the federal government gains more powers over the cantons. The revised law has been in force since 2016.
121958.m: The Epidemics Act has three situations.

121959.q: Which influenza subtype caused the Spanish flu of 1918?
121959.e: The Spanish flu was caused by an influenza A virus of subtype H1N1. It killed tens of millions of people worldwide.
121959.m: The Spanish flu was an H1N1 virus.

121960.q: What do the letters H and N stand for in the names of influenza A subtypes?
a: The surface proteins haemagglutinin and neuraminidase
121960.e: Haemagglutinin helps the virus attach to cells. Neuraminidase helps the new viruses leave the cell.
121960.m: H and N stand for two surface proteins of flu viruses.

121961.q: Which pandemic in the 14th century killed an estimated third of Europe's population?
121961.e: The Black Death was a plague pandemic from about 1347 to 1351. Estimates suggest around a third of people in Europe died.
121961.m: The Black Death killed about a third of Europeans.

121962.q: Which flu pandemic did the WHO declare in 2009?
121962.e: Swine flu was caused by a new influenza A virus carrying genes that came from pigs. For most people it was fairly mild.
121962.m: In 2009 the WHO declared the swine flu pandemic.

121963.q: Which antibody class drives the classic immediate-type allergy?
121963.e: Allergen-specific immunoglobulin E sits on mast cells and, at renewed contact with the allergen, triggers the release of messenger substances.
121963.m: IgE plays the main role in immediate-type allergy.

121964.q: Against which invaders is immunoglobulin E originally mainly directed?
121964.e: Together with mast cells and eosinophil granulocytes, IgE helps to fight worms and other parasites. In allergies, this defence is directed against harmless substances.
121964.m: Originally, IgE serves to fight parasites.

121965.q: Which antibody was discovered in the 1960s and explained how allergic reactions are triggered?
121965.e: The married couple Ishizaka in the USA and Johansson and Bennich in Sweden described IgE in 1966 and 1967. This identified the antibody that drives immediate-type allergies.
121965.m: IgE was discovered in the 1960s as the allergy antibody.

121966.q: Why is IgE found only in very small amounts in the blood, even though it is so important in allergies?
a: Most of it is attached firmly to mast cells
It is excreted through the kidneys at once
It is only found in the gut
It breaks down when blood is taken
121966.e: IgE is the rarest antibody class in serum. Most of it is bound to mast cells and basophil granulocytes and waits there for the allergen.
121966.m: IgE is the rarest antibody class in the blood.

121967.q: Which messenger substance is released from mast cells during an allergic reaction and causes itching and swelling?
121967.e: When an allergen binds to IgE on mast cells, they release histamine. Antihistamines block its effect.
121967.m: Histamine from mast cells causes allergic symptoms.

121968.q: What is an allergy treatment called in which you receive increasing amounts of the allergen over years?
121968.e: In desensitisation, also called specific immunotherapy, the immune system slowly gets used to the allergen. The IgE-driven reaction becomes weaker as a result.
121968.m: Desensitisation gets the immune system used to an allergen.

121969.q: Which cells make IgE and other antibodies?
121969.e: Activated B cells mature into plasma cells and produce antibodies. Messenger substances from T helper cells, such as interleukin-4, get them to make IgE.
121969.m: Plasma cells produce antibodies, including IgE.

121970.q: Which medicine is injected first in a severe allergic shock?
121970.e: In anaphylaxis, triggered by IgE and mast cells, adrenaline narrows the blood vessels and widens the airways. People with allergies often carry an emergency auto-injector for this.
121970.m: In an allergic shock, adrenaline helps first.

121971.q: Which messenger substance is stored in the granules of mast cells and causes itching and swelling?
121971.e: Histamine widens blood vessels, makes them leakier and irritates nerve endings. This leads to redness, weals and itching.
121971.m: Mast cells store large amounts of histamine.

121972.q: In which kind of reaction do mast cells play a central role?
121972.e: Mast cells carry antibodies of the IgE type on their surface. When an allergen such as pollen binds to them, they release histamine within minutes.
121972.m: Mast cells trigger immediate allergic reactions.

121973.q: Where does the name “mast cell” come from?
a: They were thought to be well-fed cells
They are found mainly in the gut
They were first found in animals being fattened
They are shaped like a ship's mast
121973.e: Their discoverer believed that the cells, packed with granules, were “fattened” (German “gemästet”) and served to nourish the tissue. The name stayed, even though the idea was wrong.
121973.m: The mast cell's name comes from its fattened appearance.

121974.q: What is it called when an activated mast cell releases its stored granules?
121974.e: In degranulation, the storage granules merge with the cell membrane and release histamine and other mediators. This happens within seconds to minutes.
121974.m: An activated mast cell empties its granules by degranulation.

121975.q: Where do the precursors of mast cells develop?
121975.e: Mast cells come from blood-forming stem cells in the bone marrow. Their precursors move into the tissue and only mature there.
121975.m: The precursors of mast cells come from the bone marrow.

121976.q: What is a disease called in which mast cells multiply abnormally and build up in the tissue?
121976.e: In mastocytosis, mast cells build up in the skin, bone marrow or other organs. Those affected have a higher risk of severe allergic reactions.
121976.m: In mastocytosis there are too many mast cells.

121977.q: Which medicines block the effect of histamine from mast cells, for example in hay fever?
121977.e: Antihistamines occupy the histamine receptors so that the released histamine has less effect. Sneezing, itching and watery eyes ease off.
121977.m: Antihistamines damp down the effect of histamine.

121978.q: Which life-threatening reaction can occur when very many mast cells throughout the body release histamine at the same time?
121978.e: In anaphylaxis, the blood vessels throughout the body widen, blood pressure falls and the airways can swell shut. It is treated immediately with adrenaline.
121978.m: A massive release of histamine can trigger anaphylactic shock.

121979.q: What is hyposensitisation also called in technical language?
121979.e: In specific immunotherapy, the body receives the allergen that causes the problem in increasing doses. The aim is for the immune system to tolerate the substance again.

121980.q: How long does hyposensitisation usually last?
121980.e: So that the immune system changes for the long term, specialist societies recommend treatment for about three to five years. Shorter treatments work for less long.
121980.m: Hyposensitisation needs several years of patience.

121981.q: How is the allergen given in sublingual immunotherapy?
121981.e: Sublingual means “under the tongue”. Drops or tablets with the allergen are absorbed there instead of being injected.
121981.m: In sublingual therapy, the allergen goes under the tongue.

121982.q: For which allergy is hyposensitisation carried out especially often?
121982.e: Hay fever caused by grass or tree pollen is one of the most common allergies. Hyposensitisation can clearly ease the symptoms for years.
121982.m: Hay fever is often treated with hyposensitisation.

121983.q: Which messenger substance causes itching, sneezing and swelling in an allergic reaction?
121983.e: On contact with the allergen, mast cells release histamine. It widens vessels and irritates nerves, which causes the typical symptoms.
121983.m: Histamine causes the typical allergy symptoms.

121984.q: Why do patients usually have to stay at the surgery for about 30 minutes after a hyposensitisation injection?
a: Because of the risk of anaphylaxis
Because the allergen first has to take effect
So that the doctor can lower the blood pressure
Because the injection is removed again
121984.e: The injection contains the allergen and can rarely trigger a severe allergic reaction. Such reactions usually happen early and can then be treated immediately.
121984.m: After the injection, you wait at the surgery because of possible anaphylaxis.

121985.q: For which allergy is hyposensitisation especially effective and can even save lives?
121985.e: In insect venom allergies, the treatment protects most of those treated from severe reactions if they are stung again. It is not suitable for the other complaints named.
121985.m: Hyposensitisation works especially well against insect venom allergy.

121986.q: What is the first phase of hyposensitisation called, in which the dose of allergen is gradually increased?
121986.e: First the dose is increased up to the maximum dose. Then comes the maintenance phase with a constant dose at longer intervals.
121986.m: Hyposensitisation starts with the build-up phase.

a: An inherited tendency to make IgE against substances in the environment
An allergy that only occurs in adults
An inflammation of the joints caused by autoantibodies
An inborn inability to make antibodies
121987.e: People with atopy make IgE more easily against harmless substances such as pollen or house dust mites. This can lead to hay fever, asthma or eczema.
121987.m: Atopy is an inherited readiness for IgE-driven allergies.

121988.q: Which condition usually comes first in the so-called “atopic march”?
121988.e: The atopic march often begins in infancy with atopic eczema. Later, food allergies, hay fever and asthma can follow.
121988.m: The atopic march usually starts with atopic eczema.

121989.q: What does the Greek word “atopia”, from which the term atopy comes, mean?
a: Being out of place or unusual
121989.e: Atopia literally means “without a place” and referred to something unusual. In 1923 Coca and Cooke chose the word for the strange oversensitivity to harmless substances.

121990.q: What does the hygiene hypothesis say about how allergies develop?
a: Little contact with microbes in childhood increases the risk of allergy
Allergies are passed on by bacteria
121990.e: The hypothesis assumes that the immune system must get to know many microbes early on. If this contact is missing, it is later more likely to react to harmless substances.
121990.m: Early contact with microbes probably protects against allergies.

121991.q: According to studies from Switzerland, Austria and Germany, which children have allergies less often?
a: Children from traditional farms with livestock
Children from flats in big cities
Children who have never had pets
121991.e: Studies such as the ALEX study showed that early contact with cowsheds and raw milk lowers the risk of allergy. This is explained by the variety of microbes in the surroundings.
121991.m: Farm children get allergies less often.

121992.q: Against which substances do people with atopy typically develop allergies?
121992.e: In atopy, the immune system reacts with IgE to substances in the environment that are actually harmless, such as pollen, animal hair or house dust mites.
121992.m: People with atopy react to harmless substances in the environment.

121993.q: Which skin test is often used to check which allergens someone reacts to?
121993.e: In the skin prick test, drops containing allergens are put on the forearm and the skin is pricked lightly. If a weal forms, the person is sensitised.
121993.m: The skin prick test shows allergies on the skin.

121994.q: Which term describes the rise in allergies in industrialised countries since the middle of the 20th century?
121994.e: In many industrialised countries, the share of people with hay fever and asthma has risen sharply. Experts therefore speak of an allergy epidemic.
121994.m: Allergies have risen sharply in industrialised countries.

121995.q: Which feature typically distinguishes bronchial asthma from COPD?
a: The narrowing of the airways is largely reversible
Asthma only affects the air sacs
Asthma is always caused by smoking
There is no inflammation at all in asthma
121995.e: In asthma, the narrowing of the bronchi improves clearly on its own or with medicines. In COPD it largely remains.
121995.m: In asthma, the narrowing of the airways is reversible.

121996.q: Which spirometry value shows how much air you can breathe out forcefully in the first second?
121996.e: FEV1 stands for forced expiratory volume in one second. During an asthma attack this value drops considerably.

121997.q: Which simple device can people with asthma use to monitor their breathing at home?
121997.e: The peak flow meter measures the highest speed at which you can breathe out. Falling values give early warning of things getting worse.
121997.m: A peak flow meter is used to check asthma at home.

121998.q: Which substance is a typical short-acting reliever inhaler that quickly widens the bronchi during an asthma attack?
121998.e: Salbutamol is a beta-2 agonist and relaxes the muscles of the bronchi within a few minutes. It eases the attack but does not treat the inflammation.
121998.m: Salbutamol quickly widens the bronchi when you are short of breath.

121999.q: Which group of medicines treats the inflammation of the airways in asthma in the long term?
121999.e: Inhaled corticosteroids damp down the chronic inflammation directly in the bronchi. They are taken regularly, even when there are no symptoms.
121999.m: Inhaled steroids fight the inflammation in asthma.

122000.q: What is a severe asthma attack called that does not ease despite the usual emergency medicines?
122000.e: In status asthmaticus, the severe breathlessness continues and can become life-threatening. It must be treated in hospital.
122000.m: A severe asthma attack that does not end is called status asthmaticus.

122001.q: Which whistling breathing sound when breathing out is typical of an asthma attack?
122001.e: Wheezing happens when air is forced through narrowed small bronchi. It is heard mainly when breathing out.
122001.m: Whistling wheezing when breathing out is typical of asthma.

122002.q: Why should you rinse your mouth after inhaling a steroid spray for asthma?
a: To prevent a fungal infection in the mouth
So that the spray works more strongly
To prevent tooth decay from sugar
So that the bronchi widen faster
122002.e: Some of the steroid stays in the mouth and throat and weakens the local defence there. Rinsing prevents fungal infections and hoarseness.
122002.m: Rinse your mouth after using a steroid spray.

122003.q: Which white blood cells are typically found in greater numbers in the phlegm in allergic asthma?
122003.e: In allergic asthma, eosinophil granulocytes move into the wall of the bronchi and keep the inflammation going. Their number is raised in the sputum and often in the blood too.
122003.m: In allergic asthma, eosinophils are increased.

122004.q: Which antibody class triggers immediate-type allergy?
122004.e: In immediate-type allergy, IgE antibodies sit on mast cells. When the allergen meets them, the mast cells release histamine.
122004.m: Immediate-type allergies are triggered by IgE.

122005.q: How quickly does an immediate-type allergy typically start after contact with the allergen?
a: After about one to two days
122005.e: Because the IgE is already waiting on the mast cells, histamine is released almost at once. That is why this form is called the immediate type.

122006.q: What is the most severe form of immediate-type allergy, affecting the whole body, called?
122006.e: In anaphylactic shock, blood pressure and circulation drop, and the airways can swell shut. Without quick treatment it can be fatal.
122006.m: Anaphylactic shock is the most severe immediate-type reaction.

122007.q: Which medicine is the most important emergency treatment for anaphylactic shock?
122007.e: Adrenaline narrows the blood vessels, stabilises the circulation and widens the bronchi. People at risk therefore often carry an adrenaline auto-injector.

122008.q: Which skin test is most often used to check for an immediate-type allergy?
122008.e: In the skin prick test, a drop of allergen solution is put on the skin and the skin is pricked lightly. A weal after about 15 to 20 minutes points to sensitisation.
122008.m: The skin prick test shows immediate-type allergies on the skin.

122009.q: Why can someone with a birch pollen allergy get a tingling in the mouth when eating a raw apple?
a: Because of a cross-allergy caused by similar proteins
Because apples produce a lot of histamine
Because of poisoning from fruit acid
122009.e: The main birch allergen resembles a protein in apples, so the IgE recognises both. Cooking usually destroys this apple protein.
122009.m: Birch pollen allergy and apple allergy are often cross-allergies.

122010.q: What is the inflammation called that can appear again a few hours after the first immediate-type reaction?
122010.e: Besides histamine, mast cells also make substances that attract inflammatory cells. These cause a second wave of symptoms hours later.
122010.m: A late-phase reaction can follow the immediate reaction.

122011.q: Why does an allergy usually only show itself at repeated contact with the allergen?
a: At the first contact, the body first has to make the matching antibodies
At the first contact, the allergen is still too small
The body does not notice the first contact at all
Allergens are excreted at once the first time
122011.e: At the first contact, the immune system is sensitised and makes IgE. Only at a later contact does the allergic reaction happen.

122012.q: What does the word “allergy” literally mean in Greek?
122012.e: Allergy comes from the Greek allos for “other” and ergon for “activity”. It means a changed reaction of the body to substances that are actually harmless.
122012.m: Allergy literally means a different reaction.

122013.q: Which joints are typically affected first, and on both sides, in rheumatoid arthritis?
a: The knuckles and middle finger joints
The joints of the lower spine
122013.e: The inflammation usually begins symmetrically in the small joints of the hands. The joints nearest the fingertips, by contrast, are typically spared.
122013.m: Rheumatoid arthritis first affects the knuckles and middle finger joints.

122014.q: Which pattern of complaints in the morning is typical of rheumatoid arthritis?
a: Long-lasting morning stiffness of the joints
122014.e: The inflamed joints are often stiff for more than half an hour in the morning. In osteoarthritis, stiffness when getting going usually lasts only a few minutes.
122014.m: Long morning stiffness points to rheumatoid arthritis.

122015.q: To which kind of disease does rheumatoid arthritis belong?
a: Inherited diseases caused by a single gene
122015.e: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system wrongly attacks the body's own tissue in the joints. This leads to lasting inflammation.
122015.m: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the body's own joints.

122016.q: What fundamentally distinguishes rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis?
a: It is an inflammation, not wear and tear
It is caused by an accident
It only affects the bones, never the joints
122016.e: Osteoarthritis develops through wear of the cartilage. Rheumatoid arthritis, on the other hand, is an inflammatory disease of the immune system.
122016.m: Arthritis means inflammation, osteoarthritis means wear and tear.

122017.q: Why should rheumatoid arthritis be treated as early as possible?
a: So that the joints are not permanently destroyed
Because otherwise it turns into osteoarthritis
Because medicines are banned later on
122017.e: The inflammation gradually attacks cartilage and bone. Early treatment slows this process and keeps the joints moving.
122017.m: If treated early, the joints stay healthy for longer.

122018.q: What do most medicines against rheumatoid arthritis do?
a: They damp down the overactive immune system
They kill bacteria in the joint
122018.e: Because the immune system attacks the joints, the medicines slow down the defence in a targeted way. As a result, inflammation, pain and swelling ease.
122018.m: Medicines for rheumatism slow down the immune system.

122019.q: Which tissue layer in the joint is inflamed first in rheumatoid arthritis?
a: The inner lining of the joint
The outer lining of the bone
The tendon sheath of the calf
122019.e: The inflamed inner lining of the joint (synovium) grows excessively and forms what is known as pannus. This gradually destroys cartilage and bone.
122019.m: Rheumatoid arthritis starts in the inner lining of the joint.

122020.q: Who gets rheumatoid arthritis more often?
122020.e: Women are affected about two to three times more often than men. The disease usually starts in middle adulthood.
122020.m: More women than men get rheumatoid arthritis.

122021.q: What are the firm lumps under the skin called that appear in some people with rheumatoid arthritis on outer surfaces such as the elbow?
122021.e: Rheumatoid nodules are inflamed lumps of tissue at places under pressure. Heberden's nodes, by contrast, belong to osteoarthritis of the joints nearest the fingertips.
122021.m: Rheumatoid nodules often sit on the elbows.

122022.q: Which skin sign on the face is typical of systemic lupus erythematosus?
122022.e: The redness stretches across the cheeks and the bridge of the nose and looks like a butterfly. It often gets worse after exposure to the sun.
122022.m: A butterfly rash on the face is typical of lupus.

122023.q: What are many autoantibodies directed against in systemic lupus erythematosus?
a: Parts of the cell nucleus such as DNA
122023.e: In lupus, the immune system makes antibodies against parts of the body's own cell nuclei. Antibodies against double-stranded DNA are especially typical.
122023.m: In lupus, antibodies attack parts of the body's own cell nuclei.

122024.q: Which screening test for autoantibodies against cell nuclei is almost always positive in lupus?
122024.e: Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are found in almost all patients with systemic lupus. A negative test therefore makes the diagnosis very unlikely.
122024.m: In lupus, antinuclear antibodies can almost always be detected.

122025.q: What does the Latin word “lupus” in the name of the disease mean?
122025.e: The name dates back to the Middle Ages, when skin ulcers were compared to wolf bites. Erythematosus means “reddened”.
122025.m: Lupus is the Latin word for wolf.

122026.q: Roughly how many out of ten people with systemic lupus erythematosus are women?
122026.e: Lupus affects women around nine times more often than men. It usually starts in young adulthood.

122027.q: How do most medicines against lupus work?
a: They damp down the immune system
122027.e: Because the immune system turns against the body itself, it is slowed down with drugs such as hydroxychloroquine, cortisone or other immunosuppressants.
122027.m: In lupus, the immune system is damped down.

122028.q: What is the dangerous organ involvement called in which lupus attacks the kidneys?
122028.e: In lupus nephritis, immune complexes are deposited in the filtering units of the kidneys and inflame them. Without treatment, kidney function can fail.

122029.q: Which environmental factor can trigger skin rashes and flare-ups in lupus?
122029.e: Many people with lupus are sensitive to light. UV light damages skin cells, whose parts then stimulate the misguided immune system.
122029.m: In lupus, consistent sun protection is important.

122030.q: How does lupus caused by medicines usually develop?
a: It fades after the drug is stopped
It gets worse and worse over time
It is passed on to the children
122030.e: Substances such as hydralazine or procainamide can cause lupus symptoms. After the drug is stopped, these usually disappear.
122030.m: Drug-induced lupus usually fades after the drug is stopped.

122031.q: What kind of disease is Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
a: An autoimmune disease of the thyroid
A viral infection of the liver
An iodine deficiency of the adrenal gland
A bacterial infection of the lungs
122031.e: In Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the body's own immune system attacks the thyroid. It becomes chronically inflamed and is gradually destroyed.
122031.m: Hashimoto's is an autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid.

122032.q: Against which thyroid enzyme are the typical antibodies in Hashimoto's thyroiditis directed?
122032.e: Anti-TPO antibodies are directed against thyroid peroxidase, which builds iodine into the thyroid hormones. They are raised in most of those affected.
122032.m: In Hashimoto's, antibodies against thyroid peroxidase are found.

122033.q: Which disorder of function does Hashimoto's thyroiditis usually lead to in the long run?
122033.e: The immune system gradually destroys the thyroid tissue. As a result, too few hormones are made.
122033.m: Hashimoto's usually leads to an underactive thyroid.

122034.q: How is an underactive thyroid caused by Hashimoto's thyroiditis treated?
122034.e: The missing hormone T4 is replaced with a tablet. The treatment usually lasts for life.
122034.m: In Hashimoto's, the missing thyroid hormone is replaced.

122035.q: How does the TSH level in the blood change when Hashimoto's thyroiditis has led to an underactive thyroid?
a: It drops to zero every day
122035.e: The pituitary gland notices the lack of hormone and releases more TSH to drive the thyroid. A raised TSH is therefore an early sign.
122035.m: With an underactive thyroid, TSH is raised.

122036.q: Which cells are found in huge numbers in the thyroid tissue in Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
122036.e: The tissue is densely filled with lymphocytes, some of which form real lymph follicles. That is why the disease is also called chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis.
122036.m: In Hashimoto's, lymphocytes move into the thyroid.

122037.q: Which complaint typically fits an underactive thyroid in Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
122037.e: Without enough thyroid hormone, the metabolism runs more slowly; you feel cold easily, are tired and put on weight. A racing heart and trembling fit an overactive thyroid better.
122037.m: With an underactive thyroid, you feel cold easily.

122038.q: In countries with enough iodine, such as Switzerland, what is the most common cause of an underactive thyroid?
122038.e: Because table salt in Switzerland is iodised, iodine deficiency hardly plays a role any more. The most common cause is then Hashimoto's autoimmune inflammation.
122038.m: Where there is enough iodine, Hashimoto's is the most common cause of an underactive thyroid.

a: The body's own antibodies constantly stimulate the thyroid
A lack of iodine makes the thyroid shrink
A tumour of the pituitary gland makes too much TSH
122039.e: Graves' disease is an autoimmune disease. Antibodies imitate the control hormone TSH and drive the thyroid constantly, so that it becomes overactive.
122039.m: In Graves' disease, antibodies constantly stimulate the thyroid.

122040.q: Which three signs are typical of Graves' disease (known in German as Basedow's disease)?
a: Goitre, bulging eyes and a racing heart
Thirst, needing to pass urine and weight gain
122040.e: In 1840 Carl von Basedow described the enlarged thyroid, the bulging eyes and the fast pulse. Not all patients show all three signs.
122040.m: Goitre, bulging eyes and a racing heart are typical of Graves' disease.

122041.q: Which trace element does the thyroid need to make its hormones?
122041.e: Thyroid hormones such as thyroxine contain iodine atoms. That is why iodine is added to table salt in Switzerland.
122041.m: Without iodine, the thyroid cannot make hormones.

122042.q: What makes the eye involvement in Graves' disease clearly worse?
122042.e: In Graves' disease, tissue and muscles behind the eye swell and push it forward. Smoking makes this inflammation clearly worse.
122042.m: Smoking worsens the eye involvement in Graves' disease.

122043.q: What are medicines called that slow down hormone production by the thyroid in Graves' disease?
122043.e: Antithyroid drugs such as thiamazole block the building of iodine into the thyroid hormones. As a result, hormone production falls.
122043.m: Antithyroid drugs slow down the overactive thyroid.

122044.q: Which treatment for Graves' disease destroys thyroid tissue in a targeted way using a radioactive substance?
122044.e: The thyroid takes up the radioactive iodine-131, which irradiates it from the inside. In this way the overactivity is ended permanently.
122044.m: Radioiodine therapy makes use of the thyroid's uptake of iodine.

122045.q: What is the TSH level like in an overactive thyroid caused by Graves' disease?
a: It is raised but cannot be measured
122045.e: The large amounts of thyroid hormones inhibit the pituitary gland, which therefore releases hardly any TSH. The antibodies still keep driving the thyroid.
122045.m: In Graves' disease, TSH is suppressed.

122046.q: Which complaint typically fits the overactive thyroid in Graves' disease?
122046.e: The metabolism runs at full speed, so those affected lose weight despite a good appetite. Restlessness, sweating and trembling often come on top.
122046.m: With an overactive thyroid, you lose weight despite your appetite.

122047.q: Which defence cells trigger a contact allergy?
122047.e: Contact allergy is driven by T cells, not by antibodies. It therefore belongs to the delayed-type allergies (type IV).
122047.m: In contact allergy, T cells are at work.

122048.q: Which substance is one of the most common causes of contact allergy in Europe?
122048.e: Nickel is found in costume jewellery, belt buckles and buttons. That is why European law limits how much nickel such objects may release.
122048.m: Nickel is a very common cause of contact allergy.

122049.q: Which test is used to detect a contact allergy?
122049.e: In the patch test, test substances are stuck onto the back with plasters. The result is read after about two to three days.
122049.m: Contact allergies are detected with the patch test.

122050.q: How long after contact does it usually take for allergic contact eczema to become visible?
122050.e: T cells first have to move to the spot and release messenger substances. That is why the eczema appears with a delay.
122050.m: Contact eczema only shows after days.

122051.q: What are small molecules called that only become a complete allergen by binding to the body's own proteins?
122051.e: Haptens such as nickel ions are too small on their own to trigger an immune response. Bound to skin proteins, they are recognised by T cells.
122051.m: Haptens only become allergens together with proteins.

122052.q: Which component of cement used to cause “bricklayer's itch” (cement eczema) very often?
122052.e: Hexavalent chromium in cement is a strong contact allergen. Since cement has been made low in chromate, bricklayer's itch has become rarer.
122052.m: Chromate in cement causes bricklayer's itch.

122053.q: Why do experts warn against “black henna” for temporary tattoos?
a: It can cause a strong contact allergy
It colours the skin for ever
It makes the skin sensitive to light as with sunburn
122053.e: The dye p-phenylenediamine (PPD) is often added to black henna. It can cause severe eczema and a lifelong allergy, for example to hair dyes.
122053.m: Black henna can cause a lifelong contact allergy.

122054.q: Apart from preservatives, which group of substances in cosmetics causes contact allergies especially often?
122054.e: Fragrances are among the most common contact allergens. In the patch test, several of them are tested together as a fragrance mix.
122054.m: Fragrances are among the common contact allergens.

122055.q: At which receptor do the classic antihistamines against allergies act?
122055.e: Anti-allergy antihistamines occupy the H1 receptor so that histamine has less effect there. Itching, sneezing and weals ease.
122055.m: Anti-allergy antihistamines act at the H1 receptor.

122056.q: Which side effect is especially common with first-generation antihistamines?
122056.e: Older antihistamines easily reach the brain and reduce alertness there. Newer substances hardly cross the blood-brain barrier.
122056.m: Old antihistamines often make you drowsy.

122057.q: Which substance is a second-generation antihistamine?
122057.e: Cetirizine makes you much less drowsy than older first-generation substances. It is often used for hay fever.
122057.m: Cetirizine is a modern antihistamine that causes little drowsiness.

122058.q: What are H2 antihistamines such as famotidine used for?
122058.e: H2 receptors are found, among other places, on the acid-producing cells of the stomach. If they are blocked, less acid is made.

122059.q: Which Swiss-born pharmacologist received the Nobel Prize in 1957, partly for developing the first antihistamines?
122059.e: Daniel Bovet was born in 1907 in Fleurier in the canton of Neuchâtel. He researched the first antihistamines in Paris and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1957.
122059.m: Daniel Bovet from Neuchâtel was a pioneer of antihistamines.

122060.q: What is the antihistamine dimenhydrinate often taken for?
122060.e: Dimenhydrinate damps down the vomiting centre and the organ of balance. It is therefore taken before car or boat journeys.

122061.q: Which first-generation antihistamine is contained in many over-the-counter sleeping pills because of its sedating effect?
122061.e: Diphenhydramine easily reaches the brain and blocks H1 receptors there, which promote alertness. This side effect is used on purpose in sleeping pills.
122061.m: Diphenhydramine is used as a sleeping aid because it makes you drowsy.

122062.q: In an allergy, which cells release the histamine whose effect antihistamines slow down?
122062.e: Mast cells sit in the skin and mucous membranes and store histamine in granules. When an allergen binds to their IgE antibodies, they release the histamine.
122062.m: Mast cells release histamine in allergies.

122063.q: What does the acronym “laser” stand for?
a: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Absorption by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation
Linear Amplification by Synchronized Electron Radiation
Light Acceleration by Stimulated Electron Resonance
122063.e: A laser amplifies light through the stimulated emission of radiation. The initial letters of these words form its name.
122063.m: Laser means light amplification by stimulated emission.

122064.q: Which physical process, described in theory by Albert Einstein in 1917, is the basis of the laser?
122064.e: An incoming photon prompts an excited atom to emit a second photon of the same kind. In this way light with the same direction, frequency and phase is multiplied.
122064.m: The laser is based on stimulated emission.

122065.q: Which condition must exist in the active medium of a laser for light to be amplified?
122065.e: In a population inversion there are more particles in the excited state than in the lower state. Only then does stimulated emission outweigh absorption.
122065.m: Without population inversion a laser cannot amplify.

122066.q: What is the job of a laser's resonator, which usually consists of two mirrors?
a: It makes the light pass through the active medium many times
It splits the light into colours
122066.e: The light bounces back and forth between the mirrors and is amplified further on each pass. One of the mirrors is partly transparent and lets the beam out.
122066.m: In the resonator the laser light is amplified again and again.

122067.q: Which two properties most clearly distinguish laser light from the light of a filament bulb?
a: It is coherent and almost a single colour
122067.e: Laser light has a fixed phase relationship (coherence) and a very narrow wavelength. A filament bulb, by contrast, emits a broad spectrum with no fixed phase.
122067.m: Laser light is coherent and monochromatic.

122068.q: What colour is the light of a classic helium-neon laser, as used in physics lessons?
122068.e: The helium-neon laser shines red, at a wavelength of about 633 nm. Green laser pointers, by contrast, mostly use frequency-doubled solid-state lasers.

122069.q: Roughly how much energy does a photon from a green laser with a wavelength of 532 nm have (using E in eV ≈ 1240 / λ in nm)?
122069.e: 1240 divided by 532 gives about 2.33 eV. This rule of thumb follows from E = h·c/λ.
122069.m: A shorter wavelength means more energetic photons.

122070.q: What is the name of the forerunner of the laser, which amplifies microwaves instead of light using the same principle?
122070.e: Charles Townes and colleagues built the first maser using ammonia molecules in 1954. The M stands for microwave.
122070.m: The maser amplifies microwaves using the laser principle.

122071.q: According to the Rayleigh criterion, which formula describes the smallest resolvable angle of a telescope with a circular aperture D?
122071.e: Two points count as separate if the maximum of one diffraction pattern falls on the first minimum of the other. This gives θ ≈ 1.22 λ/D in radians.
122071.m: The larger the aperture, the finer the resolution.

122072.q: One telescope has a mirror twice as large as another. According to the Rayleigh criterion, how does the smallest resolvable angle change?
122072.e: According to the Rayleigh criterion, θ ≈ 1.22 · λ / D. The angle is inversely proportional to the diameter, so a mirror twice as large separates details twice as fine.
122072.m: The larger the aperture, the finer the resolution.

122073.q: Which German physicist worked out the resolution limit of the light microscope in 1873?
122073.e: Ernst Abbe showed that the smallest resolvable structure is about λ/(2·NA). He worked closely with Carl Zeiss in Jena.
122073.m: Ernst Abbe found the resolution limit of the microscope.

122074.q: According to Abbe, the smallest resolvable distance is d = λ / (2 · NA). What is d for light of 500 nm and a numerical aperture NA = 1.25?
122074.e: d = 500 nm / (2 · 1.25) = 500 nm / 2.5 = 200 nm. Smaller structures blur in an ordinary light microscope.
122074.m: Light microscopes can hardly resolve below 200 nanometres.

122075.q: Why does immersion oil between the objective and the specimen improve a microscope's resolution?
a: It shortens the focal length of the eyepiece
It makes the light source stronger
122075.e: The oil has a higher refractive index than air, so even slanting light rays get into the objective. This raises the numerical aperture n·sin α.
122075.m: Immersion oil increases the numerical aperture.

122076.q: Roughly what angle can a healthy human eye just about resolve?
122076.e: An eye with normal vision separates two points that are about one arcminute apart. This corresponds to a visual acuity of 1.0.
122076.m: The eye resolves about one arcminute.

122077.q: In principle, how can you improve the resolving power of a microscope?
a: With light of a shorter wavelength
With brighter light of the same colour
122077.e: The diffraction limit is proportional to the wavelength. Blue or ultraviolet light therefore resolves finer structures than red light.

122078.q: Why do electron microscopes achieve a much finer resolution than light microscopes?
a: Electrons have a much smaller wavelength than light
122078.e: The electron microscope is also limited by diffraction. But fast electrons have a wavelength many thousands of times smaller than that of visible light.
122078.m: A smaller wavelength means finer resolution.

122079.q: Why can an electron microscope show much finer details than a light microscope?
a: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light
Electrons are larger than particles of light
122079.e: Resolving power depends on the wavelength. Fast electrons have a wavelength a thousand times shorter than that of visible light.
122079.m: A shorter wavelength allows finer resolution.

122080.q: What is used to focus the electron beams in an electron microscope?
122080.e: Coils carrying a current create magnetic fields that deflect moving electrons. In this way they act like converging lenses.
122080.m: Electron microscopes focus with magnetic fields.

122081.q: Why must there be a high vacuum inside an electron microscope?
a: Air molecules would scatter the electrons
Electrons only form in a vacuum
122081.e: Electrons easily collide with gas molecules and are deflected. Without a vacuum the beam would be blurred or stopped completely.
122081.m: An electron beam needs a high vacuum.

122082.q: Roughly what is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V?
122082.e: λ = h / √(2·m·e·U) = 6.63·10^-34 / √(2 · 9.11·10^-31 · 1.60·10^-19 · 100) ≈ 1.23·10^-10 m. That is several thousand times shorter than visible light.
122082.m: Fast electrons have very short wavelengths.

122083.q: What does a scanning electron microscope typically detect to produce an image of the surface?
122083.e: The finely focused electron beam scans the surface point by point and knocks out secondary electrons. Their number gives the brightness of each pixel.
122083.m: The scanning electron microscope uses knocked-out secondary electrons.

122084.q: Which Swiss biophysicist from the University of Lausanne won the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for cryo-electron microscopy?
122084.e: Jacques Dubochet developed a way of freezing water so quickly that it sets like glass instead of forming crystals. This allows biomolecules to be imaged in their natural shape in the electron microscope.
122084.m: Jacques Dubochet made cryo-electron microscopy possible.

122085.q: Why must samples for a transmission electron microscope be extremely thin?
a: The electrons have to pass through them
So that they do not evaporate in the vacuum
So that they fit in the sample holder
122085.e: Electrons are strongly scattered and absorbed by matter. Only slices from a few to about a hundred nanometres thick let enough electrons through.
122085.m: In a TEM the electrons must pass through the sample.

122086.q: How does the wavelength of the electrons change if you increase the accelerating voltage?
a: It first gets longer, then shorter
122086.e: A higher voltage gives the electrons more momentum, and according to de Broglie λ = h/p. This increases the possible resolving power.
122086.m: More voltage means shorter electron waves.

122087.q: Where was the scanning tunnelling microscope developed in 1981?
a: At the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon
At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen
122087.e: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer built the device at the IBM research laboratory near Zurich. It was the first microscope to make individual atoms on surfaces visible.
122087.m: The scanning tunnelling microscope comes from the IBM lab in Rüschlikon.

122088.q: Which quantum mechanical effect is the scanning tunnelling microscope based on?
122088.e: Electrons can cross a narrow gap between the tip and the sample even though, classically, their energy would not be enough. The current that flows is called the tunnelling current.
122088.m: The scanning tunnelling microscope uses the tunnelling effect.

122089.q: How does the tunnelling current depend on the distance between the tip and the sample?
a: It does not depend on distance
It falls with the square of the distance
122089.e: A change in distance of only about 0.1 nm changes the current by roughly an order of magnitude. This sensitivity makes atomic resolution possible.
122089.m: The tunnelling current reacts exponentially to distance.

122090.q: What condition must a sample meet for the classic scanning tunnelling microscope?
122090.e: A tunnelling current must be able to flow between the tip and the sample. Insulators cannot be studied directly in this way.
122090.m: A scanning tunnelling microscope needs conducting samples.

122091.q: What moves the fine tip of a scanning tunnelling microscope with atomic precision?
122091.e: Piezo crystals expand by tiny, easily controlled amounts when a voltage is applied. This lets the tip be moved by fractions of a nanometre.
122091.m: Piezo elements move the tip with atomic precision.

122092.q: What did Don Eigler manage to do for the first time with a scanning tunnelling microscope in 1989?
a: Split an atom into two halves
122092.e: Eigler pushed individual xenon atoms into place on a nickel surface with the tip, spelling out the letters “IBM”. It was the first deliberate arrangement of individual atoms.
122092.m: With a scanning tunnelling microscope you can move individual atoms.

122093.q: Which device did Gerd Binnig, Calvin Quate and Christoph Gerber develop in 1986 to scan non-conducting samples with atomic precision too?
122093.e: The atomic force microscope measures the forces between a fine tip and the sample instead of a current. That is why it also works with insulators and biological samples.
122093.m: The atomic force microscope can scan insulators too.

122094.q: Ideally, how should the tip of a scanning tunnelling microscope end?
a: In a ball one millimetre across
In a bundle of carbon fibres
122094.e: Because the current depends so strongly on distance, it flows almost only through the frontmost atom. The sharper the tip, the sharper the image.
122094.m: A good tunnelling tip ends in a single atom.

122095.q: In which canton was the physicist Heinrich Rohrer born in 1933?
122095.e: Heinrich Rohrer was born in 1933 in Buchs in the St Gallen Rhine Valley. He later became one of the best-known Swiss physicists.
122095.m: Heinrich Rohrer came from Buchs in the canton of St Gallen.

122096.q: In which year did Heinrich Rohrer win the Nobel Prize in Physics?
122096.e: Rohrer and Gerd Binnig were honoured in 1986 for the scanning tunnelling microscope, only five years after it was developed.
122096.m: Heinrich Rohrer won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.

122097.q: Which two famous physicists did Heinrich Rohrer attend lectures by as a student?
122097.e: Rohrer began studying physics in 1951 and learned from Wolfgang Pauli and Paul Scherrer. Both shaped physics in Zurich for decades.
122097.m: Heinrich Rohrer studied under Wolfgang Pauli and Paul Scherrer.

122098.q: At which university did Heinrich Rohrer study and earn his doctorate?
122098.e: Rohrer studied physics at ETH Zurich from 1951 and also wrote his doctoral thesis there in low-temperature physics.
122098.m: Heinrich Rohrer was a graduate of ETH Zurich.

122099.q: For which invention did Heinrich Rohrer win the Nobel Prize together with Gerd Binnig?
122099.e: Rohrer and Binnig developed the scanning tunnelling microscope in 1981 at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon. For the first time it made it possible to image individual atoms on surfaces.
122099.m: Heinrich Rohrer co-invented the scanning tunnelling microscope.

122100.q: Which field of research did Heinrich Rohrer work on in his doctoral thesis at ETH?
122100.e: Rohrer studied changes in the length of superconductors as they passed into the superconducting state. Only later did he turn to surface physics.
122100.m: Heinrich Rohrer began his research with superconductors.

122101.q: Which field did Heinrich Rohrer's invention help to move forward decisively?
122101.e: With the scanning tunnelling microscope it became possible for the first time to image and move individual atoms. This is seen as one of the starting points of nanotechnology.
122101.m: Rohrer's microscope opened the door to nanotechnology.

122102.q: In which year did Heinrich Rohrer die?
122102.e: Heinrich Rohrer died in 2013 at the age of 79 in Wollerau in the canton of Schwyz. To the end he championed the nanosciences.

122103.q: Where is the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope?
122103.e: The VLT stands in the Atacama Desert in northern Chile at an altitude of about 2,600 m. The air there is very dry and the sky is almost always clear.
122103.m: The Very Large Telescope stands in Chile's Atacama Desert.

122104.q: Which organisation runs the Very Large Telescope?
122104.e: ESO is an intergovernmental organisation for ground-based astronomy. Switzerland has been a member since 1982.
122104.m: The VLT belongs to the European Southern Observatory.

122105.q: How many large main telescopes make up the Very Large Telescope?
122105.e: The VLT has four main telescopes, each with a mirror 8.2 m across. There are also smaller auxiliary telescopes.
122105.m: The VLT has four large main telescopes.

122106.q: What is the diameter of the main mirror of each of the large VLT telescopes?
122106.e: Each main mirror is a single piece of glass ceramic 8.2 m across and only about 18 cm thick. Active supports keep it in shape.
122106.m: The VLT main mirrors each measure 8.2 metres.

122107.q: How does the VLT make up for the shimmering of the air that blurs images of stars?
a: With adaptive optics that constantly adjust deformable mirrors
With a dome that sucks out the air
By observing only during the day
122107.e: Sensors measure the disturbance caused by the air many hundreds of times a second. Small actuators bend a mirror so that the disturbance is cancelled out.
122107.m: Adaptive optics makes telescope images sharp despite the shimmering air.

122108.q: What is the name of the mode in which the light from several VLT telescopes is combined to achieve a much higher resolution?
122108.e: In the VLTI the light paths of the telescopes are precisely matched and overlaid. The resolution then almost equals that of a telescope as large as the distance between the mirrors.
122108.m: The VLTI links several telescopes into one interferometer.

122109.q: What did researchers prove at the centre of the Milky Way through years of observations at the VLT?
122109.e: Reinhard Genzel's team tracked the orbits of stars around Sagittarius A*. This revealed a mass of about four million solar masses in a tiny space, which earned the Nobel Prize in 2020.
122109.m: A giant black hole sits at the centre of the Milky Way.

122110.q: How large will the main mirror of the Extremely Large Telescope be, which ESO is building near the VLT?
122110.e: The ELT is being built on Cerro Armazones and will have a mirror of about 39 m made up of hundreds of segments. It will be the largest optical telescope in the world.
122110.m: The ELT will have a mirror of about 39 metres.

122111.q: When and on what was the James Webb Space Telescope launched?
a: On 24 April 2004 on a Space Shuttle
122111.e: The European Ariane 5 carried the telescope into space on Christmas Day 2021 from the spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana. The precise launch saved a lot of fuel.
122111.m: The James Webb Telescope was launched at Christmas 2021.

122112.q: How many hexagonal segments make up the main mirror of the James Webb Telescope?
122112.e: The 18 gold-coated beryllium segments together form a mirror 6.5 m across. It was folded for launch and unfolded in space.
122112.m: The Webb mirror consists of 18 segments.

122113.q: In which wavelength range does the James Webb Space Telescope mainly observe?
122113.e: Webb observes from visible red light to the mid-infrared. That is where cool objects and very distant, redshifted galaxies shine.
122113.m: The James Webb Telescope is an infrared telescope.

122114.q: Why is the James Webb Telescope's mirror coated with a thin layer of gold?
a: Gold reflects infrared light particularly well
Gold carries electricity to the instruments
122114.e: Gold reflects almost all light in the infrared. The layer is only about 100 nanometres thick, so less than 50 grams of gold were needed in total.
122114.m: Gold makes the Webb mirror a good infrared mirror.

122115.q: How many layers of foil make up the James Webb Telescope's sunshield?
122115.e: Five wafer-thin layers of coated plastic keep out the heat of the Sun and the Earth. This lets the instrument side cool to below -220 degrees Celsius.
122115.m: A five-layer sunshield keeps the Webb Telescope cold.

122116.q: Why do you need an infrared telescope to observe the first galaxies after the Big Bang?
a: Their light is strongly redshifted by the expansion of the universe
They only give off heat radiation
Visible light is faster than infrared
Infrared is amplified by the Earth's atmosphere
122116.e: While the light is travelling, space expands and stretches the waves. Ultraviolet and visible light from the early galaxies therefore reaches us as infrared.
122116.m: Light from the earliest galaxies reaches us as infrared.

122117.q: Which three space agencies built the James Webb Space Telescope together?
122117.e: NASA led the project, while the European ESA and the Canadian CSA contributed instruments and the launch. Canada supplied the fine guidance sensor, for example.
122117.m: The Webb Telescope is a joint project of NASA, ESA and CSA.

122118.q: In which year was the Hubble Space Telescope put into space?
122118.e: The Space Shuttle Discovery released Hubble into Earth orbit in April 1990. Since then it has been one of the most successful scientific instruments.
122118.m: Hubble has been in space since 1990.

122119.q: What is the diameter of the Hubble Space Telescope's main mirror?
122119.e: The 2.4 m mirror was designed to fit the Space Shuttle's cargo bay. Without the disturbing atmosphere it still delivers very sharp images.

122120.q: Which fault made the first images from the Hubble Telescope blurred?
a: Spherical aberration of the main mirror
A crack in the secondary mirror
122120.e: The mirror had been ground about 2 micrometres too flat at the edge. In 1993 the fault was fixed with corrective optics during a servicing mission.
122120.m: A wrongly ground mirror made Hubble short-sighted at first.

122121.q: Which Swiss astronaut took part in servicing missions to the Hubble Space Telescope?
122121.e: Claude Nicollier flew on the first repair mission in 1993 and operated the robotic arm. In 1999 he went out to the telescope himself during another servicing mission.

122122.q: What kind of orbit does the Hubble Space Telescope travel in?
a: In a low Earth orbit about 500 km high
In an orbit around the Moon
122122.e: Hubble circles the Earth in about 95 minutes. This low orbit allowed Space Shuttles to service the telescope.
122122.m: Hubble circles the Earth at a low altitude.

122123.q: Which astronomer is the Hubble Space Telescope named after?
122123.e: In the 1920s Edwin Hubble showed that there are galaxies outside the Milky Way and that the universe is expanding.
122123.m: The Hubble Telescope honours Edwin Hubble.

122124.q: What is the name of the famous long-exposure image from 1995, for which Hubble looked at an apparently empty patch of sky and found thousands of galaxies?
122124.e: Over ten days Hubble exposed a tiny patch of sky in the Plough. About 3,000 distant galaxies appeared on it.
122124.m: The Hubble Deep Field shows thousands of distant galaxies.

122125.q: Which important cosmological quantity did Hubble help to determine more precisely with measurements of Cepheid stars?
122125.e: Cepheids are pulsating stars whose brightness reveals their distance. With them Hubble determined the expansion rate of the universe much more precisely than before.
122125.m: Hubble improved the measurement of the expansion of the universe.

122126.q: Who invented the principle of holography in 1947 and won the Nobel Prize for it in 1971?
122126.e: The Hungarian-British physicist Dennis Gabor wanted to use it to improve the resolution of electron microscopes. Usable holograms only became possible with the laser.

122127.q: Compared with an ordinary photograph, what does a hologram also store?
a: The phase of the light wave
122127.e: A photograph only records brightness. A hologram also stores the phase through an interference pattern, and with it the spatial information.
122127.m: A hologram stores the amplitude and phase of the light.

122128.q: When a hologram is recorded, the overlapping of which two waves creates the interference pattern?
122128.e: Part of the laser light lights up the object, another part falls directly on the plate. Their overlap creates the stored pattern.
122128.m: A hologram is made from an object wave and a reference wave.

122129.q: Why is laser light used to record classic holograms?
122129.e: Only coherent light produces a stable interference pattern across the whole plate. Ordinary light has far too short a coherence length for this.

122130.q: What do you see if you break a piece off a classic transmission hologram and light it with laser light?
a: The whole image, but less sharp and from a narrower viewing angle
Only the matching section of the image
122130.e: Every point on the plate contains light from all points of the object. A fragment therefore acts like a smaller window onto the whole object.
122130.m: Every piece of a hologram contains the whole image.

122131.q: What does the Greek word part “holos” in the term holography mean?
122131.e: Holography means roughly “recording the whole”. The idea is that the complete wave information is stored.

122132.q: What are holograms used for especially often in everyday life?
a: As protection against forgery on ID cards and bank cards
122132.e: Holograms are hard to copy because making them needs a complex optical recording. That is why they protect passports, payment cards and branded products.
122132.m: Holograms are often used to prevent forgery.

122133.q: Why can holograms on ID cards and payment cards also be viewed in ordinary white light?
a: They reflect only certain colours depending on the viewing angle
They glow by themselves in the dark
They are made of a colour photo
122133.e: In reflection and embossed holograms, fine structures act like colour filters. Depending on the viewing angle, only certain light from the white light is reflected back.
122133.m: Some holograms also work with white light.

122134.q: Which famous experiment with an interferometer in 1887 found no sign of a luminiferous ether?
122134.e: Albert Michelson and Edward Morley expected the Earth's motion through the ether to shift the interference pattern. No shift appeared, which later supported the theory of relativity.
122134.m: The Michelson-Morley experiment disproved the luminiferous ether.

122135.q: Which component in a Michelson interferometer splits the light beam into two partial beams?
122135.e: The semi-transparent beam splitter lets part of the light through and reflects the rest. After reflection from two mirrors it combines the beams again.
122135.m: A beam splitter divides and recombines the light in an interferometer.

122136.q: One mirror of a Michelson interferometer is moved by 1 µm and the wavelength is 500 nm. How many interference fringes pass by?
122136.e: The light path changes by twice the mirror's movement, so by 2 µm. 2,000 nm divided by 500 nm gives 4 fringes.
122136.m: A mirror movement counts twice in the light path.

122137.q: How long are the arms of the LIGO detectors, which first detected gravitational waves in 2015?
122137.e: The two laser arms of each LIGO detector are at right angles and each 4 km long. A gravitational wave changes their length by far less than the diameter of a proton.
122137.m: LIGO measures gravitational waves with arms 4 kilometres long.

122138.q: Which physicist became the first American to win the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1907, partly for his interferometers?
122138.e: Albert Michelson was honoured for his precision optical instruments and the measurements he made with them. He also determined the speed of light very precisely.
122138.m: Albert Michelson was the first American Nobel Prize winner in physics.

122139.q: What are interferometers often used for in technology and research?
122139.e: Even a change in path of a fraction of a wavelength shifts the interference pattern. This allows lengths to be measured to within nanometres.
122139.m: Interferometers measure lengths using the wavelength of light as a scale.

122140.q: What does an interferometer show when the light path in one arm gets longer by exactly half a wavelength?
a: The image becomes twice as bright
122140.e: A path difference of half a wavelength shifts the phase by 180 degrees. Where there was constructive interference before, the waves now cancel each other out.
122140.m: A path difference of half a wavelength reverses the interference pattern.

122141.q: Why is laser light mostly used in interferometers?
a: Laser light is coherent and has practically a single wavelength
Laser light is faster than other light
Laser light is not reflected by mirrors
122141.e: A stable interference pattern needs a fixed phase relationship between the partial beams. Laser light provides this even over long path differences.
122141.m: Laser light suits interferometers because of its coherence.

122142.q: Which disturbance does adaptive optics on large telescopes make up for?
122142.e: Warm and cold layers of air constantly distort the light waves, so that stars twinkle. Adaptive optics continuously measures and corrects this distortion.
122142.m: Adaptive optics makes up for the twinkling caused by the atmosphere.

122143.q: Which component of an adaptive optics system constantly changes its shape to correct the light wave?
122143.e: Behind a thin mirror sit many small actuators. They bend the surface so that the distortion of the wave is cancelled out.
122143.m: A deformable mirror smooths out the light wave.

122144.q: What does the wavefront sensor of an adaptive optics system measure?
a: How strongly the light wave is distorted by the air
How far away the star is
How fast the telescope is turning
122144.e: The sensor constantly detects how the atmosphere distorts the light wave. From this data a computer calculates how the deformable mirror must adjust.
122144.m: The wavefront sensor measures the distortion of the light.

122145.q: How is an artificial guide star made for adaptive optics?
a: A laser makes sodium atoms about 90 km up glow
A balloon carries a lamp into the stratosphere
A satellite sends a flash of light
The Moon's light is reflected back
122145.e: The laser makes sodium atoms in the upper atmosphere glow. This bright point serves as a reference when there is no bright star near the target object.
122145.m: Laser guide stars replace missing bright stars in the sky.

122146.q: Why does a space telescope like Hubble not need adaptive optics against atmospheric turbulence?
a: Because it observes from above the Earth's atmosphere
Because it only works at night
122146.e: Atmospheric turbulence arises in the Earth's atmosphere. A telescope in space is not affected by it, but it is much more expensive than a large ground-based telescope with adaptive optics.
122146.m: There is no atmospheric turbulence in space.

122147.q: Roughly how many times a second does astronomical adaptive optics have to adjust its correction?
a: Hundreds to over a thousand times
122147.e: The turbulence in the air changes within milliseconds. That is why the system has to measure and readjust very quickly.
122147.m: Adaptive optics corrects hundreds of times a second.

122148.q: In which medical field is adaptive optics used to make individual cells visible?
122148.e: The eye also distorts light through small irregularities. With adaptive optics, individual light-sensitive cells of the retina can be imaged.
122148.m: Adaptive optics makes cells in the retina visible.

122149.q: What do astronomers call the image sharpness of a ground-based telescope that is limited by atmospheric turbulence?
122149.e: Seeing is usually given as an angle in arcseconds. At good sites it is below one arcsecond, and adaptive optics improves it further.
122149.m: Seeing describes the blurring of images by atmospheric turbulence.

122150.q: What does the abbreviation CCD stand for?
122150.e: In a charge-coupled device, the collected charges are passed on from pixel to pixel.

122151.q: Which invention from 1969 made digital cameras possible and won its inventors the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics?
122151.e: Willard Boyle and George Smith designed the CCD in 1969 at Bell Labs, originally as a memory component. It soon turned out to be excellent as an image sensor.
122151.m: The CCD sensor made digital photography possible.

122152.q: Which physical effect turns the incoming light into electric charge in a CCD pixel?
122152.e: Photons lift electrons in the silicon into the conduction band. These electrons are collected in a potential well under each pixel.
122152.m: In a CCD, light creates charges through the photoelectric effect.

122153.q: How are the charges of a CCD sensor read out?
a: They are shifted row by row to the readout amplifier
Each pixel has its own radio chip
They are scanned with a laser
122153.e: By cleverly switching voltages, the charge packets move on as in a bucket chain. At the edge they are converted into voltage one after another.
122153.m: A CCD passes the charges to the output like a bucket chain.

122154.q: Why are CCD cameras in astronomy often cooled down a lot?
a: So that heat produces fewer unwanted signals
So that the pixels become larger
So that the colours become stronger
So that the camera becomes lighter
122154.e: Heat creates electrons in the silicon even without light, which makes the image noisy. At low temperatures this so-called dark current falls sharply and faint objects become visible.
122154.m: Cooling reduces the noise of a CCD sensor.

122155.q: How does a single CCD sensor get colour information?
a: Through a colour filter mosaic such as the Bayer filter
By measuring the temperature of the pixels
122155.e: In front of the pixels lie alternating red, green and blue filters, with green appearing twice as often. The full colours are then calculated from the neighbouring pixels.
122155.m: A Bayer filter gives an image sensor colour.

122156.q: Which type of sensor has replaced the CCD sensor in most mobile phone cameras?
122156.e: CMOS sensors amplify the signal directly in each pixel, are cheaper and use less power. CCDs remain important in some scientific cameras.
122156.m: Mobile phones today mostly contain CMOS sensors.

122157.q: What happens in a CCD sensor when a very bright star heavily overexposes a pixel?
a: Charge spills over into neighbouring pixels and forms streaks
122157.e: Each pixel can only store a certain amount of charge. When it is full, the charge spills over into the neighbouring pixels along the readout direction. This is called blooming.
122157.m: Too much light makes charge in a CCD spill into neighbouring pixels.

122158.q: Which property made CCD sensors far superior to photographic film in astronomy?
a: They turn a much larger share of the light into signal
They have a much larger image area
They are insensitive to red light
122158.e: A good CCD turns a large share of the incoming photons into signal, film only a few per cent. This is called high quantum efficiency. It makes much fainter objects visible.
122158.m: CCD sensors make much better use of light than film.

122159.q: According to current research, which factor most strongly determines the position of the natural tree line worldwide?
a: Lack of warmth during the growing season
Lack of nitrogen in the soil
Air pressure that is too low
122159.e: Worldwide, the tree line lies where the growing season becomes too cool for trees to form enough new tissue. Other factors only shift the line locally.
122159.m: The tree line is mainly a warmth limit.

122160.q: Why do dwarf shrubs still grow above the tree line, but no trees?
a: Dwarf shrubs grow in the warmer zone close to the ground
All trees there are eaten by chamois
The soil there contains too much oxygen
122160.e: Tall trees reach up into the cold, windy air and are linked to the cool soil. Dwarf shrubs benefit from the warmth of the sunlit ground surface. At the tree line, the soil is only about 6 to 7 °C in summer.
122160.m: It is warmer close to the ground, which is why dwarf shrubs survive there.

122161.q: Which two tree species typically form the tree line in the central Alps, for example in the Engadine?
122161.e: Swiss stone pine and larch cope particularly well with cold and short summers. That is why they grow highest in the inner Alps.
122161.m: Swiss stone pine and larch are the trees of the tree line in the central Alps.

122162.q: Why is the tree line higher in the inner Alps, for example in Valais or the Engadine, than on the northern edge of the Alps?
a: Because of the mass elevation effect
Because of soil richer in lime
122162.e: Large connected mountain masses warm up more and have a sunnier, more continental climate. This raises the limits of warmth and vegetation.
122162.m: Large mountain masses raise the tree line.

122163.q: Roughly at what altitude is the natural tree line in the central Alps of Valais and the Grisons?
122163.e: In the inner Alps, trees grow up to about 2,200 to 2,400 m. On the northern edge of the Alps, the line is much lower.
122163.m: In the central Alps, trees grow up to over 2,000 m.

122164.q: How does the height of the tree line change from the subtropics towards the polar regions?
a: It drops until it is close to sea level
It stays the same height everywhere
122164.e: The tree line is highest in the subtropics. The further you go towards the poles, the cooler the summers, and in the subarctic trees only grow at low altitudes.
122164.m: Towards the poles, the tree line drops lower and lower.

122165.q: Which conifer, often growing like a shrub, forms a belt of crooked wood above the forest, especially on limestone?
122165.e: The dwarf mountain pine is a low-lying form of the mountain pine. Its flexible branches are pressed down by the snow without breaking.
122165.m: The dwarf mountain pine forms dense crooked wood in the mountains.

122166.q: Why is today’s forest line in many Alpine valleys lower than the tree line that the climate would allow?
a: Because of centuries of Alpine pasture farming
Because of volcanic eruptions in the Middle Ages
122166.e: For pastures, the upper forest was cleared and grazed for centuries. This artificially pushed the forest line down.
122166.m: Alpine pasture farming has lowered the forest line in many places.

122167.q: What has been observed at the tree line in the Alps in many places since the 20th century?
a: Young trees are growing further up
Trees are dying off up to 500 m lower
The tree line is completely unchanged
Broadleaved trees are pushing out the larches there
122167.e: Warmer summers and the abandonment of Alpine pastures let young trees grow higher up. That is why the tree line is rising in many places.
122167.m: With warming and less grazing, the forest is moving uphill.

122168.q: At which university did the plant ecologist Christian Körner teach as a professor for many years?
122168.e: Christian Körner headed plant ecology at the Botanical Institute of the University of Basel for decades.
122168.m: Christian Körner did research as a professor in Basel.

122169.q: Which standard work on the ecology of high mountain plants was written by Christian Körner?
122169.e: “Alpine Plant Life” sums up how plants function in high mountains and is a textbook used worldwide.
122169.m: Körner’s textbook is called “Alpine Plant Life”.

122170.q: According to Christian Körner, which factor mainly determines the position of the natural tree line worldwide?
a: The temperature during the growing season
122170.e: Körner showed that the tree line worldwide lies at similarly low temperatures during the growing season. Trees can then no longer build enough new tissue.
122170.m: The tree line is determined mainly by temperature.

122171.q: What was the crane in the forest at Hofstetten near Basel, where Körner's group did research, used for?
a: For adding CO2 to tree crowns
122171.e: With the Swiss Canopy Crane, extra CO2 was released into the crowns of tall trees. This made it possible to test whether a mature forest grows faster with more CO2.
122171.m: The Basel crane was used to study the effect of more CO2 on old trees.

122172.q: How does Christian Körner define the alpine zone in the same way everywhere in the world?
a: As the area above the natural tree line
As the area above 2000 m above sea level
As the area with snow in July
As the area above the snow line
122172.e: Because fixed altitudes do not fit at every latitude, Körner uses the climatic tree line as the lower limit of the alpine zone.
122172.m: The alpine zone begins above the natural tree line.

122173.q: According to Körner, which environmental factor changes with altitude in the same regular way everywhere on Earth, unlike rainfall, for example?
122173.e: Körner distinguished factors that depend directly on altitude, such as air pressure and temperature, from factors linked to altitude only in some regions, such as rainfall or wind.
122173.m: Air pressure falls evenly with altitude everywhere.

122174.q: According to Körner's theory, which process limits plant growth first in the cold?
122174.e: At low temperatures a plant can still make sugar but can hardly turn it into new tissue. Tissue formation, the so-called sink, is the bottleneck.
122174.m: In the cold, plants do not lack sugar but cell growth.

122175.q: Which country does the plant ecologist Christian Körner originally come from?
122175.e: Christian Körner was born in Austria and studied in Innsbruck before moving to Basel.
122175.m: Christian Körner was born in Austria.

122176.q: What does the international programme GLORIA study on mountain summits?
a: How plant life is changing due to climate change
How fast the glaciers are melting
How many climbers visit the summits
How rock is weathered by frost
122176.e: GLORIA is a worldwide network that observes the plant life of mountain summits over the long term to detect the effects of climate change.
122176.m: GLORIA observes the plants on mountain summits around the world.

122177.q: Why are mountain summits especially good places to observe the effects of climate change on plants?
a: Cold-adapted species there react sensitively to warming
Most of Europe's plant species grow there
No rain or snow ever falls on summits
Summit plants grow exactly the same every year
122177.e: On summits, species live at their cold limit. Even small changes in temperature shift which species can grow there. The GLORIA network is coordinated from Vienna.
122177.m: Summit plants show early how climate change is working.

122178.q: Why does GLORIA record the plants on the same plots again and again?
a: To detect changes over the years
Because the plants would otherwise die
To measure the height of the summits again
122178.e: In each region, several summits at different altitudes are studied. The surveys are repeated on the same plots every few years, so changes become visible.

122179.q: On what principle are the summits of a GLORIA region chosen?
a: In steps from the tree line up to the nival zone
All summits at exactly the same altitude
Only the highest summits in each country
Only summits with a cable car
122179.e: The summits range from around the tree line up into the nival zone. In this way a whole altitude gradient is covered.
122179.m: GLORIA summits form a staircase from the tree line to the permanent snow.

122180.q: What are permanently marked plots called, on which researchers record the plants again and again over many years?
122180.e: Permanent monitoring plots are marked precisely and surveyed regularly. In GLORIA they are squares with sides of one metre just below the summits.
