122662.e: Arthropods such as Marrella make up a large part of the finds. Today this group includes insects, spiders and crustaceans.

122663.q: Which animal is regarded as a large predator of the Cambrian seas and is also known from the Burgess Shale?
122663.e: Anomalocaris probably reached well over half a metre in length and had grasping head appendages and a round mouth. It was one of the largest animals of its time.
122663.m: Anomalocaris was a large predator of the Cambrian.

122664.q: Which fossil from the Burgess Shale was first reconstructed the wrong way round, so that it seemed to walk on its spines?
122664.e: Hallucigenia was described in 1977 with the spines pointing down. Later finds showed that the spines were on its back and the legs came in pairs.
122664.m: Hallucigenia was at first reconstructed upside down.

122665.q: Which scientist made the Burgess Shale known to a wide audience in 1989 with the book “Wonderful Life”?
122665.e: In “Wonderful Life”, Stephen Jay Gould interpreted the Burgess animals as evidence of the role of chance in evolution. Some of his interpretations were later criticised.
122665.m: Stephen Jay Gould made the Burgess Shale famous with “Wonderful Life”.

122666.q: Why is the small animal Pikaia from the Burgess Shale interesting for the origin of vertebrates?
a: It is seen as an early relative of vertebrates
It was the first land animal
It is the ancestor of all insects
122666.e: Pikaia probably had a notochord, a forerunner of the backbone, and muscle blocks like today's lancelets. It is therefore placed among the early chordates.
122666.m: Pikaia is seen as an early relative of vertebrates.

122667.q: In which country are the Ediacara Hills, after which the Ediacaran fauna is named?
122667.e: The Ediacara Hills lie in the Flinders Ranges in South Australia. There the geologist Reginald Sprigg described the first fossils of this community in 1946.
122667.m: The Ediacaran fauna is named after hills in South Australia.

122668.q: What kind of living things are typical of the Ediacaran fauna?
a: Soft-bodied sea creatures without hard shells
Large land animals with bony skeletons
122668.e: The Ediacaran organisms had no shells or bones. They are only preserved as impressions in sandstone, first described by the geologist Reginald Sprigg in South Australia in 1946.
122668.m: The Ediacaran fauna consisted of soft-bodied sea creatures.

122669.q: In which period did the Ediacaran fauna live?
122669.e: The Ediacaran fauna lived about 575 to 539 million years ago at the end of the Precambrian. It is among the oldest known complex living things.
122669.m: The Ediacaran fauna lived shortly before the Cambrian.

122670.q: Which finding in 2018 supported the interpretation of Dickinsonia as an animal?
a: Detection of cholesterol breakdown products in the fossil
122670.e: Researchers found traces of cholesteroids in Dickinsonia fossils, which are typical of animals. Plants and fungi produce other sterols.
122670.m: Traces of cholesterol show that Dickinsonia was an animal.

122671.q: Why was the discovery of the fossil Charnia in England in 1957 a sensation?
a: It came from rock older than the Cambrian
It was the first dinosaur fossil found
It was a still living animal
122671.e: At that time people believed there had been no larger living things before the Cambrian. Charnia was the first recognised Precambrian fossil of a multicellular organism.
122671.m: Charnia proved that multicellular organisms existed before the Cambrian.

122672.q: What is special about the Ediacaran in the geological time scale?
a: In 2004 it was introduced as the first new system in over 100 years
It is the youngest period of Earth's history
122672.e: The International Union of Geological Sciences officially introduced the Ediacaran in 2004. It was the first new period in over a century.
122672.m: The Ediacaran was officially added to the time scale in 2004.

122673.q: Why is the interpretation of many Ediacaran organisms still disputed today?
a: Their body shapes hardly resemble today's animal groups
Only a single fossil has been found
They were only discovered a few years ago
All their fossils have been destroyed
122673.e: Many Ediacaran organisms look like quilted air mattresses or fern fronds. The palaeontologist Adolf Seilacher considered them a separate, extinct group; others see early animals in them.
122673.m: Many Ediacaran organisms fit into no animal group of today.

122674.q: Which present-day animal group may, according to some researchers, already have had forerunners in the Ediacaran fauna?
122674.e: The Ediacaran organism Kimberella had an oval body and left scratch marks as if grazing on microbial mats. Many see it as a mollusc-like organism.
122674.m: Kimberella is seen as a possible early relative of molluscs.

122675.q: In which country was the fossil Tiktaalik found in 2004?
122675.e: A team led by Neil Shubin found Tiktaalik on Ellesmere Island in the Canadian territory of Nunavut. The description appeared in the journal Nature in 2006.
122675.m: Tiktaalik was found in the Canadian Arctic.

122676.q: Roughly how old are the fossils of Tiktaalik?
122676.e: Tiktaalik lived in the late Devonian about 375 million years ago. The team searched specifically for rocks of this age because transitional forms were to be expected there.
122676.m: Tiktaalik lived about 375 million years ago in the Devonian.

122677.q: Which transition in evolution does Tiktaalik illustrate?
122677.e: Tiktaalik combines fish features such as scales and fins with features of four-legged animals. It is therefore often called a “fishapod”.
122677.m: Tiktaalik shows the transition from fish to land vertebrates.

122678.q: Which feature sets Tiktaalik apart from typical fish and links it to land vertebrates?
122678.e: In fish, the head is firmly joined to the shoulder girdle. Tiktaalik, however, could move its head independently of its body.
122678.m: Tiktaalik was one of the first to have a movable neck.

122679.q: What was special about Tiktaalik's pectoral fins?
a: They contained bones like an upper arm, ulna and wrist-like elements
They were made only of cartilage without bone
122679.e: The sturdy fins had bones that correspond to the upper arm, forearm and wrist of four-legged animals. With them Tiktaalik could probably prop itself up in shallow water.
122679.m: Tiktaalik's fins had bones like an arm and wrist.

122680.q: What does the name Tiktaalik mean in the language of the Inuit?
122680.e: The name comes from Inuktitut and refers to a large freshwater fish, the burbot. The researchers asked the elders of Nunavut for a suitable name.
122680.m: In Inuktitut, Tiktaalik means large freshwater fish.

122681.q: Which book did Neil Shubin write about Tiktaalik and the traces of our fish past in the human body?
122681.e: In “Your Inner Fish”, Shubin explains how parts of our body go back to early fish. The book was also made into a television series.
122681.m: Neil Shubin wrote the book “Your Inner Fish”.

122682.q: Which breathing organs did Tiktaalik probably have?
122682.e: Tiktaalik had gills, but also features that point to breathing air with lungs. That was an advantage in shallow, low-oxygen waters.
122682.m: Tiktaalik could probably breathe with gills and lungs.

122683.q: How many million years ago did the Permian-Triassic mass extinction happen?
122683.e: The event is dated to about 252 million years ago. It marks the boundary between the Palaeozoic and the Mesozoic.
122683.m: The Permian-Triassic mass extinction happened about 252 million years ago.

122684.q: Where does the Permian-Triassic mass extinction rank among the great mass extinctions?
a: It was the largest in Earth's history
It was the smallest of the big five
122684.e: At the end of the Permian, the great majority of marine species and a large part of land vertebrates disappeared. It is therefore also called the “Great Dying”.
122684.m: The Permian-Triassic mass extinction was the largest in Earth's history.

122685.q: Which cause is now seen as the main trigger of the Permian-Triassic mass extinction?
a: An ice age caused by sunspots
122685.e: Huge lava flows in Siberia released enormous amounts of carbon dioxide and other gases. The results were strong warming, acidification and a lack of oxygen in the oceans.
122685.m: Volcanism of the Siberian Traps triggered the Permian-Triassic extinction.

122686.q: Which animal group disappeared for good with the Permian-Triassic mass extinction?
122686.e: Trilobites had survived for almost 300 million years. At the end of the Permian their last representatives died out.
122686.m: Trilobites died out for good at the end of the Permian.

122687.q: Which well-known animal group arose during the Triassic, after the Permian-Triassic mass extinction?
122687.e: The mass extinction made room for new animal groups. The first dinosaurs appeared about 230 million years ago in the Triassic.
122687.m: Dinosaurs arose in the Triassic after the Permian-Triassic extinction.

122688.q: What is special about insects in the Permian-Triassic mass extinction?
a: It is the only known mass extinction of insects
122688.e: Insects usually came through other crises well. At the end of the Permian, however, several orders of insects disappeared.
122688.m: At the end of the Permian even insects suffered a mass extinction.

122689.q: What consequences did the strong warming at the end of the Permian have for the oceans?
a: Sea level falling by several kilometres
122689.e: Warm water can hold less oxygen, and a lot of carbon dioxide makes the sea more acidic. Both were deadly for many sea creatures.
122689.m: At the end of the Permian the oceans suffered from lack of oxygen and acidification.

122690.q: What makes fossil sites such as the Messel Pit so valuable for research?
a: Soft parts such as skin, feathers or stomach contents are also preserved
Only especially large bones lie there
The animals there are still frozen alive
The fossils are all made of gold
122690.e: Usually only bones, teeth or shells of animals are preserved. In rare sites, however, soft parts survive too, revealing a lot about appearance and way of life.
122690.m: Some fossil sites even preserve soft parts.

122691.q: Which fossil site near Darmstadt has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995?
122691.e: In the Messel Pit, animals about 47 million years old from the Eocene are preserved, often with fur, feathers and stomach contents. In 1995 it became Germany's first World Heritage Site in the natural heritage category.
122691.m: The Messel Pit has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995.

122692.q: Which famous fossil of an early bird comes from the limestone slabs of Solnhofen?
122692.e: The fine-grained limestone slabs of the Solnhofen area in Bavaria preserved Archaeopteryx together with feather impressions. The first skeleton was described in 1861.
122692.m: Archaeopteryx comes from the limestone slabs of Solnhofen.

122693.q: Why are animals at the bottom of low-oxygen lakes often especially well preserved as fossils?
a: Without oxygen, bacteria and scavengers hardly break down the bodies
The water there is always frozen
The water contains a lot of sugar, which preserves
The animals are dried there by sunlight
122693.e: On an oxygen-free lake bed there are no scavengers, and decay is very slow. Fine mud covers the bodies so that even delicate structures are preserved.
122693.m: Lack of oxygen protects bodies from decay.

122694.q: What are the fossils from the Devonian Hunsrück Slate near Bundenbach known for?
a: Their soft parts are preserved by pyrite
122694.e: In the Hunsrück Slate, starfish, sea lilies and arthropods were replaced by pyrite. As a result, even legs and antennae become visible on X-rays.
122694.m: In the Hunsrück Slate, fossils are preserved by pyrite.

122695.q: What is the Posidonia Shale of Holzmaden in Baden-Württemberg especially known for?
a: Ichthyosaurs with embryos in their bodies
122695.e: In the Lower Jurassic shale, ichthyosaurs are preserved, some with skin outline and unborn young. This shows that they gave birth to live young.
122695.m: Ichthyosaurs with embryos were found in Holzmaden.

122696.q: Which geological period do the Chengjiang and Burgess Shale fossil sites come from, showing the sudden appearance of many animal phyla?
122696.e: About 540 to 500 million years ago, almost all of today's animal phyla appeared in a short time. This is called the Cambrian explosion.
122696.m: Chengjiang and the Burgess Shale show the Cambrian explosion.

122697.q: In which fossil site in Los Angeles were ice age animals such as sabre-toothed cats preserved in natural asphalt?
122697.e: In the asphalt pits of Rancho La Brea, animals got stuck in the sticky tar. Millions of bones have been dug up there for over a hundred years.
122697.m: In the La Brea Tar Pits, ice age animals were preserved in asphalt.

122698.q: Roughly how far back in time does the EPICA Dome C ice core from Antarctica reach?
122698.e: The EPICA Dome C core provides a climate archive covering about 800,000 years. It shows eight ice age cycles and the link between temperature and CO2.
122698.m: The EPICA Dome C ice core reaches back about 800,000 years.

122699.q: What information do the trapped air bubbles in ice cores provide?
a: The earlier composition of the atmosphere
The earlier depth of the sea
The age of the rocks under the ice
The number of volcanoes on the Moon
122699.e: Air trapped in ice is a direct sample of the atmosphere of earlier times. From it, the concentrations of CO2 and methane, for example, can be measured.
122699.m: Air bubbles in ice show the earlier composition of the atmosphere.

122700.q: Which Bernese physicist is regarded as a pioneer of ice core research on carbon dioxide?
122700.e: Hans Oeschger developed methods at the University of Bern for measuring gases in ice. The Oeschger Centre for Climate Change Research in Bern bears his name.
122700.m: Hans Oeschger from Bern was a pioneer of ice core research.

122701.q: What is the method called that uses tree rings to determine climate and age?
122701.e: The width of tree rings depends on the temperature and rainfall in each year. By overlapping pieces of wood, chronologies spanning thousands of years are built.
122701.m: Dendrochronology reads climate from tree rings.

122702.q: What does the Milanković theory explain?
a: How variations in the Earth's orbit and axis control ice ages
How volcanic eruptions trigger ice ages
How sunspots determine the daily weather
How ocean currents are caused by the Moon
122702.e: The shape of the Earth's orbit, the tilt of its axis and its wobble change in long cycles. This changes how solar radiation is distributed, which helps control the switch between ice ages and warm periods.
122702.m: Variations in the Earth's orbit and axis control the ice age cycles.

122703.q: What can researchers read from the limestone shells of tiny sea creatures in old marine deposits?
122703.e: Depending on the water temperature, the creatures build different amounts of heavy oxygen into their shells. Earlier temperatures can be worked out from these oxygen isotopes.
122703.m: Limestone shells of sea creatures reveal earlier sea temperatures.

122704.q: What happened during the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum about 56 million years ago?
a: A rapid global warming of several degrees
An almost complete glaciation of the Earth
The asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs
A strong cooling caused by volcanic ash
122704.e: During the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM), the global temperature rose by several degrees within a short time. It serves as a natural comparison for a rapid release of carbon.
122704.m: About 56 million years ago there was a strong warming called the PETM.

122705.q: What does the “Snowball Earth” hypothesis describe?
a: An almost complete glaciation of the Earth in the late Precambrian
The impact of an icy comet in the Jurassic
The Little Ice Age in the Middle Ages
122705.e: In the Cryogenian, about 720 to 635 million years ago, glaciers probably reached as far as the tropics. Evidence includes glacial deposits in areas that were once near the equator.
122705.m: Snowball Earth describes an almost global glaciation in the Precambrian.

a: The processes from an organism's death to its fossilisation
122706.e: Taphonomy studies the decay, transport, burial and transformation of living things after death. It explains why some organisms become fossils and others do not.
122706.m: Taphonomy studies how dead living things become fossils.

122707.q: What does the Greek word “taphos”, found in the term taphonomy, mean?
122707.e: Taphonomy combines “taphos” (grave) and “nomos” (law). So it is about the laws of being buried, all the way to becoming a fossil.
122707.m: Taphonomy roughly means the study of the laws of the grave.

122708.q: Why are often only single, scattered bones found from a dead animal on land?
a: Scavengers and water carry the parts away
Animals usually have only a few bones
The bones move by themselves in the soil
122708.e: Between death and burial, scavengers break up the body, and water or wind carry the remains away. Complete skeletons are therefore rare.
122708.m: Before burial, dead animals are often scattered.

122709.q: What is a fossil called that consists of the inside of a shell filled with sediment that has hardened?
122709.e: If an empty shell fills with sediment and the shell later dissolves, the inner shape is preserved as an internal mould. It shows, for example, where the mussel's muscles were attached.
122709.m: An internal mould is the fossilised filling of a shell.

122710.q: Which process leads to the formation of petrified wood?
a: Drying out in the desert without minerals
122710.e: Mineral-rich water gets into the cells and deposits silica there, for example. In this way the cell structures of the wood are preserved in stone.
122710.m: Petrified wood forms when minerals such as silica are deposited.

122711.q: Why are living things with hard shells strongly over-represented in the fossil record?
a: Hard parts decay much more slowly than soft parts
Soft-bodied animals did not exist in the past
122711.e: Soft tissue is quickly destroyed by bacteria and scavengers. Shells, bones and teeth, however, last long enough to be buried.
122711.m: Hard parts have a much greater chance of becoming fossils.

122712.q: Which condition especially favours the preservation of soft parts in fossils?
a: Rapid burial in a low-oxygen environment
Long storage in the open air
122712.e: Without oxygen, decomposers hardly work, and quick burial protects against scavengers. Such conditions existed, for example, at the bottom of calm, low-oxygen basins.
122712.m: Rapid burial without oxygen protects soft parts from decay.

122713.q: What is the process called in which plant remains are turned into a thin film of carbon without air?
122713.e: In carbonisation, volatile substances escape and carbon becomes concentrated. Typical examples are leaf impressions with a black film in Carboniferous shales.
122713.m: In carbonisation, a film of carbon is left behind from plants.

a: Single-celled organisms, usually with a shell
122714.e: Foraminifera are single-celled organisms that usually build a shell of lime or cemented grains. They catch food with fine false feet.
122714.m: Foraminifera are single-celled organisms, usually with a limestone shell.

122715.q: Where does the name foraminifera come from?
a: From the name of their discoverer
122715.e: The Latin “foramen” means hole and “ferre” means to carry. The name refers to the openings between the chambers of the shell.

122716.q: Which rock containing large foraminifera were the pyramids of Giza mostly built from?
122716.e: The limestone of Giza is rich in nummulites, disc-shaped foraminifera from the Eocene. Even the ancient geographer Strabo thought the coin-like objects were petrified lentils.
122716.m: The pyramids of Giza are mostly made of nummulitic limestone.

122717.q: Why are foraminifera so important in oil exploration and biostratigraphy?
a: They are common and make good index fossils
122717.e: Foraminifera occur in large numbers and evolved quickly. Even small drill samples are enough to determine the age of rock layers.
122717.m: Foraminifera are important index fossils for dating.

122718.q: Which ways of life are mainly distinguished among foraminifera?
a: Benthic on the sea floor and planktonic drifting in the water
Only in fresh water and in caves
Only on plants and in the soil
122718.e: Most species live benthically on or in the sea floor. Planktonic species drift in the water and are particularly important for palaeoclimate research.
122718.m: Foraminifera live benthically on the floor or planktonically in the water.

122719.q: Why do the limestone shells of fossil foraminifera help to reconstruct past climate?
a: Their composition reveals the water temperature at the time
They only grow at full moon
They contain trapped air bubbles from the atmosphere
They turn blue in the cold
122719.e: When the shell is built, more or less heavy oxygen is taken up depending on the water temperature. From drill cores from the sea floor, temperatures over millions of years can be read.
122719.m: Foraminifera shells are a climate archive.

122720.q: What do foraminifera use to catch their food?
a: Net-like false feet made of cell plasma
122720.e: Foraminifera stretch fine, branching false feet of cell plasma through the openings of their shell. Algae, bacteria and small particles get caught in them.
122720.m: Foraminifera catch food with net-like false feet.

122721.q: What happens to the limestone shells of planktonic foraminifera after they die?
a: They sink and form lime mud on the sea floor
They dissolve immediately at the surface
They are washed onto beaches as sand
They grow into new coral reefs
122721.e: The tiny shells trickle down and cover large parts of the ocean floor as lime mud. Over millions of years, limestone can form from it.
122721.m: Sunken foraminifera shells form lime mud.

122722.q: Which dinosaur from China, described in 1996, was the first non-bird dinosaur with proven feather-like structures?
122722.e: Sinosauropteryx from north-eastern China showed a fringe of simple filaments. The find revived the debate about the origin of birds.
122722.m: Sinosauropteryx was the first known feathered non-bird dinosaur.

122723.q: Which Chinese province do many fossils of feathered dinosaurs from the Cretaceous come from?
122723.e: The Yixian Formation in Liaoning formed in lakes that were often covered by volcanic ash. As a result, feathers and soft parts were superbly preserved.
122723.m: Many feathered dinosaurs come from Liaoning in China.

122724.q: Which small dinosaur had long feathers on its arms and legs and is therefore called “four-winged”?
122724.e: Microraptor had flight feathers on its front and back legs. It could probably glide with them and perhaps also flap actively.
122724.m: Microraptor had flight feathers on its arms and legs.

122725.q: Which large tyrannosaur, about nine metres long, was described with feathers in 2012?
122725.e: Yutyrannus huali is the largest known dinosaur with directly proven feather-like structures. Its name means roughly “beautiful feathered tyrant”.
122725.m: Yutyrannus was a large feathered tyrannosaur.

122726.q: How were researchers able to reconstruct the feather colours of dinosaurs such as Anchiornis?
a: From paint remains in cave paintings
122726.e: Melanosomes are tiny pigment bodies whose shape and arrangement are linked to certain colours. For Anchiornis this revealed black and white plumage with a reddish crest.
122726.m: Fossil melanosomes reveal the colours of dinosaur feathers.

122727.q: What were feathers on dinosaurs probably first used for, before they were used for flying?
122727.e: Many feathered dinosaurs could not fly. Their feathers kept them warm and were probably also used to impress or for brooding.
122727.m: Feathers probably first arose as insulation and decoration.

122728.q: Which find from Myanmar made headlines in 2016 in connection with feathered dinosaurs?
a: A feathered dinosaur tail in amber
A dinosaur egg with a living embryo
A coat of feathers made of gold
A cave painting of a raptor
122728.e: A piece of tail with feathers and vertebrae was trapped in amber about 99 million years old. However, the trade in amber from Myanmar is ethically disputed because of the civil war.
122728.m: A feathered dinosaur tail was found in amber from Myanmar.

122729.q: What conclusion do palaeontologists draw today from the many feathered dinosaurs?
a: Birds are descendants of theropod dinosaurs
122729.e: Shared features such as feathers, a wishbone and hollow bones link birds with theropods such as Velociraptor. Birds are therefore regarded as living dinosaurs.
122729.m: Birds are the living descendants of the theropods.

a: Trace fossils such as tracks, burrows and feeding marks
122730.e: Ichnology studies traces of life, that is, evidence of the behaviour of organisms. These include footprints, dwellings, crawling traces and droppings.

122731.q: What does Adolf Seilacher's concept of ichnofacies describe?
a: Typical trace communities indicate settings such as water depth
Each trace belongs to exactly one animal species
Traces show the exact age in years
122731.e: Certain combinations of trace fossils occur in typical environments, such as the tidal zone or the deep sea. In this way traces help to reconstruct earlier habitats.
122731.m: Ichnofacies are typical trace communities of certain habitats.

122732.q: How can you typically recognise the tracks of predatory dinosaurs (theropods)?
a: Narrow three-toed prints with claw marks
122732.e: Theropods walked on their hind legs and usually put down three toes, often with sharp claws. Such tracks are assigned, for example, to the trace genus Grallator.
122732.m: Theropods left three-toed tracks with claw marks.

122733.q: Which trace genus from the Triassic got its name because its prints look like human hands?
122733.e: Chirotherium means “hand animal”. The tracks became known in 1834 near Hildburghausen in Thuringia; they were probably made by relatives of crocodiles.
122733.m: Chirotherium means hand animal because the tracks look like hands.

122734.q: Which traces did trilobites typically leave on the sea floor?
a: Two-lobed crawling traces from their many legs
122734.e: With their many legs, trilobites dug furrowed, two-lobed crawling traces into the mud. These trace fossils are called Cruziana and are typical of old marine deposits.

122735.q: What do the branching burrows that mark the start of the Cambrian show?
a: Animals began to dig deliberately through the sea floor
The first animals moved onto land
Birds searched the mud for food
122735.e: The base of the Cambrian is defined by the first appearance of branching burrows (Treptichnus pedum). They show a new, complex digging behaviour of animals.
122735.m: New burrows mark the beginning of the Cambrian.

122736.q: Why did the roughly 395-million-year-old tracks of Zachełmie in Poland cause a stir in 2010?
a: They are older than known transitional forms such as Tiktaalik
They were found on the Moon
122736.e: The prints come from early four-legged animals and are much older than transitional forms such as Tiktaalik. Four-legged animals must therefore have arisen earlier than thought.
122736.m: The tracks of Zachełmie show that four-legged animals arose earlier than thought.

122737.q: What is the churning of sediment by living things called?
122737.e: Burrowing animals such as worms and mussels mix up sediment layers. Heavily bioturbated rocks hardly show any layering.
122737.m: Bioturbation is the churning of sediment by living things.

122738.q: Where was the skeleton of Ticinosuchus ferox found?
a: On Monte San Giorgio in Ticino
122738.e: Ticinosuchus comes from the Middle Triassic rocks of Monte San Giorgio. Its name means roughly “fierce Ticino crocodile”.
122738.m: Ticinosuchus was found on Monte San Giorgio in Ticino.

122739.q: Which animal group does Ticinosuchus belong to?
122739.e: Ticinosuchus belongs to the pseudosuchians, the line that leads to today's crocodiles. It is often placed among the rauisuchians.
122739.m: Ticinosuchus was a relative of crocodiles.

122740.e: The skeleton points to an animal about two and a half metres long. It walked with upright legs and was a predator.
122740.m: Ticinosuchus was about two and a half metres long.

122741.q: In which geological period did Ticinosuchus live?
122741.e: Ticinosuchus dates from the Middle Triassic, about 240 million years ago. The fossils of Monte San Giorgio from this time are famous.

122742.q: What way of life did Ticinosuchus probably have?
a: It was a plant-eater in the sea
It lived as a filter feeder
122742.e: Its build, with strong legs under the body and sharp teeth, suggests a predator on land. It was one of the great hunters of its time.
122742.m: Ticinosuchus was a predator that lived on land.

122743.q: Why is it remarkable that Ticinosuchus was found on Monte San Giorgio?
a: The site consists of marine deposits
The site lies in a glacier
The site is a volcanic crater
122743.e: On Monte San Giorgio, mainly sea animals such as fish and marine reptiles are found. A land animal is rare there and was probably washed into the basin after death.
122743.m: Ticinosuchus is a rare land animal in marine deposits.

122744.q: Which Swiss university carried out the large excavations on Monte San Giorgio in which Ticinosuchus was also recovered?
122744.e: From 1924, the Palaeontological Institute of the University of Zurich dug on Monte San Giorgio under Bernhard Peyer. Many of the finds are now on display in the Palaeontological Museum in Zurich.
122744.m: The University of Zurich dug for fossils on Monte San Giorgio.

122745.q: What does the species name “ferox” in Ticinosuchus ferox mean?
122745.e: The Latin “ferox” means fierce or wild. It refers to the predatory appearance of the animal.

122746.q: What are the marine reptiles of the Mesozoic with four paddles and often a very long neck called?
122746.e: Plesiosaurs moved through the water with four flipper-like paddles. Many species had an extremely long neck with a small head.
122746.m: Plesiosaurs were marine reptiles with four paddles and a long neck.

122747.q: Which vertebrates were the first to master powered flight in the Mesozoic?
122747.e: Pterosaurs already flew in the late Triassic with a wing membrane stretched along a greatly lengthened fourth finger. Birds and bats only learned to fly later.
122747.m: Pterosaurs were the first vertebrates with powered flight.

122748.q: Where does the name Triassic come from?
a: From the threefold division of rocks in Germany
122748.e: In 1834 Friedrich von Alberti grouped Buntsandstein, Muschelkalk and Keuper together as the Triassic. The Greek word means a group of three.
122748.m: The Triassic is named after the three parts Buntsandstein, Muschelkalk and Keuper.

122749.q: Which finding led Luis and Walter Alvarez to the impact hypothesis for the end of the Cretaceous in 1980?
a: An iridium anomaly in the boundary layer
A dinosaur skeleton with burn marks
122749.e: In the thin clay layer at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary they found greatly increased iridium levels. Iridium is much more common in asteroids than in the Earth's crust.
122749.m: An iridium anomaly pointed to an asteroid impact at the end of the Cretaceous.

122750.q: Where is the crater that is linked with the mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous?
a: On the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico
In the Nördlinger Ries in Germany
122750.e: The Chicxulub crater has a diameter of about 180 kilometres. It formed about 66 million years ago from the impact of a body about ten kilometres across.
122750.m: The Chicxulub crater is on the Yucatán Peninsula.

122751.q: Which important group of plants arose and spread in the Cretaceous?
122751.e: Angiosperms, or flowering plants, appeared in the early Cretaceous. By the end of the Cretaceous they had become dominant in many habitats.
122751.m: Flowering plants spread in the Cretaceous.

122752.q: Which supercontinent broke apart during the Mesozoic?
122752.e: Pangaea began to break apart in the Triassic. Among other things, the Atlantic opened and today's continents took shape.
122752.m: The supercontinent Pangaea broke apart in the Mesozoic.

122753.q: In which period of the Mesozoic did the first mammals appear?
122753.e: The first true mammals, or their closest forerunners, appeared in the late Triassic. They mostly stayed small throughout the Mesozoic.
122753.m: The first mammals appeared in the Triassic.

122754.q: Which sea at times covered large parts of today's Switzerland in the Mesozoic?
122754.e: At that time the Tethys separated Africa and Europe. Its deposits now form many limestones of the Alps and the Jura.
122754.m: In the Mesozoic, Switzerland at times lay in the Tethys sea.

122755.q: What is the method called that uses pollen in bog and lake deposits to work out earlier vegetation and climate?
122755.e: Pollen is very tough and is preserved in low-oxygen sediments. From the share of different plants, the temperature and rainfall of earlier times can be worked out.
122755.m: Pollen analysis shows the vegetation and climate of past times.

122756.q: After the Permian-Triassic mass extinction, how long did it take for ecosystems to largely recover?
122756.e: Communities stayed poor in species for a long time in the early Triassic, and reefs and coal swamps were largely missing. Only after several million years did varied ecosystems form again.
122756.m: Recovery after the Permian-Triassic extinction took several million years.

122757.q: Which organelle is found in plant cells but is missing in animal cells?
122757.e: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis; animal cells have no chloroplasts.
122757.m: Only plant cells and algae have chloroplasts.

122758.q: Which small organelle breaks down long-chain fatty acids and splits toxic hydrogen peroxide with the enzyme catalase?
122758.e: Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes; the hydrogen peroxide produced is broken down by catalase into water and oxygen.
122758.m: Peroxisomes detoxify hydrogen peroxide with catalase.

122759.q: Which structure separates the contents of the nucleus from the cytoplasm?
122759.e: The nuclear envelope consists of two membranes and is pierced by nuclear pores through which substances are exchanged.
122759.m: The nuclear envelope with its nuclear pores surrounds the genetic material.

122760.q: What is the membrane called that surrounds the large central vacuole of a plant cell?
122760.e: The tonoplast separates the cell sap of the vacuole from the cytoplasm and regulates the exchange of substances.
122760.m: The vacuole of the plant cell is surrounded by the tonoplast.

122762.q: Why is part of the endoplasmic reticulum called the “rough ER”?
a: It is surrounded by a cell wall
122762.e: Under the electron microscope the rough ER looks grainy because many ribosomes are attached to the outside of its membranes.
122762.m: The rough ER is studded with ribosomes.

122763.q: What is the main task of the rough endoplasmic reticulum?
a: Making membrane proteins and proteins for secretion
122763.e: Proteins are made at the rough ER that are built into membranes or exported from the cell; in the process they enter the inside of the ER.
122763.m: Proteins for membranes and for export are made at the rough ER.

122764.q: Which substances are mainly made at the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
a: Lipids such as phospholipids and steroids
122764.e: The smooth ER has no ribosomes; it synthesises lipids, including membrane phospholipids and steroid hormones.
122764.m: The smooth ER is the lipid factory of the cell.

122765.q: Which structure is the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum directly connected to?
122765.e: The ER emerges directly from the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope; its interior is connected to the space between the two nuclear membranes.
122765.m: The ER and the nuclear envelope form one continuous membrane system.

122766.q: What task does the especially extensive smooth ER perform in liver cells?
122766.e: In liver cells, the smooth ER contains enzymes that chemically convert medicines and toxins so that they can be excreted.
122766.m: The smooth ER of the liver helps with detoxification.

122767.q: How do newly made proteins get from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus?
a: In membrane vesicles that bud off
122767.e: Transport vesicles bud off from the ER, fuse with the membranes of the Golgi apparatus and release their cargo.
122767.m: Vesicles transport proteins from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.

122768.q: What causes a ribosome to bind to the ER during protein synthesis?
a: A signal peptide on the new protein
A start codon on the mRNA
A poly-A tail on the mRNA
122768.e: A signal sequence at the start of the growing chain is bound by a recognition particle (SRP), which guides the ribosome to the ER membrane.
122768.m: A signal peptide sends proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum.

122769.q: What is a single stack of flattened membrane cisternae of the Golgi apparatus called?
122769.e: The Golgi apparatus of a cell consists of one or more dictyosomes, that is, stacks of flat membrane sacs.
122769.m: A Golgi stack is called a dictyosome.

122770.q: In which cells did Camillo Golgi discover the organelle named after him in 1898?
122770.e: Camillo Golgi stained nerve cells with silver salts and discovered a fine network inside the cell. In 1906 he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
122770.m: Golgi discovered his organelle in nerve cells.

122771.q: Which side of the Golgi apparatus receives the vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum?
122771.e: The cis side faces the ER and serves as the receiving side; vesicles are sent off from the opposite trans side.
122771.m: The Golgi apparatus receives on the cis side and dispatches on the trans side.

122772.q: What is the main task of the Golgi apparatus?
a: Storing and reading the genetic material
122772.e: In the Golgi apparatus, proteins from the ER are processed further, given address labels and packed into vesicles for their destination.
122772.m: The Golgi apparatus is the post office and packing station of the cell.

122773.q: Which chemical change do many proteins undergo in the Golgi apparatus?
a: They are split into amino acids
They are reduced to fatty acids
122773.e: In the Golgi apparatus, the sugar chains attached in the ER (glycosylation) are modified and extended; this produces glycoproteins.
122773.m: In the Golgi apparatus, many proteins receive their final sugar chains.

122774.q: How are secretory proteins packed by the Golgi apparatus released from the cell?
122774.e: Secretory vesicles move to the cell membrane, fuse with it and empty their contents outside.
122774.m: In exocytosis, vesicles fuse with the cell membrane.

122775.q: Which organelle is formed when vesicles bud off from the Golgi apparatus?
122775.e: Vesicles containing digestive enzymes bud off from the trans side of the Golgi apparatus and become lysosomes.
122775.m: Lysosomes come from the Golgi apparatus.

122776.q: What task do Golgi vesicles perform in plant cells after nuclear division?
122776.e: The vesicles supply material for the new cell wall and fuse in the middle of the cell to form the cell plate, which separates the daughter cells.
122776.m: Plant cells form a cell plate between the daughter cells.

122777.q: In which cells is the Golgi apparatus particularly well developed?
a: In gland cells with a lot of secretion
122777.e: Cells that release many substances, such as goblet cells or cells of the pancreas, need a lot of packing and dispatch capacity.
122777.m: Cells that secrete a lot have a large Golgi apparatus.

122778.e: Ribosomes are complexes of ribosomal RNA and numerous proteins, made up of a large and a small subunit.
122778.m: Ribosomes consist of RNA and proteins.

122779.q: What sedimentation coefficient do the ribosomes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells have?
122779.e: Eukaryotic ribosomes in the cytoplasm sediment at 80 Svedberg; their subunits are 60S and 40S.
122779.m: 80S ribosomes work in the cytoplasm of eukaryotes.

122780.q: Which step of protein biosynthesis do ribosomes carry out?
122780.e: At the ribosome, the base sequence of the mRNA is translated into a chain of amino acids.
122780.m: Ribosomes translate the mRNA into proteins.

122781.q: What is a group of ribosomes called that read the same mRNA at the same time?
122781.e: Several ribosomes can work one after another on one mRNA; in this way many copies of a protein are made at once.
122781.m: A polysome consists of several ribosomes on one mRNA.

122782.q: Which RNA brings the amino acids to the ribosome?
122782.e: Transfer RNA carries an amino acid and uses its anticodon to recognise the matching codon of the mRNA.
122782.m: The tRNA delivers the amino acids to the ribosome.

122783.q: Why can antibiotics such as tetracycline harm bacteria without seriously disturbing protein synthesis in the human cytoplasm?
122783.e: The ribosomes of bacteria differ in size and structure from the cytoplasmic ribosomes of humans, so some drugs bind specifically only to the bacterial ones.
122783.m: Many antibiotics specifically attack the ribosomes of bacteria.

122784.q: What distinguishes ribosomes from organelles such as lysosomes or mitochondria?
a: They are larger than the nucleus
122784.e: Ribosomes are molecular complexes without a surrounding membrane and are found in all cells, including bacteria.
122784.m: Ribosomes are not surrounded by a membrane.

122785.q: Roughly what pH is found inside a lysosome?
122785.e: Lysosomes are acidic; their digestive enzymes work best at a pH of around 4.5 to 5.
122785.m: The inside of a lysosome is acidic.

122786.q: What kind of enzymes do lysosomes contain?
122786.e: Lysosomes contain dozens of hydrolytic enzymes that split proteins, nucleic acids, fats and carbohydrates.
122786.m: Lysosomes digest substances with acid hydrolases.

122787.q: Why are lysosomes sometimes called the “stomach” of the cell?
a: They produce stomach acid for the body
They take up food from the intestine
122787.e: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes and break down cell components and particles taken in. They were discovered by the Belgian researcher Christian de Duve.
122787.m: Lysosomes are the digestive vesicles of the cell.

122788.q: What is the process called in which a cell breaks down its own damaged components in lysosomes?
122788.e: In autophagy, cell components are enclosed by a membrane and digested with lysosomes; Yoshinori Ohsumi received the Nobel Prize for this in 2016.
122788.m: In autophagy, the cell recycles its own components.

122789.q: What is the cause of lysosomal storage diseases such as Tay-Sachs disease?
a: A fault in the nuclear envelope
122789.e: If a particular breakdown enzyme is missing, undigested substances build up in the lysosomes; in Tay-Sachs these are gangliosides in nerve cells.
122789.m: In storage diseases, the lysosomes lack a breakdown enzyme.

122790.q: How is the acidic environment in the lysosome maintained?
a: By proton pumps in the membrane
122790.e: An ATP-dependent proton pump (V-ATPase) continuously transports hydrogen ions into the lysosome.
122790.m: Proton pumps keep the lysosome acidic.

122791.q: Why do lysosomal enzymes that get into the cytoplasm usually cause only little damage?
a: They are hardly active at neutral pH
They are immediately converted into ATP
122791.e: The hydrolases need an acidic environment; in the almost neutral cytoplasm (pH about 7.2) they work only weakly.
122791.m: Lysosomal enzymes only work properly in acidic conditions.

122792.q: What is the vesicle called that forms when a phagosome fuses with a lysosome?
122792.e: Phagocytes take bacteria into a phagosome; after fusion with a lysosome, the bacteria are digested in the phagolysosome.
122792.m: Phagocytes digest their prey in the phagolysosome.

122793.q: Which three types of filament make up the cytoskeleton of animal cells?
a: Microtubules, actin filaments and intermediate filaments
Microtubules, collagen fibres and elastin fibres
122793.e: The cytoskeleton consists of microtubules, actin filaments (microfilaments) and intermediate filaments.
122793.m: The cytoskeleton consists of three kinds of filament.

122794.q: Which protein are microtubules made of?
122794.e: Microtubules are hollow tubes made of dimers of alpha and beta tubulin.

122795.q: What tasks does the cytoskeleton perform?
a: It gives the cell its shape and makes movement possible
122795.e: The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres. It supports the cell, transports substances and makes movements such as cell division possible.
122795.m: The cytoskeleton is the scaffold and transport network of the cell.

122796.q: Which structure made of microtubules pulls the chromosomes apart during cell division?
122796.e: During mitosis, microtubules form the spindle apparatus. Its fibres attach to the chromosomes and pull the halves to the poles of the cell.
122796.m: The spindle apparatus distributes the chromosomes during cell division.

122797.q: Which protein forms the intermediate filaments in the epithelial cells of the skin?
122797.e: Keratins are typical intermediate filaments of epithelial cells and make skin, hair and nails tough.

122798.q: From which structure do most microtubules originate in animal cells?
122798.e: The centrosome with its two centrioles is the most important organising centre for microtubules in animal cells.

122799.q: Which arrangement of microtubules does a cross-section through a cilium or flagellum of eukaryotes show?
122799.e: Nine doublet microtubules surround two single central microtubules; the motor protein dynein makes the doublets slide against each other.
122799.m: Cilia have nine doublet microtubules around two central ones.

122800.q: Which protein of the cytoskeleton works together with myosin in the muscle cell?
122800.e: During muscle contraction, myosin heads pull on the actin filaments. As a result the filaments slide into each other and the muscle shortens.
122800.m: Actin and myosin make the muscle contract.

122801.q: In which order do the classic phases of mitosis take place?
122801.e: Mitosis begins with prophase, followed by metaphase, anaphase and finally telophase.
122801.m: The phases of mitosis are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.

122802.q: In which phase of mitosis are the sister chromatids pulled to the poles of the cell?
122802.e: In anaphase, the sister chromatids are separated from each other and pulled by the spindle fibres to opposite poles.
122802.m: In anaphase, the chromatids move apart.

122803.q: To which protein structure of the chromosomes do the spindle fibres attach?
122803.e: The kinetochore is a protein complex at the constriction of the chromosome to which the microtubules of the spindle bind.
122803.m: Spindle fibres attach at the kinetochore.

122804.q: What is the division of the cytoplasm after nuclear division called?
122804.e: Nuclear division (karyokinesis) is followed by cytokinesis, in which the cell body splits into two daughter cells.
122804.m: After nuclear division, cytokinesis divides the cell body.

122805.q: In which phase of mitosis do the chromosomes condense enough to become visible under a light microscope?
122805.e: At the beginning of mitosis the chromatin condenses strongly; the chromosomes become recognisable as threads.
122805.m: In prophase, the chromosomes become visible.

122806.q: In which phase of mitosis do new nuclear envelopes form around the two sets of chromosomes?
122806.e: In telophase the chromosomes uncoil again and new nuclear envelopes and nucleoli form.
122806.m: In telophase, two new nuclei are formed.

122807.q: How is the cytoplasm divided in animal cells at the end of mitosis?
a: By the breakdown of the nucleus
122807.e: A ring of actin and myosin contracts beneath the membrane and pinches the cell in two along a cleavage furrow.
122807.m: Animal cells pinch in two when they divide.

122808.q: In which phase of the cell cycle is the DNA copied?
122808.e: In the synthesis phase (S phase) of interphase, all the DNA is replicated.
122808.m: The DNA is copied in the S phase.

122809.q: What is the state called into which many specialised cells, such as nerve cells, leave the cell cycle?
122809.e: Cells in the G0 phase no longer divide but remain metabolically active; some can re-enter the cycle.
122809.m: Resting cells are in the G0 phase.

122810.q: Which proteins rise and fall periodically in the cell cycle and activate certain kinases that control the process?
122810.e: Cyclins bind to kinases (CDKs) and so allow the transition to the next phase of the cycle; afterwards they are broken down.
122810.m: Cyclins set the rhythm of the cell cycle.

122811.q: Which protein is called the “guardian of the genome” because it stops the cell cycle when DNA is damaged?
122811.e: When DNA is damaged, p53 stops the cycle until the damage is repaired, or triggers programmed cell death; its gene is mutated in many tumours.
122811.m: The protein p53 protects the cell from dividing with damaged DNA.

122812.q: Which stage makes up most of the cell cycle in most dividing cells?
122812.e: Interphase, with the G1, S and G2 phases, usually lasts many hours, while the actual nuclear division takes only about an hour.
122812.m: The cell spends most of its time in interphase.

122813.q: What are genes called that normally slow down cell division and whose failure can contribute to cancer?
122813.e: Tumour suppressor genes inhibit division or promote repair; if both copies fail, this brake is missing.
122813.m: Tumour suppressor genes act as a brake on cell division.

122814.q: What is the limited number of divisions that normal human body cells can go through in cell culture called?
122814.e: In 1961 Leonard Hayflick showed that normal fibroblasts divide only about 40 to 60 times and then stop.
122814.m: Normal body cells cannot divide endlessly.

122815.q: Which ends of the chromosomes become shorter with every cell division in many body cells?
122815.e: DNA polymerase cannot fully copy the end of a strand; that is why, without the enzyme telomerase, the telomeres shorten with each division.
122815.m: Telomeres protect the ends of chromosomes and become shorter with age.

a: The random thermal motion of the particles
122816.e: Particles move randomly because of their thermal energy (Brownian motion); this results in a net flow from the place of higher to the place of lower concentration.
122816.m: Diffusion is based on the random movement of particles.

122817.q: What does Fick's first law state?
a: The flow of particles is proportional to the concentration gradient
The flow of particles is independent of concentration
The pressure is proportional to the temperature
122817.e: According to Adolf Fick, the steeper the concentration gradient, the more substance flows per unit of time.
122817.m: A steeper concentration gradient speeds up diffusion.

122818.q: How does a rise in temperature affect the speed of diffusion?
122818.e: At higher temperatures the particles move faster, and the diffusion coefficient increases.

122819.q: How does glucose passively enter many body cells via GLUT transport proteins?
122819.e: GLUT transporters let glucose pass through the membrane along its concentration gradient without using ATP.
122819.m: Facilitated diffusion uses transport proteins but no energy.

122820.q: Which substance can diffuse most easily straight through the lipid bilayer of a membrane?
122820.e: Small non-polar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂ dissolve in the fatty interior of the membrane; ions and large polar molecules need transport proteins.
122820.m: Small non-polar molecules pass through membranes easily.

122821.q: Why is the huge surface area of the alveoli so important for gas exchange?
a: The amount of diffusion increases with the exchange surface
A large surface raises body temperature
Active transport takes place on large surfaces
122821.e: The flow of diffusing gas is proportional to the area; many small alveoli create a surface of roughly 100 square metres.
122821.m: Large surfaces make fast gas exchange possible.

122822.q: How does the time particles need to diffuse across a distance change if the distance is doubled?
122822.e: The average diffusion time grows with the square of the distance; twice the distance means about four times the time. That is why diffusion is only efficient over short distances.
122822.m: Diffusion is only fast over short distances.

122823.q: What happens once the concentrations have evened out in diffusion?
a: Particles keep moving, but there is no net flow
122823.e: At equilibrium, the same number of particles move in both directions; the concentration therefore stays the same everywhere.
122823.m: Diffusion equilibrium is a dynamic equilibrium.

122824.q: What happens to red blood cells that are placed in distilled water?
a: They shrink into a spiky shape
122824.e: The inside of the cell is more concentrated than pure water; water flows in until the membrane tears (haemolysis).
122824.m: Red blood cells burst in pure water.

122825.q: What is it called when the protoplast pulls away from the cell wall after a plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution?
122825.e: In the hypertonic solution the vacuole loses water, the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the rigid cell wall.
122825.m: Plant cells undergo plasmolysis in a concentrated solution.

122826.q: What is the internal pressure of a plant cell against its cell wall, which keeps herbaceous plants upright, called?
122826.e: Through osmotic uptake of water, the vacuole presses the cell contents against the cell wall; if water is lacking, the plant wilts.
122826.m: Turgor makes plant parts firm and plump.

122827.q: Which membrane proteins allow water to pass through especially quickly?
122827.e: Aquaporins are water channels; Peter Agre received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2003 for discovering them.
122827.m: Aquaporins are the water channels of the cell membrane.

122828.q: What concentration does a physiological saline solution have, which is roughly isotonic with blood?
122828.e: A solution with 0.9 g of sodium chloride per 100 ml has roughly the same osmotic value as blood plasma.
122828.m: Physiological saline contains 0.9 per cent salt.

122829.q: How does the osmotic pressure of a solution change if the concentration of dissolved particles is doubled?
122829.e: Osmotic pressure is proportional to the number of dissolved particles. Twice as many particles produce about twice the pressure.
122829.m: More dissolved particles mean more osmotic pressure.

122830.q: Why do strawberries release juice when you sprinkle them with sugar?
a: Water moves out by osmosis towards the sugar solution
The sugar dissolves the cell walls
The sugar is actively pumped into the cells
122830.e: The sugar forms a very concentrated solution on the outside; water flows out of the fruit cells.
122830.m: Sugar draws water out of fruit by osmosis.

a: It uses an ion gradient that was built up beforehand
It splits ATP directly at the transporter
It only takes place in plant cells
It works without a transport protein
122831.e: A secondary active transporter couples the movement of a substance to the backflow of ions whose gradient was built up by an ATP-driven pump.
122831.m: Secondary active transport uses the energy from ATP indirectly.

122832.q: What is transport called in which two substances are carried in the same direction at the same time?
122832.e: In symport, two substances move together in the same direction through the same transport protein.
122832.m: In symport, two substances travel together in the same direction.

122833.q: What fundamentally distinguishes active transport from diffusion?
a: It works against a concentration gradient
122833.e: Active transport can move substances from a place of lower to a place of higher concentration and needs energy for this, usually from ATP.
122833.m: Active transport needs energy and can work against the gradient.

122834.q: What is the uptake of droplets of fluid by infolding of the cell membrane called?
122834.e: In pinocytosis (“cell drinking”), the membrane pinches off small vesicles of fluid towards the inside; this vesicle transport needs energy.
122834.m: In pinocytosis, the cell drinks small amounts of fluid.

122835.q: Which medicines inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase of the parietal cells and so reduce stomach acid?
122835.e: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole block the pump that transports hydrogen ions into the stomach.
122835.m: Proton pump inhibitors slow down acid production in the stomach.

122836.q: Which German physicist built the first electron microscope with Max Knoll from 1931 and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1986?
122836.e: Ernst Ruska developed the electron microscope with Max Knoll at the Technical University of Berlin and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.
122836.m: Ernst Ruska is regarded as the inventor of the electron microscope.

122837.q: Which Swiss biophysicist from the University of Lausanne received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for contributions to cryo-electron microscopy?
122837.e: Jacques Dubochet developed a method of freezing samples in a flash in glass-like ice; he shared the prize with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.
122837.m: Jacques Dubochet made biomolecules in ice visible for the electron microscope.

122838.q: Why does an electron microscope achieve a much higher resolution than a light microscope?
a: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength
122838.e: Resolving power depends on the wavelength; fast electrons have a wavelength of only a few picometres.

122839.q: Why must there be a high vacuum in the electron microscope?
a: Air molecules would scatter the electrons
Electrons only form from light in a vacuum
122839.e: Electrons are deflected by even a few gas molecules; without a vacuum the beam would become blurred and weakened.
122839.m: Electron microscopes work in a vacuum.

122840.q: Which type of microscope produces three-dimensional-looking images of surfaces, such as the head of a fly?
a: Stereo magnifier with a light source
122840.e: The SEM scans the surface with a fine beam of electrons and analyses the electrons knocked out; this produces images that look three-dimensional.
122840.m: The scanning electron microscope shows surfaces in three dimensions.

122841.q: What is used to focus the electron beam in an electron microscope?
122841.e: Electrons are deflected by magnetic fields; coils carrying a current therefore act as electromagnetic lenses.

122842.q: Why do images from the electron microscope originally appear only in shades of grey?
a: Electrons have no colour as visible light does
The electrons are sent through colour filters
122842.e: Colours arise from different wavelengths of visible light. Electron images only show how strongly electrons are scattered; coloured images have been coloured in afterwards.
122842.m: Coloured electron microscope images are coloured in afterwards.

122843.q: Which cell structure can be clearly seen in the electron microscope but not in the light microscope?
122843.e: Ribosomes measure only around 20 to 30 nm and are therefore far below the resolution limit of the light microscope of about 200 nm.
122843.m: Ribosomes can only be seen in the electron microscope.

122844.q: Which plastids store large amounts of starch in potato tubers?
122844.e: Amyloplasts are colourless plastids that build glucose into starch grains and store them.
122844.m: Amyloplasts are the starch stores of the plant cell.

122845.q: Which plastids give ripe tomatoes and carrots their red to orange colour?
122845.e: Chromoplasts contain carotenoids such as lycopene or beta-carotene and colour fruits, roots and flowers.

122846.q: What are the reaction spaces of a eukaryotic cell that are separated by membranes called?
122846.e: Membranes divide the cell into compartments so that opposing metabolic processes such as building up and breaking down can take place at the same time.
122846.m: Membranes divide the cell into separate reaction spaces.

122847.q: What are the fine channels called that connect neighbouring plant cells through the cell wall?
122847.e: Plasmodesmata are channels lined with membrane through which the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells is connected.
122847.m: Plasmodesmata connect plant cells to each other.

122848.q: Which proteins inside the rough ER help newly made chains to find their correct shape?
122848.e: Chaperones such as BiP bind to unfolded protein chains in the ER and support their correct folding; misfolded proteins are sorted out.
122848.m: Chaperones help proteins to fold correctly.

122849.q: At which constricted point are the two sister chromatids of a chromosome joined?
122849.e: The centromere is the constriction of the chromosome; there the chromatids remain joined until they are separated.
122849.m: Sister chromatids are joined at the centromere.

122850.q: What is the result of mitosis?
a: Four cells with half a set of chromosomes
Two cells with different genetic material
One cell with a double nucleus
122850.e: In mitosis, each chromosome is distributed evenly between two nuclei. The daughter cells have the same genetic material as the parent cell. Four cells with half a set are produced in meiosis.
122850.m: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells.

122851.q: What is transport called in which two substances are carried in opposite directions at the same time?
122851.e: An antiporter exchanges substances, for example the sodium-calcium exchanger, which carries calcium out of the cell while sodium flows in.
122851.m: In antiport, two substances are exchanged for each other.

122852.q: Why do drinking solutions for diarrhoea contain a little sugar as well as salt?
a: Sugar helps the intestine take up sodium and therefore water
Sugar stops the movement of the intestine
Sugar makes the solution keep longer
122852.e: In the small intestine, glucose and sodium are taken up together by a transporter. Water follows, so the body loses less fluid.
122852.m: Sugar and salt together help the intestine to take up water.

122853.q: Which pump uses ATP to transport sodium out of the cell and potassium into the cell?
122853.e: The sodium-potassium pump carries three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. It maintains the resting potential of the cells.
122853.m: The sodium-potassium pump works with energy from ATP.

122854.q: What disadvantage does electron microscopy have compared with light microscopy for biological samples?
a: No preparation at all is needed
122854.e: There is a vacuum in the electron microscope, and samples are fixed, sliced or frozen. Living cells in motion cannot be viewed in this way.
122854.m: You cannot see living cells in the electron microscope.

122855.q: A voltage of 230 V is applied to a resistor of 46 Ω. What is the current?
122855.e: According to Ohm's law, I = U/R, so 230 V / 46 Ω, which gives 5 A.
122855.m: Current is voltage divided by resistance.

122856.q: A current of 0.25 A flows through a resistor of 480 Ω. What voltage is across it?
122856.e: U = R·I, so 480 Ω · 0.25 A, which gives 120 V.
122856.m: Voltage is the product of resistance and current.

122858.q: An ohmic resistor draws a current of 0.5 A at 12 V. What current flows at 30 V?
122858.e: The resistance is 12 V / 0.5 A, so 24 Ω. At 30 V, 30 V / 24 Ω flows, so 1.25 A.
122858.m: With constant resistance, the current grows in the same ratio as the voltage.

122859.q: What is the unit ohm in SI base units?
122859.e: One volt is kg·m²/(s³·A); divided by one ampere, this gives kg·m²/(s³·A²) for the ohm.
122859.m: One ohm is one volt per ampere.

122860.q: What is the electrical conductance of a resistor of 40 Ω?
122860.e: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, so 1/40 Ω, which gives 0.025 S or 25 millisiemens.
122860.m: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance.

122861.q: What is the resistance of a copper wire 20 m long with a cross-section of 0.75 mm² (ρ = 0.0178 Ω·mm²/m)?
122861.e: R = ρ·l/A gives 0.0178 · 20 / 0.75, so about 0.47 Ω.
122861.m: The resistance of a wire grows with its length and falls with its cross-section.

122862.q: Which metal has the lowest resistivity at room temperature?
122862.e: At about 0.016 Ω·mm²/m, silver has the lowest value of all metals, just ahead of copper; because of the price, copper is mostly used.
122862.m: Silver conducts best of all metals.

122863.q: What is the SI unit of resistivity?
122863.e: From ρ = R·A/l the unit is Ω·m²/m, so Ω·m; in engineering Ω·mm²/m is also common.

122864.q: A wire is replaced by a wire of the same kind with twice the length and twice the diameter. How does the resistance change?
122864.e: Twice the diameter means four times the cross-section. With twice the length this gives 2/4, so half the resistance.
122864.m: The cross-section grows with the square of the diameter.

122865.q: How long must a constantan wire with a cross-section of 0.2 mm² (ρ = 0.50 Ω·mm²/m) be for it to have 10 Ω?
122865.e: From R = ρ·l/A it follows that l = R·A/ρ, so 10 · 0.2 / 0.50, which gives 4 m.
122865.m: The length of wire needed follows from resistance, cross-section and material.

122866.q: Why is the alloy constantan used for precision resistors?
a: Its resistance hardly depends on temperature
122866.e: Constantan (copper and nickel) has an almost vanishing temperature coefficient; its resistance stays nearly constant when it heats up.
122866.m: Constantan hardly changes its resistance when heated.

122867.q: A Pt100 sensor has exactly 100 Ω at 0 °C and a temperature coefficient of 0.00385 1/K. Roughly what is its resistance at 50 °C?
122867.e: With R = R₀·(1 + α·ΔT) you get 100 Ω · (1 + 0.00385 · 50), so about 119.3 Ω.
122867.m: In metals, resistance rises with temperature.

122868.q: Currents of 3 A and 1.5 A flow into a junction, and one branch carries 2 A out. What current flows out in the fourth branch?
122868.e: According to the junction rule, the sum of the currents flowing in equals the sum of the currents flowing out: 4.5 A minus 2 A gives 2.5 A.
122868.m: As much current flows out of a junction as flows in.

122869.q: Two resistors are connected in series to 12 V. There is a voltage drop of 7.5 V across the first. What voltage is across the second?
122869.e: According to the loop rule, the sum of the partial voltages equals the source voltage: 12 V minus 7.5 V gives 4.5 V.
122869.m: In a loop the partial voltages add up to the source voltage.

122870.q: Which physical principle is the junction rule based on?
a: Constancy of the speed of light
122870.e: No charge can pile up or disappear at a junction, so the same amount of charge per unit time must flow in as flows out.
122870.m: The junction rule follows from the fact that charge is not lost.

122871.q: Which conservation law is the loop rule based on?
122871.e: A charge that travels once round a closed loop arrives back at the same potential. The energy gained and given off must balance, so the sum of the voltages is zero.
122871.m: The loop rule follows from the conservation of energy.

122872.q: Two batteries of 9 V and 3 V are connected against each other in a loop, and the total resistance is 20 Ω. What current flows?
122872.e: Sources connected against each other are subtracted: 9 V minus 3 V gives 6 V, and 6 V / 20 Ω gives 0.3 A.
122872.m: Voltage sources connected against each other weaken each other.

122873.q: A 40 Ω resistor is connected in parallel with a 10 Ω resistor, and the total current is 1 A. What current flows through the 10 Ω resistor?
122873.e: The currents divide in inverse proportion to the resistances: I₁ = 1 A · 40/(10 + 40), so 0.8 A.
122873.m: The larger share of the current flows through the smaller resistor.

122874.q: Which quantity is the same in all branches of a parallel circuit?
122874.e: Each parallel branch forms a loop without a source with the others; that is why the same voltage is across all branches.
122874.m: Components connected in parallel have the same voltage.

122875.q: What is the equivalent resistance of 47 Ω, 33 Ω and 20 Ω in series?
122875.e: In a series circuit the resistances add up: 47 + 33 + 20 gives 100 Ω.
122875.m: In series the resistances add up.

122876.q: What is the equivalent resistance of 60 Ω and 30 Ω in parallel?
122876.e: For two resistors in parallel, R = R₁·R₂/(R₁ + R₂), so 1800/90, which gives 20 Ω.
122876.m: Resistors in parallel give a smaller total resistance.

122877.q: Three resistors of 12 Ω each are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
122877.e: For n equal resistors in parallel, the result is R/n, so 12 Ω / 3, which gives 4 Ω.
122877.m: Equal resistors in parallel divide their value by their number.

122878.q: A 10 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel combination of 30 Ω and 60 Ω. What is the equivalent resistance?
122878.e: The parallel combination gives 30·60/90, so 20 Ω; adding 10 Ω in series gives 30 Ω in total.
122878.m: Mixed circuits are worked out step by step from the inside outwards.

122879.q: What is always true of the equivalent resistance of a parallel circuit?
a: It is smaller than the smallest single resistance
It is larger than the largest single resistance
122879.e: Each extra branch opens another path for the current; the total conductance is the sum of the individual conductances.
122879.m: More parallel paths lower the total resistance.

122880.q: A series combination of 25 Ω and 35 Ω is in parallel with 40 Ω. What is the equivalent resistance?
122880.e: The series branch has 60 Ω; in parallel with 40 Ω this gives 60·40/100, so 24 Ω.
122880.m: First combine the series branches, then the parallel circuit.

122881.q: Which resistor must be connected in parallel with 120 Ω so that the equivalent resistance is 40 Ω?
122881.e: From 1/R = 1/40 minus 1/120 it follows that 1/R = 2/120, so R = 60 Ω.
122881.m: In parallel circuits the reciprocals of the resistances add up.

122882.q: What is the equivalent resistance of a series of 2 Ω, a parallel combination of 6 Ω and 3 Ω, and 4 Ω?
122882.e: 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω gives 18/9, so 2 Ω. In series with 2 Ω and 4 Ω this gives 8 Ω.
122882.m: Parts of a circuit are combined step by step into one equivalent resistance.

122883.q: Two equal resistors give 40 Ω in series. What is their equivalent resistance when connected in parallel?
122883.e: Each resistor has 20 Ω; in parallel, two equal resistors give half of a single one, so 10 Ω.
122883.m: Two equal resistors in parallel have half the single value.

122884.q: An unloaded voltage divider made of R₁ = 1 kΩ and R₂ = 2 kΩ is connected to 12 V. What voltage is across R₂?
122884.e: U₂ = U · R₂/(R₁ + R₂), so 12 V · 2/3, which gives 8 V.
122884.m: The larger voltage drop is across the larger resistor.

122885.q: An unloaded divider connected to 9 V has R₁ = 10 kΩ. How large must R₂ be so that exactly 3 V is across R₂?
122885.e: There is a drop of 6 V across R₁ and 3 V across R₂. The voltages are in the same ratio as the resistances, so R₂ = 10 kΩ · 3/6, which gives 5 kΩ.
122885.m: The partial voltages are in the same ratio as the partial resistances.

122886.q: What happens to the output voltage of a voltage divider if you connect a load in parallel with R₂?
122886.e: The load forms a parallel combination with R₂ that has a smaller resistance; as a result, less voltage drops across this part.
122886.m: A load lowers the output voltage of a voltage divider.

122887.q: A divider with R₁ = R₂ = 10 kΩ is connected to 12 V. A load of 10 kΩ is connected in parallel with R₂. What is the output voltage?
122887.e: R₂ in parallel with the load gives 5 kΩ. The output voltage is 12 V · 5/(10 + 5), so 4 V.
122887.m: A loaded voltage divider delivers less voltage than when unloaded.

122888.q: Which component is an adjustable voltage divider with a sliding contact?
122888.e: In a potentiometer, a movable wiper divides a resistance track into two parts; this allows the voltage picked off to be adjusted smoothly.
122888.m: A potentiometer is an adjustable voltage divider.

122889.q: In an unloaded divider connected to 20 V, R₁ is three times as large as R₂. What voltage is across R₂?
122889.e: R₂ has a quarter of the total resistance, so a quarter of the voltage is across it: 20 V / 4 gives 5 V.
122889.m: Each partial resistor gets its share of the total voltage.

122890.q: In a twilight switch, a light-dependent resistor (LDR) forms the lower part of a voltage divider. What happens to its voltage when it gets dark?
122890.e: In the dark the resistance of the LDR rises sharply; this gives it a larger share of the total voltage.
122890.m: A light-dependent resistor has a high resistance in the dark.

122891.q: An unloaded divider made of 1.5 kΩ and 4.5 kΩ is connected to 24 V. What voltage drops across the 1.5 kΩ resistor?
122891.e: The current is 24 V / 6 kΩ, so 4 mA. Across the 1.5 kΩ resistor there is a drop of 4 mA · 1.5 kΩ, so 6 V.
122891.m: The shared current determines the partial voltages.

122892.q: A battery with an open-circuit voltage of 1.5 V and an internal resistance of 0.5 Ω delivers 0.4 A. What is the terminal voltage?
122892.e: Across the internal resistance there is a drop of 0.4 A · 0.5 Ω, so 0.2 V. The terminal voltage is 1.5 V minus 0.2 V, so 1.3 V.
122892.m: Under load the terminal voltage of a source falls.

122893.q: A car battery has an open-circuit voltage of 12 V and an internal resistance of 0.02 Ω. What is the short-circuit current?
122893.e: In a short circuit only the internal resistance limits the current: 12 V / 0.02 Ω gives 600 A.
122893.m: The internal resistance limits the short-circuit current.

122894.q: A source shows 9.0 V with no load and still 8.0 V with a load of 0.5 A. What is its internal resistance?
122894.e: The voltage loss of 1.0 V occurs across the internal resistance: Rᵢ = 1.0 V / 0.5 A, so 2 Ω.
122894.m: The drop in voltage under load tells you the internal resistance.

122895.q: At what load resistance does a voltage source deliver the greatest possible power to the load?
a: When it equals the internal resistance
When it is twice the internal resistance
122895.e: With impedance matching, that is when the load resistance equals the internal resistance, the power in the load is at its maximum; the efficiency is then only 50 per cent.
122895.m: Power matching means equal load and internal resistance.

122896.q: A source with an open-circuit voltage of 6 V has an internal resistance of 3 Ω. What is the maximum power it can deliver to a load?
122896.e: With power matching, P = U₀²/(4·Rᵢ), so 36/12, which gives 3 W.
122896.m: The maximum load power depends on the open-circuit voltage and the internal resistance.

122897.q: Why do the headlights often dim briefly when a car is started?
a: The high starter current causes a voltage drop across the internal resistance
The alternator switches off the lamps
122897.e: The starter motor draws several hundred amperes; even a small internal resistance makes the terminal voltage drop noticeably.
122897.m: Large currents lower the terminal voltage of a battery.

122898.q: A source with an open-circuit voltage of 4.5 V and an internal resistance of 1 Ω supplies a load resistance of 8 Ω. What current flows?
122898.e: The internal and load resistances are in series: I = 4.5 V / (1 Ω + 8 Ω), so 0.5 A.
122898.m: The internal resistance is in series with the load.

122899.q: A 12 V car lamp draws 5 A. What is its power?
122899.e: P = U·I gives 12 V · 5 A, so 60 W.
122899.m: Electric power is voltage times current.

122900.q: What current flows through a 2000 W kettle connected to 230 V?
122900.e: I = P/U gives 2000 W / 230 V, so about 8.7 A.

122901.q: What power does a heating resistor of 52.9 Ω take at 230 V?
122901.e: P = U²/R gives 52,900 V² / 52.9 Ω, so 1000 W.
122901.m: At a fixed voltage the power grows when the resistance gets smaller.

122902.q: A current of 3 A flows through a 20 Ω resistor. How much power is converted?
122902.e: P = I²·R gives 9 A² · 20 Ω, so 180 W.
122902.m: Power rises with the square of the current.

122903.q: A lamp rated 60 W at 230 V is run at 115 V. What is its power if the resistance stays constant?
122903.e: Because P = U²/R, half the voltage gives a quarter of the power: 60 W / 4 gives 15 W.
122903.m: Half the voltage means a quarter of the power at the same resistance.

122904.q: Two 230 V filament bulbs, one of 100 W and one of 25 W, are connected in series to 230 V. Which one shines more brightly?
122904.e: The 25 W bulb has four times the resistance. In series the same current flows, so according to P = I²·R it converts more power.
122904.m: In a series circuit the larger resistance gets more power.

122905.q: An electric motor takes 1.5 kW of electrical power and gives out 1.2 kW of mechanical power. What is its efficiency?
122905.e: Efficiency is useful power divided by power supplied: 1.2 kW / 1.5 kW gives 0.8, so 80 per cent.
122905.m: Efficiency compares the useful power with the power taken in.

122906.q: A 230 V socket is protected by a 10 A fuse. What is the maximum total power that may be connected?
122906.e: P = U·I gives 230 V · 10 A, so 2300 W; more power would trip the fuse.
122906.m: The fuse limits the power that can be connected.

122907.q: A 2 kW fan heater runs for 3 hours. How much electrical energy does it use?
122907.e: W = P·t gives 2 kW · 3 h, so 6 kWh.
122907.m: Electrical energy is power times time.

122908.q: A 1.5 kW hairdryer runs for 10 minutes a day. What does that cost over 30 days, assuming 30 centimes per kWh?
122908.e: Per day that is 1.5 kW · 1/6 h, so 0.25 kWh, and in 30 days 7.5 kWh. That costs 7.5 · 0.30 francs, so 2.25 francs.
122908.m: Electricity costs are energy times the tariff.

122909.q: An appliance constantly uses 5 W on standby. How much energy is that in a year of 365 days?
122909.e: 5 W · 24 h · 365 gives 43,800 Wh, so 43.8 kWh.
122909.m: Even small continuous users add up over the year.

122910.q: A smartphone battery has a nominal voltage of 3.7 V and a capacity of 4000 mAh. Roughly how much energy does it store?
122910.e: Energy is voltage times charge: 3.7 V · 4.0 Ah gives 14.8 Wh.
122910.m: Battery energy is nominal voltage times capacity.

122911.q: An appliance works for 30 minutes at 12 V and 2 A. How much electrical work is done?
122911.e: W = U·I·t gives 12 V · 2 A · 1800 s, so 43,200 J or 43.2 kJ.
122911.m: Electrical work is voltage times current times time.

122912.q: How long does a 2 kW kettle with no losses take to heat 1 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C (c = 4190 J/(kg·K))?
122912.e: You need 4190 · 1 · 80, so about 335 kJ. Divided by 2000 W this gives about 168 s.
122912.m: Heating time is the heat needed divided by the power.

122913.q: How much energy does a 2.2 kW oven use in 45 minutes of continuous operation?
122913.e: 45 minutes is 0.75 h; 2.2 kW · 0.75 h gives 1.65 kWh.
122913.m: For kilowatt hours, minutes must be converted into hours.

122914.q: What is the microscopic cause of Joule heating in a metal wire?
a: Collisions of the electrons with the particles of the lattice
Friction of the protons in the nucleus
122914.e: The conduction electrons give up energy when they collide with the vibrating metal ions; the lattice vibrates more strongly and the wire heats up.
122914.m: Electrical heating comes from electrons colliding in the metal lattice.
